Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 1:

﴿Wa-l-Qur'ani dhi l-dhikr﴾ The waw (wa) is for oath: He swears by the Qur'an, an oath that glorifies it (qasam tanwih bihi).

It is described as "dhi l-dhikr" (possessor of remembrance) because "dhi" (possessor of) is attached to exalted things, so it applies to a matter that is intended to be highlighted and honored.

And al-dhikr means reminding (al-tadhkir), that is, reminding people of what they are heedless of. It is also permissible that al-dhikr be understood as mention by the tongue (dhikr al-lisan), and then it carries the meaning of "that which is mentioned" (al-mudhakkar), in the passive form, that is, the Qur'an that is mentioned, i.e., the praiseworthy, deserving of praise, according to one of the two interpretations of His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you a Book in which is your remembrance﴾ [al-Anbiya': 10], that is, your honor.

The commentators have differed in determining the response of the oath (jawab al-qasam), giving seven or eight opinions. The best of what has been said here is one of two views. The first is that it is omitted, indicated by the letters ṣ, for the intended purpose is the challenge (al-tahaddi) with the inimitability of the Qur'an and their inability to oppose it, since it is speech in their own language, composed of its letters; so how could they be unable to oppose it? The sense is: "By the Qur'an, possessor of remembrance, that it is indeed from Allah, for this you were unable to produce its like." The second, which I consider the more likely, is that the response is also omitted, indicated by the turning away (al-idrab) in His words, ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾ [Sad: 2], after the Qur'an has been described as "dhi l-dhikr," since that description implies that it is a reminder and an awakener of minds. It is as if it was said: "Indeed it is a reminder, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition, denying that it is a reminder and saying: 'It is fabricated sorcery,' while they know that it is true," like His words, exalted is He, ﴿For they do not deny you, but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 33]. So the response of the oath is omitted, indicated by the context, and the letter ṣ is not the thing sworn to placed before the oath; that is, the indication of the response is not from the wording but from the meaning and context.

The purpose of omitting the response of the oath here is to turn away from it toward what is more worthy of mention, namely the description of those who disbelieved and denied the Qur'an out of obstinacy or opposition on their part.

﴿بَلِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا فِي عِزَّةٍ وَشِقاقٍ﴾ [ص: ٢]. (Bal) is used for al-idrab al-ibtali (the "nullifying" or retractive particle of disregard, which cancels a preceding statement). This is a type of al-idrab al-ibtali, which al-Raghib noted in al-Mufradat fi Gharib al-Qur'an and to which al-Zamakhshari alluded in al-Kashshaf. Its explanation is that it is not a pure nullification of the preceding speech, such that the particle bal functions as a negation particle, as is most common with al-idrab al-ibtali. Nor is it a transitional al-idrab (al-idrab al-intiqali). Rather, it nullifies a misconception arising from the preceding speech. The description of the Qur'an as ﴿dhi al-dhikr﴾ [Sad: 1] indicates that the Qur'an reminds its hearers with an effective reminder. So it follows up by removing the misconception of one who thinks that the disbelievers' failure to heed it is due to a weakness in the Qur'an's reminder, rather than because they are arrogant and defiant. Thus the particle bal in such a context functions as the particle of istidrak (corrective addition), and its purpose is to establish that the Qur'an is indeed possessed of remembrance, and to remove the doubt that may arise about this.

A similar case is His saying, ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qaf: 1], ﴿Nay, but they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them﴾ [Qaf: 2], meaning:

[p. 205]
Their refusal to believe in the Qur'an is not due to a deficiency in its exaltedness and glory, but because they wonder that a man from among them has come to them with it.

It is also possible to make bal an al-idrab al-intiqali, shifting from beginning to extol the Qur'an to explaining the cause of the turning away of those who turn away from it, because explaining that cause also confirms the extolling of the Qur'an. This is like the saying: "Leave that aside and take up a story..." And like the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*So leave that aside, and banish your sorrow with a swift she-camel, when the day fasts and grows hot.*

And Zuhayr said:

*Leave that aside and count the speech about Harim, the best of the desert-dwellers and the lord of the settled folk.*

And the words of al-A'sha:

*So leave that aside, but look at the opinion of a foe who sees between us, from his ignorance, the fine point of a dagger.*

And the words of al-'Ajjaj:

*Leave that aside and make illustrious a noble lineage made glorious.*

The meaning is that the speech began praising the Qur'an, then broke off from that to what is more important, namely explaining the cause of the turning away of those who turn away from it, due to their pride in themselves and their defiance. Thus there occurred a deviation from the answer to the oath, being sufficient with what conveys the same meaning as that answer.

The phrase "alladhina kafaru" was used rather than "al-kafirun" because of what the relative clause implies, namely the information that they are in arrogance and defiance. Its usages in speech revolve around the meanings of invincibility, dominance and haughtiness. If it operates on actual causes, it is true honor (al-'izza al-haqiqiyya). If it arises from delusion and self-admiration, it is false honor ('izza muzawwara). He said, ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride takes hold of him for sin﴾ [al-Baqara: 206], meaning pride and intensity of disobedience seized him. Here it is also false honor, since it is refusal of the truth and self-admiration. The opposite of honor is humiliation. He said, ﴿humble towards the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 54]. And al-Samaw'al or another said:

*And it did us no harm that we are few, while our neighbor is mighty, and the neighbor of the many is humiliated.*

[p. 206]
The particle fi (in) is for figurative location, metaphorically used to express the intensity of being clothed in honor. The meaning: they are clothed in honor against the truth.

Al-shiqaq means opposition and contention. What is intended: defiance of God through polytheism and of His Messenger ﷺ through denial. The meaning: what stands between them and being reminded by the Qur'an is what lies in the depths of their souls of honor and defiance.

﴿How many generations We destroyed before them! And they cried out, but it was no longer the time for escape.﴾ This is a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'naf bayani*), since arrogance toward the truth and opposition to Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) raise in the listener's mind the question of what the recompense for that is, so this verse comes as an explanation of it. This clause is inserted between the clause ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾ [Sad: 2] and the clause ﴿And they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves﴾ [Sad: 4].

This explanation was a statement accompanied by a proof of the type of analogical reasoning (*qiyas tamthil*), because His saying "before them" (*min qablihim*) indicates that they are like them in arrogance and opposition. It also contains a warning against delaying in responding to the call to the truth, meaning: the punishment will descend upon them, and repentance and regret will not benefit them, just as they did not benefit the generations before them. The implied meaning is: they will be requited for their arrogance and opposition with destruction, just as many nations before them were requited for the same; so let them beware, for if the word of punishment is fulfilled against them, repentance will not benefit them, just as repentance did not benefit those before them when they saw the punishment.

*(Kam)* is a noun indicating a large number. *Min qarnin* is a specifier (*tamyiz*) clarifying the vagueness of the number, meaning: a great number of generations. It is in the accusative position as the object of *ahlakna* (We destroyed).

*Al-qarn* means a nation, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We brought into being after them other generations﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 42]. *Min qablihim* may be a fixed adverbial phrase (*zarf mustaqarr*) made an attribute of *qarn* and placed before it, so it became a circumstantial (*hal*). It was placed first for the sake of emphasis on its content, to convey emphasis, hinting that they are an example for them in arrogance and opposition, and that this is the cause of their destruction.

It may also be connected to *ahlakna* as a non-essential adverbial (*zarf laghw*), and placed before the object of its verb, with the object being more deserving of precedence over the rest of the verb's complements, so that placing it first would be an emphasis on it, hinting at destruction, as in the first case.

He then made the destruction a basis for the fact that they cried out, but their crying out did not benefit them, as a warning lest these people fall into the same situation the generations before them fell into, when they squandered the opportunity and then cried out after it had passed, so their crying out and their supplication did not avail them.

What is meant by the crying out in *fa-nadaw* (and they cried out) is their calling upon Allah, exalted is He, in humility, which is supplication, as is related of them in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12],

and His saying: ﴿Until, when We seize their affluent ones with punishment, behold, they cry out for help﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 64].

The clause ﴿and it was no longer the time for escape﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and the *waw* is the *waw* of circumstance, meaning: they cried out in a state in which there was no time for escape for them.

*La-ta* (لاتَ) is a particle of negation with the meaning of *la* (لا) that is assimilated to *laysa* (لَيْسَ), and *la-ta* is a particle specific to negating nouns of time and what includes the meaning of time, such as demonstratives and the like.

It is composed of the negating *la* (لا) to which a superfluous *ta'* (تاء) is attached, which does not indicate feminine gender, since it is not a *ha'* (ه), but is like the addition of the *ta'* in their saying *rubbat* and *thummat*.

Negation with it for other than time and the like is an error in the language, into which Abu al-Tayyib fell when he said:

I have endured patiently until there is no longer any endurance (*la-ta mus'tabar*), and now I am thrust forward until there is no longer any thrusting forward (*la-ta muqtaham*).

All the commentators of his Diwan overlooked this, although he placed *la-ta* before a non-time noun. In any case, by the obligatory addition of the *ta'* at its end, *la* became an independent particle specific to negating nouns of time, and so it departed from the pattern of *rubbat* and *thummat*.

Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam claimed that the *ta'* in ﴿and it was no longer the time for escape﴾ is joined to *hin* (حِينَ), and that he saw it in the Mushafs of 'Uthman joined to *hin*. He claimed that this *ta'* enters upon *hin*, *awan* (أوانٍ) and *an* (آنٍ), meaning that the *ta'* attaches to the first part of the noun that follows *la*, but he did not explain what meaning its entry conveys. The scholars excused the joining of the *ta'* to *hin* in some copies of the Imam Mushaf by saying that the orthography of the Mushaf may deviate from analogy. Moreover, this does not occur in any other Mushaf except the one Abu 'Ubayd saw among the Mushafs contemporary with that Mushaf and written after it.

*Al-manas* means escape and flight, and it is a noun of place/time of the *mimi* type. It is said: *nasahu*, when it escaped him.

The meaning is: they cried out, supplicating, in a state that is not a time of escape and flight, meaning that destruction had become binding upon them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might; this is the way of Allah which has passed among His servants﴾ [Ghafir: 85].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 4–5:

﴿And they wondered that a warner from among themselves has come to them.﴾ This is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿Those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾ [Sad: 2]. It is therefore a discourse that comes with idrab (iḍrāb, a shift of topic signalled by "bal" or its sense) to move on to a new subject, as occurred in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an. Nay, but they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them﴾ [Qaf: 1–2].

The meaning is that the impossibility of a messenger being sent from among themselves was firmly fixed in their minds, and this is another cause of their turning away from being reminded by the Qur'an.

The true nature of ʿajab (ʿajab, wonder) is: an emotion in the soul that arises from knowledge of a matter whose occurrence is not expected by the soul. It is also applied, metaphorically, to denying something rare, by way of the relation of necessary consequence (ʿalaqat al-luzum), as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They said, "Do you wonder at the command of Allah?"﴾ [Hud: 73] in Surah Hud, where the object of reproach is that the wife of Ibrahim deemed it impossible that she should bear a child while she was an old woman. Likewise is its usage here. The meaning is: they denied and deemed impossible that a warner from among themselves had come to them.

The warner (al-mundhir) is the messenger, i.e., one who warns them of a punishment for deeds in which they are engaged.

The Messenger ﷺ is referred to by the description "warner," and he is described as "from among them" to indicate the poverty of their view in their wondering; for it is the nature of a warner to be from the people, one who gives sincere counsel to them, so his being from among them is more fitting than his being from others.

Then, if the partitive sense conveyed by the particle "min" (from) is intended to mean that he is one of the Arabs or one of the Quraysh, then the ignorance of their wonder at this warner is clear. If it is intended to mean that he is one of mankind, which is the apparent meaning, then their ignorance lies in the fact that one who is of their own kind is more worthy of giving them sincere counsel than a messenger of another kind, such as the angels, and this worthiness is a customary (ʿurfiyyah) one.

This wonder was expressed by them more than once, so it is firmly lodged in the depths of their souls, and it is the underlying motive that prompted them to turn away from affirming him. Therefore the report of their sayings, which they uttered in the assembly of the Shaykh of the Abtah (Abu Talib), as mentioned earlier in the account of the occasion of revelation, begins with it.

* * *

﴿And the disbelievers said, "This is a sorcerer, a liar." ﴾ ﴿"Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing."﴾

After what lay within their souls of arrogance and opposition, and their denial that a messenger should be sent to mankind from their own kind, has been laid bare, they are called to account for what they expressed of speech in that assembly, indicating by this order that their statement is a consequence of that belief of theirs.

In His saying "the disbelievers" there is the placing of an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun; the expected form would have been "and they said, 'This is a sorcerer,' etc." This is for the purpose of describing them as disbelievers in their Lord, in contrast to what they charged the Prophet ﷺ with, so they are described with what is an insult to them, comprising various kinds of abuse, both fundamentally and in its branches: that is disbelief, which is the sum of corrupt thinking and corrupt deeds.

By the word "this" they pointed to the Prophet ﷺ; they used the demonstrative to belittle one like him, as in His saying, ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 36]. They uttered this statement of theirs when they were leaving the assembly of Abu Talib mentioned in the occasion of revelation of the Surah. Because of the recency of their presence in his presence, they treated the Prophet ﷺ as though he were present at the time of pointing to him.

They made his state to be sorcery and lying, because when their minds could not accept what he spoke to them, they claimed that whatever they did not understand from it (such as the oneness of God, or His bringing the dead back to life) was sorcery, since they were accustomed to sorcery consisting of words that are not understood, as has preceded at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They teach people sorcery﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] in Surah al-Baqarah. And they claimed what they understood and deemed impossible, such as the claim of messengership from Allah, to be lying.

They explained this by two sentences: the first, ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾, and the second, the sentence ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ [Sad: 8].

So the sentence ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾ is an explanation of the sentence ﴿This is a sorcerer, a liar﴾, meaning that they considered him one who confounds them by reversing realities and reports, contrary to what is actual.

The hamza is for interrogation of denial and wonder, and for this reason they followed it with what serves as the cause of their saying "a sorcerer," which is ﴿Indeed, this is an astonishing thing﴾, meaning it is something to be wondered at, just as one wonders at the trickery of a magician.

ʿUjab (ʿujāb) means: "a description of a thing that is wondered at greatly," because the pattern fuʿāl with a dammed first letter indicates the firm establishment of the attribute, such as ṭuwāl, meaning one excessive in length, and kurām, meaning one greatly abundant in generosity; so it is more emphatic than karīm. They began their denial with the first principle of their disbelief, for the foundations of their disbelief are three: association (shirk), denial of the Messenger ﷺ, and denial of resurrection and recompense in the Hereafter.

[Page 211]

﴿The chiefs among them set off, saying: "Go on, and be steadfast in devotion to your gods. This is indeed a thing that is intended."﴾ ﴿"We have never heard of this in the latest religion. This is nothing but a fabrication."﴾

*Inṭilāq* (setting off) literally means departing and walking. It is used in the manner of verbs of beginning (*af'āl al-shurūʿ*), because the one who begins a matter sets off towards it. Its parallel in this usage is *dhahaba bi-fiʿl kadhā* (he went to do such-and-such), as in the verse of al-Nabahānī:

*"If you were our master, you have been our master; and if you are a mere braggart, then go away and leave."*

Likewise *qāma* (he rose) in the words of God Most High, ﴿when they rose up and said﴾ [al-Kahf: 14], in Surat al-Kahf.

It has also been said that *inṭilāq* here is in its literal sense, meaning: the chiefs among them departed from the gathering of Abū Ṭālib.

*Al-malaʾ* means the leaders of the people. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the one who said this was ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ. Others besides Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: among those who said it were Abū Jahl, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, and al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth.

The *ʾan* here is explanatory (*tafsīriyya*), because if *inṭilāq* is figurative, meaning beginning, then the intended sense is the beginning of speech, so it contains the meaning of saying without its letters, and it needs explanation by a quoted statement. If *inṭilāq* is literal, then it includes their departure following their mutual talk with their false words, ﴿This is a sorcerer﴾ up to His words ﴿a thing to be wondered at﴾, which implies that they departed while conferring with one another about what they should do. Since the departure is attributed to the chiefs among them, on the basis that they would not depart except for a plan about what to do, and this entails mutual consultation and speech, it was necessary to explain it with the clause ﴿Go on, and be steadfast in devotion to your gods﴾, and so on.

The command to walk may be literal, meaning: depart from this place, the place of dispute, and occupy yourselves with steadfastness in devotion to your gods. It may also be figurative, meaning: persist in your religion, as one says: "Walk as the noble ones walked," meaning: act as they acted. From this comes the naming of habits and customary practices as *sīra* (conduct).

*Al-ṣabr* (steadfastness) means holding firm and remaining constant. One says *ṣabara al-dābba* when he tied the animal. From this, steadfastness in the face of harm is called *ṣabr*, because it is a constancy with forbearance and deliberation, such that one is not agitated by distress. A parallel to this verse is God Most High's words, ﴿He nearly led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in them﴾ [al-Furqan: 42].

The preposition *ʿalā* indicates that *iṣbirū* (be steadfast) is implicitly given the sense of: remain devoted and hold firm. So the preposition *ʿalā* here denotes figurative elevation, which is firm establishment, like ﴿those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. It is not the usual *ʿalā* with which the verb of patience is construed, as in His words ﴿be patient over what they say﴾ [Ṣād: 17], for that is in the sense of *maʿa* (with). This is why *al-lām* can replace it in such a position, as in His words ﴿so be patient for the judgment of your Lord﴾ [al-Qalam: 48]. Here it is necessary to supply a noun in the genitive construction, meaning: upon the worship of your gods, so it does not transitively take a direct object.

﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾ is a clause giving the reason for the command to be steadfast in devotion to their gods, with the aim of strengthening their doubt about the validity of the Prophet's ﷺ call, by saying that it is a thing he intended for a purpose. That is, it is not true, but rather something contrived, intended for a goal, as one says: "This is a matter that was plotted at night." So the demonstrative *hādhā* (this) refers to what they were hearing in the gathering from the Prophet ﷺ, his call to them to say: "There is no god but God."

His words ﴿We have never heard of this in the latest religion﴾ are part of the speech of the chiefs. The demonstrative refers to what was indicated by their words ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾, that is, this statement, which is making the gods into one god.

The clause is either a new (independent) clause or explanatory of ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾, because not having heard the like of it shows that it is a contrived, invented thing.

Repeating the demonstrative is placing an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun, for the purpose of increasing its clarity. In His words "*bi-hādhā*" (of this), there is an implied genitive noun, meaning: of the like of this which he says.

The negation of hearing here is a declarative statement used as a metonymy (*kināya*) for disapproval and accusing him of lying.

*Al-milla* means religion. God Most High said ﴿The Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 120] in Surat al-Baqarah, and He said ﴿I have forsaken the religion of a people who do not believe in God and who disbelieve in the Hereafter, and I have followed the religion of my fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob﴾ [Yusuf: 37] in Surat Yusuf.

*Al-ākhira* is the feminine of *al-ākhir* (the last), which is that which comes after the passing of a period in which its like has been established, as in God's words ﴿Then God brings about the later creation﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 20].

The prepositional phrase in His words ﴿in the latest religion﴾ may be a settled adverbial complement in the position of a circumstantial state of the demonstrative, clarifying the intended meaning of the demonstrative, and it is connected to the verb "we have heard". The meaning is: we have not heard of this before today, so we do not give it any weight. On this reading, "the latest religion" may refer to the religion of the Christians. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and his companions. On this basis, the polytheists were citing as evidence against the monotheism of the one God that the religion of the Christians, which predates Islam, affirmed a plurality of gods. The negation of hearing would then be a metonymy for hearing its opposite, which is the plurality of gods.

They may also mean by "the latest religion" the religion in which they themselves are, and it refers to the statement of the chiefs of Quraysh to Abū Ṭālib at the time of his death, when the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "O uncle, say: there is no god but God, a word by which I may argue on your behalf before God." They all said to him: "Will you turn away from the religion of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib?" So their saying "in the latest religion" is a metonymy for the continuation of this negation until the final time, so it is known that its negation in their earlier religion is all the more so.

The clause ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾ explains the clause "We have never heard of this", and this is the conclusion of their speech that began with ﴿Go on, and be steadfast in devotion to your gods﴾. So this clause is like a summation of their speech.

*Al-ikhtilāq* (fabrication) is the invented lie for which the one who says it has no excuse.

[Page 211]

﴿The chiefs among them set off, saying: "Go on, and be steadfast in devotion to your gods. This is indeed a thing that is intended."﴾ ﴿"We have never heard of this in the latest religion. This is nothing but a fabrication."﴾

*Inṭilāq* (setting off) literally means departing and walking. It is used in the manner of verbs of beginning (*af'āl al-shurūʿ*), because the one who begins a matter sets off towards it. Its parallel in this usage is *dhahaba bi-fiʿl kadhā* (he went to do such-and-such), as in the verse of al-Nabahānī:

*"If you were our master, you have been our master; and if you are a mere braggart, then go away and leave."*

Likewise *qāma* (he rose) in the words of God Most High, ﴿when they rose up and said﴾ [al-Kahf: 14], in Surat al-Kahf.

It has also been said that *inṭilāq* here is in its literal sense, meaning: the chiefs among them departed from the gathering of Abū Ṭālib.

*Al-malaʾ* means the leaders of the people. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the one who said this was ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ. Others besides Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: among those who said it were Abū Jahl, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, and al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth.

The *ʾan* here is explanatory (*tafsīriyya*), because if *inṭilāq* is figurative, meaning beginning, then the intended sense is the beginning of speech, so it contains the meaning of saying without its letters, and it needs explanation by a quoted statement. If *inṭilāq* is literal, then it includes their departure following their mutual talk with their false words, ﴿This is a sorcerer﴾ up to His words ﴿a thing to be wondered at﴾, which implies that they departed while conferring with one another about what they should do. Since the departure is attributed to the chiefs among them, on the basis that they would not depart except for a plan about what to do, and this entails mutual consultation and speech, it was necessary to explain it with the clause ﴿Go on, and be steadfast in devotion to your gods﴾, and so on.

The command to walk may be literal, meaning: depart from this place, the place of dispute, and occupy yourselves with steadfastness in devotion to your gods. It may also be figurative, meaning: persist in your religion, as one says: "Walk as the noble ones walked," meaning: act as they acted. From this comes the naming of habits and customary practices as *sīra* (conduct).

*Al-ṣabr* (steadfastness) means holding firm and remaining constant. One says *ṣabara al-dābba* when he tied the animal. From this, steadfastness in the face of harm is called *ṣabr*, because it is a constancy with forbearance and deliberation, such that one is not agitated by distress. A parallel to this verse is God Most High's words, ﴿He nearly led us astray from our gods, had we not been steadfast in them﴾ [al-Furqan: 42].

The preposition *ʿalā* indicates that *iṣbirū* (be steadfast) is implicitly given the sense of: remain devoted and hold firm. So the preposition *ʿalā* here denotes figurative elevation, which is firm establishment, like ﴿those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. It is not the usual *ʿalā* with which the verb of patience is construed, as in His words ﴿be patient over what they say﴾ [Ṣād: 17], for that is in the sense of *maʿa* (with). This is why *al-lām* can replace it in such a position, as in His words ﴿so be patient for the judgment of your Lord﴾ [al-Qalam: 48]. Here it is necessary to supply a noun in the genitive construction, meaning: upon the worship of your gods, so it does not transitively take a direct object.

﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾ is a clause giving the reason for the command to be steadfast in devotion to their gods, with the aim of strengthening their doubt about the validity of the Prophet's ﷺ call, by saying that it is a thing he intended for a purpose. That is, it is not true, but rather something contrived, intended for a goal, as one says: "This is a matter that was plotted at night." So the demonstrative *hādhā* (this) refers to what they were hearing in the gathering from the Prophet ﷺ, his call to them to say: "There is no god but God."

His words ﴿We have never heard of this in the latest religion﴾ are part of the speech of the chiefs. The demonstrative refers to what was indicated by their words ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾, that is, this statement, which is making the gods into one god.

The clause is either a new (independent) clause or explanatory of ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾, because not having heard the like of it shows that it is a contrived, invented thing.

Repeating the demonstrative is placing an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun, for the purpose of increasing its clarity. In His words "*bi-hādhā*" (of this), there is an implied genitive noun, meaning: of the like of this which he says.

The negation of hearing here is a declarative statement used as a metonymy (*kināya*) for disapproval and accusing him of lying.

*Al-milla* means religion. God Most High said ﴿The Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 120] in Surat al-Baqarah, and He said ﴿I have forsaken the religion of a people who do not believe in God and who disbelieve in the Hereafter, and I have followed the religion of my fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob﴾ [Yusuf: 37] in Surat Yusuf.

This is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and his companions. On this basis, the polytheists were citing as evidence against the monotheism of the one God that the religion of the Christians, which predates Islam, affirmed a plurality of gods. The negation of hearing would then be a metonymy for hearing its opposite, which is the plurality of gods.

They may also mean by "the latest religion" the religion in which they themselves are, and it refers to the statement of the chiefs of Quraysh to Abū Ṭālib at the time of his death, when the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "O uncle, say: there is no god but God, a word by which I may argue on your behalf before God." They all said to him: "Will you turn away from the religion of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib?" So their saying "in the latest religion" is a metonymy for the continuation of this negation until the final time, so it is known that its negation in their earlier religion is all the more so.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 8:

﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ It is possible that ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ is part of the speech of the general body of the disbelievers, related by His words ﴿And the disbelievers said, "This is a magician, a great liar."﴾ [Sad: 4]. In that case it is connected to His words ﴿Has he made the gods into one god?﴾ [Sad: 5], and His words ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him﴾ serve as an explanation (bayan) of the phrase "a great liar", because its implied meaning is: "This is a liar", since it is a second predicate of "kana" (was). And because it is an explanation of what precedes it, it is not joined to it by a conjunction. The material between them, from His words ﴿And the chiefs among them went forth﴾ [Sad: 6] to His words ﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾ [Sad: 7], is then a parenthetical interjection between the two parts of the explanation.

It is also possible that it is a continuation of the speech of the chiefs (al-mala'), and that the explanation of the phrase "a great liar" is dispensed with by it, because the chiefs' utterance of it suffices for the others to agree with its ruling, so they dispense with explaining the phrase "a great liar".

The interrogation is one of denial (inkari), and the focus of the denial is the adverbial phrase ﴿from among us﴾, which is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun in ﴿upon him﴾. They denied that Muhammad ﷺ should be singled out for prophethood and the sending down of the Qur'an to the exclusion of the rest of them. This is what is related in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of the two cities, great?"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], meaning from Makkah or al-Ta'if. And by this denial they did not intend to reject the very possibility of a message from God.

Page 214

Rather, their aim was to exhaust the extent of their incredulity. For they denied the very principle of prophethood, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they wondered that a warner from among themselves had come to them﴾ [Sad: 4], and other verses. This is the second foundation of their disbelief, whose mention preceded at His saying ﴿Has he made the gods into one god?﴾ [Sad: 5], and it is the principle of denying that a messenger should be sent from among them.
* * *
﴿Nay, but they are in doubt concerning My Reminder﴾ It is possible that this is an answer to their saying ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾, meaning: their aim is not to challenge your being singled out for the message, but rather they are doubtful about the very fact of its being sent down. So "bal" is a retractive (ibtali) redirection, rejecting what appears from their denial of the Reminder being sent down upon him from among them, as explained above. That is, their real aim is only doubt as to whether God reveals to anyone a message. Thus the meaning of ﴿in doubt concerning My Reminder﴾ is doubt about its occurrence. The word "shakk" (doubt) is applied to certainty metaphorically, by a figurative relation of general and specific (al-ta'alluq al-ita'i wa al-taqyid), and so it has the same sense as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they do not deny you, but it is the wrongdoers who deny the signs of God﴾ [al-An'am: 33]. It is also possible that this is a transition from one report about them to another report, in which case it is a new sentence (isti'naf), and "bal" is a transitional redirection (al-idrab al-intiqali). The meaning would be: "and they are in doubt concerning My Reminder," that is, in doubt about the true nature of the Qur'an. So at one time they say, "He has fabricated it"; at another, "It is poetry"; at another, "It is magic"; at another, "They are tales of the ancients"; and at another, "It is the speech of a soothsayer."
Thus "doubt" is meant in its literal sense, namely hesitation in knowledge.

The attribution of "the Reminder" to the pronoun of the speaker, who is God exalted, is an attribution of honour and of confirming that it is from God.

"The Reminder" in this sense is the very referent intended by ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him﴾, and the expression used for it was the explicit noun rather than a pronoun, in order to reach the emphasis on it as being from God.

"Fi" (in) is for figurative containment: the involvement of doubt with them is made like a container enveloping what is within it, in that no side of it is free from it.

"Min" (from) in "min dhikri" ("concerning My Reminder") is for origin, since doubt is a quality of them; that is, doubt arose for them concerning the matter of My Reminder, that is, from the side of denying its occurrence, or from the side of what they attribute to it.
* * *
﴿Nay, but they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ He follows this redirection with another redirection, which makes clear that what emboldened them in this defiance is that, since the arrival of punishment upon them was delayed, they thought its threat false, so they took to abuse and mockery. Had they tasted the punishment, the sword would have stopped their mouths with stones.

"Lamma" is a particle of negation with the sense of "lam", except that "lamma" has a particularity: it indicates that what is negated by it extends in negation up to the time of speaking, unlike "lam". Therefore negation with "lamma" may be understood as implying an expectation that the negated thing will occur afterwards. The author of al-Kashshaf said, concerning His saying ﴿and faith has not yet entered into their hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14] in the surah al-Hujurat: what is in "lamma" of the sense of anticipation indicates that these people had believed afterwards; that is, it indicates by way of implication arising from the sense of the end-point of negation up to the time of speaking. That is, I do not guarantee what comes after that. And they tasted the punishment of the sword on the day of Badr, four years after the revelation of this verse.

The attribution of "punishment" (adhab) to the first-person ya' is for its being specific to God, because He is its determiner and the one who decrees it upon them, and because it occurred in a manner not following the customary course, since the usual pattern is for a strong army to annihilate a small army.

The first-person ya' has been elided for lightness at the rhyme-ending (fasila), while the kasra has been retained as evidence of it. This is an elision that is frequent in rhyme-endings and in poetry, similar to its elision in the vocative.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 9:

﴿Or do they possess the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the All-Mighty, the Bestower?﴾ (Am) is *munqati'a* (disjunctive, meaning "or rather," marking a break from what precedes), and it also indicates *idrab* (a turning away from one topic to another, here a transitional *idrab*). The *am* is followed by an interrogative sense that expresses denial and rebuke, denying their saying: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?﴾ [Sad: 8]. That is, the treasuries of God's bounty are not in their possession, so that they could take it upon themselves to deprive whomever they wish of the gifts of goodness. Gifts come from God, who bestows them on whomever He wills. He chooses for prophethood whomever He selects, and the choice does not belong to them, so that they could make those whom they did not put before themselves in their religion unfit for God to choose.

Fronting the adverbial phrase (*zarf*) serves emphasis, because it is the focus of the denial. It is like His saying: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32].

*Al-khaza'in* is the plural of *khizana*, with a kasra on the *kha'*. It is the room in which wealth or food is stored, and it is also applied to a chest of wood or iron in which wealth is kept.

*Al-khazn* means preservation and safeguarding. *Al-rahma* is that by which one shows gentleness and kindness toward another. God's mercy is likened to a precious stored thing that souls aspire to, in that it is not given except by the will of its keeper, in the manner of an implicit metaphor (*isti'ara makniyya*). Attributing treasuries to it is an imaginative representation (*takhyil*), like attributing claws to death. The idafa (construction) carries the sense of the lam of specificity (*lam al-ikhtisas*).

The turn from the Name of Majesty (*Allah*) to a descriptive attribute (*wasf*) is because the attribute is more suited to the purpose under discussion. It implies that His honoring him with prophethood is one of the effects of His attribute of lordship over him, since the description "Lord" indicates care and bringing to perfection. The attribute "the All-Mighty" (*al-'Aziz*) is applied to the Lord to nullify their interference in His dispositions, and the attribute "the Bestower" (*al-Wahhab*) is applied to nullify their making deprivation of good dependent on their own desires, independent of God's bestowal.

*Al-'Aziz* is the one whom nothing overcomes. *Al-Wahhab* is the one of many gifts. Prophethood is a great mercy, so its bestowal is not entrusted except to one of intense might and abundant giving.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 10:

﴿Or do they have the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them? Then let them ascend by the means (asbab).﴾ This is a transitional turning-away (idrab intiqali) to a refutation that comes upon all of their claims, and it encompasses, in summary, all the detailed refutations of their claims with a single comprehensive word, like the ḥawṣala (the all-gathering pouch). It resembles a concluding summary (tadhyil) for what it contains of the generality of dominion and the generality of places, which necessitates the generality of knowledge and the generality of disposal. It censures them for their saying about the unseen without knowledge, and for their presumption in ruling over the ranks of existent beings without power or self-sufficiency.

The interrogative that is implied after (am) (the disjunctive "am") is mocking (tahakkumi), not denunciatory (inkari), because the consequence of the matter of incapacitation (al-ta'jiz) upon it specifies that it is mocking.

So the meaning is: If they have dominion over the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and if they have any share of that, then let them climb up, if they are able, into the means of the heavens, so that they may be informed of the realities of things, and then speak with knowledge concerning the essence of God and His attributes, and concerning the possibility of resurrection or its absence, and concerning the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) or its opposite; and so that they may open the treasuries of mercy, and bestow from them upon whomever pleases them, and withhold from whomever they do not look upon with an eye of approval.

The imperative in "fal-yartaqu" (then let them ascend) is for incapacitation, like His saying ﴿Then let him extend a rope to the sky﴾ [al-Hajj: 15].

The definiteness in "al-asbab" (the means) is for the generic reference (ahd al-jins), because it is known that every elevated place has means by which one ascends to it, like the saying of Zuhayr:

"And whoever fears the means of death, it will reach him, even if he climbs the means of the sky with a ladder."

And the saying of al-A'sha:

"Even if you were in a fortress of eighty cubits, and you ascended the means of the sky by a ladder."

The sabab is the rope to which the one climbing a palm tree for harvesting holds on. If it is made of two ropes and the two ropes are joined by transverse cords tied firmly, or by pieces of wood between the two ropes, with the sides of the two ropes woven over them, then it is the sullam (ladder).

The particle of place (harf al-zarfiyya) is a subsequent metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya) for the firm grasp of the means, to the point that they are as if they were enclosing containers around those who ascend.

[Page 218]

﴿A host of the factions will be routed there﴾ may be a resumptive clause (*istinaf*, a sentence that continues the preceding discourse), meant to connect with the earlier speech. It follows His saying: ﴿Before them We destroyed many a generation﴾ [Sad: 3], and so on. This is because His saying ﴿But those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾ [Sad: 2] came before it, and was followed by His saying ﴿Before them We destroyed many a generation﴾ [Sad: 3], and so on. When the discourse had concluded its detailing of what belongs to those who disbelieve in terms of arrogance and opposition, and of the consequences that follow from this, the reins were turned toward

[Page 219]

detailing the generations that were destroyed, who were like them before them in disbelief, so that it would lead to His saying ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾ [Sad: 12], up to His saying "﴿so My punishment was justly due﴾ [Sad: 14]."

In that case, the clause ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾ [Sad: 12] is a substitute for the clause ﴿A host of the factions will be routed there﴾, being a substitute of part for whole (*badal ba'd min kull*, a grammatical construction in which a part replaces the whole).

It may also be an independent, initial resumptive statement (*istinaf ibtida'i*), going out in the sense of good news for the Prophet ﷺ that these are a host of the factions who will be routed, i.e., their defeat is decreed to occur in the near future. This good news is a miracle from the reports of the unseen, with which the description of their circumstances is concluded. Qatadah said: "God promised that He would defeat them while they were in Mecca, and its fulfilment came on the Day of Badr." Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: "It is an indication of the conquest of Mecca." Some exegetes said: "It is an indication of the victory on the Day of the Trench."

It is customary for reports that serve as good news or warning about a hidden matter to be coded (*marmuzah*), and the code in this good news is the demonstrative noun in His saying ﴿there﴾ (*hunalika*), for there is nothing in the speech that is fit to be pointed to without some interpretation. So let us take it as a pointer to a place which God made known to His Prophet ﷺ, and that place is Badr.

It may also be that the word *al-ahzab* (the factions) in this verse is a hidden allusion to the routing of the factions on the days of the Trench, for it became known as the Battle of the Factions. God named them "the factions" in the surah that was revealed about them, so that naming would be an inspiration (*ilham*), just as God inspired the Muslims so that they named the Prophet's ﷺ pilgrimage the Farewell Pilgrimage, while he was then among them in sound health. This belongs to the category of the hidden miracles, some of which we gathered in a separate book. Perhaps the choice of the distal demonstrative is a symbol that this defeat would occur in a distant place other than Mecca. Therefore the verse does not indicate the conquest of Mecca, because that conquest did not involve punishment for the deniers; rather, God pardoned them, and they were the "freed ones" (*al-tulaqa'*).

This pointer was known to the Prophet ﷺ, and it is among the secrets between him and his Lord, so that the future would be its interpretation, just as Jacob knew the secret of his son Joseph's dream. So he said to him: ﴿Do not relate your dream to your brothers﴾ [Yusuf: 5]. Joseph did not know its interpretation until the day he said: ﴿O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before; my Lord has made it true﴾ [Yusuf: 100], referring to his parents' prostration before him.

[Page 220]

As for the apparent meaning of the verse, which people understood on the day it was revealed, it is that the host are the disbelievers of the people of Mecca, and that the tanwin (nunation) in it is for *naw'iyya* (indicating a type or kind). That is, they are nothing but a host among the hosts who denied and were destroyed. The demonstrative ﴿there﴾ refers to a conventional, figurative place, namely the worldly and customary elevation in which they stand. The routing is a metaphor (*musta'ar*, an extended or borrowed usage) for weakening their power. On both explanations, the apparent and the interpreted, the verse is nothing other than a consolation for the Messenger ﷺ, a reinforcement for him, and good news that his religion will prevail over them.

*Al-jund* means a large group. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Has there come to you the report of the hosts﴾ [al-Buruj: 17], ﴿of Pharaoh and Thamud﴾ [al-Buruj: 18].

The word *ma* is a superfluous particle (*harf za'id*) that emphasises the meaning of what precedes it. So it is an emphasis (*tawkid*) on what *jund* indicates by its meaning. Its indefiniteness is for magnification, meaning "a great host." This is because the tanwin, although it indicates magnification, is not explicit in it, so by the emphasis it became explicit. The discussion of this has already been presented under His saying: ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a mosquito or what is smaller than it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], in Surat al-Baqarah. If the verse refers to the Day of Badr, then the magnification of *jund* is because its men were the great men of Quraysh, such as Abu Jahl and Umayyah ibn Khalaf. If it refers to the Day of the Factions, then the magnification of *jund* is because of the large number of its men from the Arab tribes.

The description of *jund* by *mahzum* (routed) is in the sense of the future, i.e., "it will be routed." The passive participle, like the active participle, is a metaphorical usage for the future, and the indicator is contextual. This is from the practice of using what is for the present in the sense of the future, to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence, so that it is as though it is so close that it is like something happening now.

*Al-ahzab* refers to those who share a single opinion, whose members rally behind one another (*yatahazzabu*). It has already been discussed in Surat al-Ahzab.

The *min* (from) is for partitive (*li-l-tab'id*, indicating a part). The meaning is: these hosts are among the nations, and this is an implicit threat that what befell the nations will befall them. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the day of the factions, like the custom of the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, and those after them"﴾ [Ghafir: 30].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 12–14:

"﴿Before them the people of Noah, and ʿĀd, and Pharaoh, the lord of the stakes, denied [their messengers]﴾ ﴿and Thamūd, and the people of Lot, and the companions of the Thicket. Those were the factions﴾ ﴿Each of them denied the messengers, so My punishment was justly due﴾" When His saying ﴿a host of factions, routed there﴾ [Ṣād: 11] was a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ and a promise to him of victory, and an allusion to a warning against those who deny him, that they are heading to what the factions of whom these are part came to, as was mentioned just before, this was followed by something that serves as an explanation of this allusion. The proof of the intended outcome is in the manner of the analogical argument of equivalence. It was mentioned just before that this sentence is either a substitute (badal) for the sentence "a host there" etc., or a resumptive new sentence (istiʾnāf), and for this reason it is separated from the one before it.

The object of "denied" (kadhdhabat) is omitted, because what clarifies it will come in His saying ﴿each of them denied the messengers﴾, as will come. And the attribution of denial specifically to Pharaoh, rather than to his people, is singled out because God sent Moses, peace be upon him, to Pharaoh so that he would release the Children of Israel, and he denied Moses. God then commanded Moses to dispute with Pharaoh in order to refute his disbelief, so the disputation in matters of belief continued, and it became necessary to make known that Pharaoh and his people were in error, lest the Children of Israel be deceived by Pharaoh's doubts. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 15:

﴿And these do not await but a single shout, with no pause for it.﴾ When His saying "﴿So My punishment was deserved﴾ [Sad: 14]" implied the threat to the polytheists of Quraysh of a punishment awaiting them, in accordance with Allah's way of recompensing those who denied His messengers, there was joined to the statement about the descent of punishment upon the earlier confederates a statement threatening with punishment those who resembled them in denial.

And "these" (ha'ula') is a reference to the disbelievers of Quraysh, because the repeated renewal of their call, their threats and their denial day after day made them as though present, so the demonstrative was understood as referring to them. I have examined the usage of the Qur'an and found that when it employs "ha'ula'" without a mentioned referent accompanying it, it intends by it the polytheists of Makkah, as I have pointed out on more than one occasion previously.

And "yanzuru" is derived from al-nazar in the sense of al-intizar (awaiting). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels come to them?﴾ [al-An'am: 158], i.e., the polytheists await nothing but a single shout. This is like His saying: ﴿So do they await anything but the like of the days of those who passed before them?﴾ [Yunus: 102].

What is apparent from the verse is that it is a threat of a thunderous shout (sayha) and the like, such as the shout of Thamud, or the shout of the blast in the Trumpet at which the resurrection for recompense occurs. However, what was mentioned just before, that His saying ﴿A host there, routed, from among the confederates﴾ [Sad: 11] is an allusion to good tidings to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that his opponents will be defeated and the sword will work among them on the day of Badr, requires that the shout be the battle cry (sayhat al-qital), namely that the warner cry out "Ya sabahah!" as the crier in Makkah cried out when the Muslims confronted the caravan of Quraysh at Badr.

Describing it as "wahidah" (single) is an indication that the thunderbolt is great and destructive, or that the blast is single, namely the blast of annihilation (nafkhat al-sa'q). And in the hidden meaning there is an allusion that the people will rush to their weapons and go out hastily to rescue others, so the great event was the event of the day of Badr, or the shout of those challenging one another to combat on that day.

The awaiting is attributed to them although they are heedless of it and deny its outward meaning, as a metaphorical attribution in the manner of the rhetorical metaphor (al-majaz al-'aqli), for the believers promised victory await this for them, or the angels appointed to gather them at the blast await them. Since they were the object of the awaiting, the verb "yanzuru" was attributed to them by way of the relation of being the object, in the manner of ﴿In a pleasing life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21].

Al-fawaq, with the fa' pronounced with fatha or damma, is a name for the interval between the two milkings of a she-camel and the two suckings of her young calf: the milker milks the she-camel, then leaves her for a while so that her calf may suckle her, so that the milk descends into the udder, then they return and milk her. The period between the two milkings is called fawaq. It is a brief while. Before beginning to milk, they let the calf suckle her so that she releases milk. Most lexicographers hold that the fatha and damma in it are equivalent, but Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' held that there is a difference between the fatha and the damma, saying: the fatha-form means relief, like jawab from ijabah, and the damma-form is the name of the duration.

The milk gathered in that portion is called al-fay'ah with the fa' pronounced with kasra, and its plural is afawiq.

The meaning of ﴿it has no pause (ma laha min fawaq)﴾ is that there is no respite after it of the length of a fawaq. This is like His saying: ﴿They await nothing but a single shout that will seize them while they dispute, so they will not be able to make a bequest﴾ [Ya-Sin: 49].

The majority of readers read "fawaq" with fatha on the fa'. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with damma on the fa'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 16:

﴿And they say, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ This describes the state of their levity regarding the Resurrection and the recompense, and their denial of that, and their denial of the Qur'an's warning to them. When the Qur'an threatened them with the punishment of God, they said: "Our Lord, hasten to us our share of the punishment in this world, before the Day of Reckoning," displaying their indifference to the warning and their denial of it, lest the Muslims think that their levity toward the warning was because they do not believe in the Resurrection. So they made clear to them that they do not believe the Prophet (ﷺ) in every warning, even the warning of punishment in this world, which they believe to be within God's disposal.

This statement was made by them in a mocking manner, and it is related here to show their vulgarity and their obstinacy in disbelief.

This is the third of the foundations of their disbelief that was mentioned earlier, namely the denial of the Resurrection and the recompense. It is thus coordinated with ﴿And the disbelievers say, "This is a sorcerer, a great liar."﴾ [Sad: 4], so He mentioned their saying ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾ [Sad: 5], then He mentioned their saying ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ [Sad: 8] and what followed it of the consequences of such statements, and the statement led on to their third foundation. It has been said: the one who said that was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith; it has also been said: Abu Jahl, while the people were present and approving, so the statement was attributed to all of them.

The qitt is the portion (qist) of a thing, and it is applied to a piece of paper, parchment or cloth on which a grant is written for someone; for this reason it is interpreted as a deed (sakk). Al-Mutalammis said, concerning the document of 'Amr ibn Hind, which he gave him to take to his governor in Bahrain, deceiving him into thinking it was an order to give him a grant, whereas it was an order to kill him; al-Mutalammis understood what it contained, so he threw it into the river and said, in the verse for which the proverb is coined:

"I threw it into the bend of the river, from the side of a disbeliever; thus does every misguided qitt get cast."

So qitt is applied to that in which a reward or punishment is written, and most commonly it is the paper of a grant. Al-A'sha said:

"Nor the king al-Nu'man, on a day when I met him, among his people, giving out the qutut and distributing."

For this reason al-Hasan said: "They only meant: hasten to us the bliss You promised us for faith, so that we may see it now and become certain."

Even if we grant that qitt is specific to a deed of grant, this does not prevent their intention of hastening the punishment, by their having called their portion of punishment a qitt as a form of mockery, as 'Amr ibn Kulthum said when he made fighting a hospitality:

"We hosted you, and we hastened your hospitality, before dawn, a crushing, pounding meal."

Thus they would have combined mockery within mockery, going to extremes in mockery.

Their calling it "the Day of Reckoning" is also a mockery, since they do not believe in reckoning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verses 17–20:

﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength. Indeed, he was constantly turning back (awwab) to Allah.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him, in the evening and at sunrise.﴾ ﴿And the birds, gathered; each was constantly turning back to him.﴾ ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom and gave him wisdom (hikmah) and decisive speech (fasl al-khitab).﴾

The narration of their statements of denial, from His saying ﴿And the disbelievers say, "This is a magician, a liar"﴾ [Sad: 4] up to here, has been followed by Allah's command to His Messenger ﷺ to be patient over their statements, since all of them were a harm: some explicit, as when they said, "a magician, a liar," and said ﴿This is nothing but an invention﴾ [Sad: 7] and ﴿Indeed, this is a thing intended﴾ [Sad: 6]; and some implicit, which is found in the rest of their statements denying what the Messenger ﷺ brought, and in their mockery when they said ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our share﴾ [Sad: 16], and in their affirmation that the God is one. It includes what they say that was not related at the beginning of this surah.

His saying ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud﴾ up to the end may be a conjunction with His saying ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾, by following His command to be patient with the example of some of the earlier prophets in what they encountered from the people, and then they had the outcome of victory and the removal of distress. It may also be a conjunction with the whole of what preceded, as a conjunction of narrative, and the purpose is the same.

Dawud is mentioned first because Allah gave him a kingdom and authority that his forefathers did not have. So in mentioning him there is an allusion that the condition of Muhammad ﷺ would come to honour and authority, though he had no predecessor and no army. Thus the condition of the Prophet ﷺ was more similar to the condition of Dawud (peace be upon him).

Woven into this is an allusion to a warning against impatience regarding the essence of Allah the Exalted, and to guarding against considering the desires of the self in governing the community, so as to keep His Messenger ﷺ far from the precipices of error and slipping, and to discipline him at the beginning and the end of his affair, lest he receive blame. Dawud also had been patient over what he suffered from the envy of Sha'ul (Talut), king of Israel, toward him for his victory over Jalut (Goliath), king of Palestine.

The inflected verbal noun from ﴿remember (udhkur) Our servant Dawud﴾ is dhikr, with a dammah on the dhal, meaning remembrance (tadhakkur). It is not the mention of the tongue, because He commanded the Prophet ﷺ to do this only to console him and to preserve his perfection, not to inform the polytheists or to inform the Muslims. Yet both aims are achieved incidentally at the time of conveying the revealed text concerning Dawud to them and reciting it to them.

The meaning of the command to remember this is to recall what the Prophet ﷺ was previously informed of concerning his virtues, and to remind him of what he may not have known of what is made known in this verse.

The description of Dawud as ﴿Our servant﴾ is a description of honour by the attribution (of servanthood to Allah), by the indication of the context, as was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿except the chosen servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat: 40] in surah al-Saffat.

Al-ayd means strength and vigour; it is the verbal noun of: "aada ya'idu" when he became strong and vigorous. From it comes ta'yid (strengthening) and taqwiyah (reinforcement). He, the Exalted, said ﴿He sheltered you and supported you with His help﴾ [al-Anfal: 26] in surah al-Anfal.

Dawud had been given extraordinary strength and wondrous courage and boldness. He would hurl a stone with a sling without missing the target, and he would bend iron with his fingers to make it into chain-mail for armour. This strength is praiseworthy, because he used it in support of the religion of monotheism.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he was constantly turning back (awwab)﴾ is a reason for the command to remember him, indicating that the purpose of the command is to take him as an example, as He, the Exalted, said ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. Thus the clause is an interjection between the clause ﴿and remember﴾ and the clause that explains it, which is ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains with him﴾.

Awwab means one who returns often, i.e., returns. The intended meaning is returning to what Allah commanded, standing at His limits, and making up for what one neglected.

The one who repents is called awwab, and this is the more common usage in the Qur'an. It is a metaphor, and repentance itself is not called awwab. The Psalms of Dawud, called in Jewish tradition the Mazamir (Psalms), contain much seeking forgiveness and what is similar in meaning to repentance.

The clause ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains with him﴾ explains the clause ﴿remember Our servant﴾, meaning: remember his virtues and what We bestowed on him, such as subjecting the mountains and such and such. The word ﴿with him﴾ is an adverb of place for ﴿glorify﴾, and it was placed before what it governs for the sake of emphasis on the mention of its accompaniment. It is not an adverb for ﴿We subjected﴾, because of the requirement of the meaning. The subjecting of the mountains and birds to Dawud has been mentioned in surah al-Anbiya.

The clause ﴿glorify﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). The imperfect verb was chosen rather than the participle, which is the usual form for the circumstantial, because the intention is to show the renewal of the mountains' glorification with him whenever he was present among them, and because the imperfect brings to mind that extraordinary state that breaks habit.

Tasbih (glorification) originally is the saying "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to Allah). Then it was applied to remembrance and to prayer. From it is the hadith of 'A'ishah: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not perform the supererogatory prayer of the morning (subhat al-subh), and I used to perform it." This meaning is not intended here, because mountains do not pray, nor do birds, and because Dawud did not pray in the mountains, since in their law prayer is valid only in the mosque. As for prayer on the earth in general, it is one of the distinctive features of Islam.

Al-'ashiyy is what comes after the afternoon prayer (asr). It is said: 'ashiyy and 'ashiyyah.

Al-ishraq is the time when the sunlight appears clearly over the earth, and it is the time of forenoon (duha). It is said: "ashraqat al-ardu" (the earth became bright), and one does not say "ashraqat al-shams" (the sun became bright). Rather, one says "sharaqat al-shams" (the sun rose), and this is of the pattern qa'ada. For this reason, the regular form of the place noun from it would be mashraq with a fathah on the ra', but it has come only with a kasrah on the ra'. The time of the sun's rising is al-shuruq, and the time of al-ishraq is the forenoon. It is said: "sharaqat al-shams wa lamma tushriq" (the sun rose and did not yet shine), and it is said: "kullama dharra shariq", meaning whenever the sun rose.

The ba' in ﴿bi-al-'ashiyy﴾ is for time (zarfiyyah), so it is determined that the intended meaning of al-ishraq is the time of al-ishraq.

Al-mahshurah means gathered around him when he recited the Psalms. The word ﴿mahshurah﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial of ﴿the birds﴾. In describing the birds with gathering (hashr), the imperfect was not used as it was used in ﴿glorify﴾, because gathering happens at once, so the context does not require an indication of renewal or of bringing the image to mind.

The tanwin in ﴿kullun lahu awwab﴾ is a replacement for the genitive noun that was omitted. The estimated meaning is: each of the gathered birds is to him one who returns often, i.e., one who comes back to him often, i.e., comes to him from a far place. This is a miracle for him, because the nature of birds is to flee from humans. The word "kull" (each) retains its original meaning of totality.

This awwab is different from the awwab in His saying ﴿Indeed, he was constantly turning back﴾, so the closing rhyme was not repeated.

The lam in ﴿lahu awwab﴾ is the lam of reinforcement, and the placement of the prepositional phrase before what it governs is for emphasis on the pronoun in the genitive.

Al-shadd means holding and firmly grasping what one holds. It is for the purpose of benefit, as here, and it may be for the purpose of harm, as in His saying ﴿and tighten upon their hearts﴾ [Yunus: 88], in surah al-A'raf.

So the tightening (shadd) of a king's rule is the strengthening of his kingdom and its safety from the harms of a revolt in his domain and from the victory of his enemies over him in his wars. Dawud reigned forty years and died at seventy years of age, under a stable kingdom.

Al-hikmah means prophethood.

Al-hikmah in the general sense is knowledge of things as they are and acting upon matters as they should be. The book of the Psalms includes many wise sayings.

Fasl al-khitab is the eloquence of speech and the gathering of the intended meaning in such a way that the listener does not need further clarification. Describing the speech as "fasl" is describing the verbal noun, meaning "decisive" (fa'il). Al-fasil is the one who separates between two things; it is the opposite of al-wasil (the connector). It is used metaphorically for that which distinguishes a thing from confusion with its opposite.

Its conjunction here with wisdom is evidence that it is used in its metaphorical meaning, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision (yawm al-fasl) was an appointed time﴾ [al-Naba': 17].

The meaning is: Dawud was given, from soundness of judgment and eloquence of speech, what made his speech, when he spoke, a discourse separating truth from falsehood, like the speech of prophets and wise men. It is enough to consider his book, the Psalms, called by the Jews the Mazamir; it is a model of eloquence of speech in their language.

It is related from Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali: "Fasl al-khitab is his saying in his sermons: 'Amma ba'du' (as for what follows)." He said: "Dawud was the first to say that." I do not think this is correct, because it is an Arabic word, and it is not known that David said in the Hebrew language anything with its meaning. That phrase was called fasl al-khitab among the Arabs because it falls between the introduction of the subject and the subject itself. So "fasl" in it is in its literal sense, and it is from the description by the verbal noun, and the genitive construction is literal. The first to say "amma ba'du" was Suhban Wa'il, orator of the Arabs. It has also been said: fasl al-khitab is judgment between disputants, but this is far-fetched, since there is no basis for its being attributed to "khitab" (discourse).

Know that Muhammad ﷺ was given of everything that Dawud was given. He was an awwab, and he said: "Indeed, my heart is veiled, so I seek the forgiveness of Allah seventy times a day." He had the mountain of Hira subjected to him despite the difficulty of its paths, and he would seclude himself in it (yatahannath) until revelation descended upon him while he was in the cave of that mountain. The mountains of Makkah were offered to him to become gold for him, but he refused and chose servanthood. The pigeons were subjected to him, and they built their nest over the cave of Thawr during his concealment in it with al-Siddiq during their journey in the migration. Allah strengthened the kingdom of Islam for him, and He sufficed him against his enemies among his kin, such as Abu Lahab and his son 'Utbah, and against his enemies such as Abu Jahl. He gave him wisdom and gave him fasl al-khitab. He said: "I was given jawami' al-kalim (comprehensive words), and speech was condensed for me into brevity." Beyond what he was given, the Book that is miraculous, rendering the eloquent Arabs unable to oppose it. He, the Exalted, said in describing the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word, and it is not jest﴾ [al-Tariq: 13].
