This strength is praiseworthy, because he used it in support of the religion of monotheism.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he was constantly turning back (awwab)﴾ is a reason for the command to remember him, indicating that the purpose of the command is to take him as an example, as He, the Exalted, said ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. Thus the clause is an interjection between the clause ﴿and remember﴾ and the clause that explains it, which is ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains with him﴾.

Awwab means one who returns often, i.e., returns. The intended meaning is returning to what Allah commanded, standing at His limits, and making up for what one neglected.

The one who repents is called awwab, and this is the more common usage in the Qur'an. It is a metaphor, and repentance itself is not called awwab. The Psalms of Dawud, called in Jewish tradition the Mazamir (Psalms), contain much seeking forgiveness and what is similar in meaning to repentance.

The clause ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains with him﴾ explains the clause ﴿remember Our servant﴾, meaning: remember his virtues and what We bestowed on him, such as subjecting the mountains and such and such. The word ﴿with him﴾ is an adverb of place for ﴿glorify﴾, and it was placed before what it governs for the sake of emphasis on the mention of its accompaniment. It is not an adverb for ﴿We subjected﴾, because of the requirement of the meaning. The subjecting of the mountains and birds to Dawud has been mentioned in surah al-Anbiya.

The clause ﴿glorify﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). The imperfect verb was chosen rather than the participle, which is the usual form for the circumstantial, because the intention is to show the renewal of the mountains' glorification with him whenever he was present among them, and because the imperfect brings to mind that extraordinary state that breaks habit.

Tasbih (glorification) originally is the saying "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to Allah). Then it was applied to remembrance and to prayer. From it is the hadith of 'A'ishah: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not perform the supererogatory prayer of the morning (subhat al-subh), and I used to perform it." This meaning is not intended here, because mountains do not pray, nor do birds, and because Dawud did not pray in the mountains, since in their law prayer is valid only in the mosque. As for prayer on the earth in general, it is one of the distinctive features of Islam.

Al-'ashiyy is what comes after the afternoon prayer (asr). It is said: 'ashiyy and 'ashiyyah.

Al-ishraq is the time when the sunlight appears clearly over the earth, and it is the time of forenoon (duha). It is said: "ashraqat al-ardu" (the earth became bright), and one does not say "ashraqat al-shams" (the sun became bright). Rather, one says "sharaqat al-shams" (the sun rose), and this is of the pattern qa'ada. For this reason, the regular form of the place noun from it would be mashraq with a fathah on the ra', but it has come only with a kasrah on the ra'. The time of the sun's rising is al-shuruq, and the time of al-ishraq is the forenoon. It is said: "sharaqat al-shams wa lamma tushriq" (the sun rose and did not yet shine), and it is said: "kullama dharra shariq", meaning whenever the sun rose.

The ba' in ﴿bi-al-'ashiyy﴾ is for time (zarfiyyah), so it is determined that the intended meaning of al-ishraq is the time of al-ishraq.

Al-mahshurah means gathered around him when he recited the Psalms. The word ﴿mahshurah﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial of ﴿the birds﴾. In describing the birds with gathering (hashr), the imperfect was not used as it was used in ﴿glorify﴾, because gathering happens at once, so the context does not require an indication of renewal or of bringing the image to mind.

The tanwin in ﴿kullun lahu awwab﴾ is a replacement for the genitive noun that was omitted. The estimated meaning is: each of the gathered birds is to him one who returns often, i.e., one who comes back to him often, i.e., comes to him from a far place. This is a miracle for him, because the nature of birds is to flee from humans. The word "kull" (each) retains its original meaning of totality.

This awwab is different from the awwab in His saying ﴿Indeed, he was constantly turning back﴾, so the closing rhyme was not repeated.

The lam in ﴿lahu awwab﴾ is the lam of reinforcement, and the placement of the prepositional phrase before what it governs is for emphasis on the pronoun in the genitive.

Al-shadd means holding and firmly grasping what one holds. It is for the purpose of benefit, as here, and it may be for the purpose of harm, as in His saying ﴿and tighten upon their hearts﴾ [Yunus: 88], in surah al-A'raf.

So the tightening (shadd) of a king's rule is the strengthening of his kingdom and its safety from the harms of a revolt in his domain and from the victory of his enemies over him in his wars. Dawud reigned forty years and died at seventy years of age, under a stable kingdom.

Al-hikmah means prophethood.

Al-hikmah in the general sense is knowledge of things as they are and acting upon matters as they should be. The book of the Psalms includes many wise sayings.

Fasl al-khitab is the eloquence of speech and the gathering of the intended meaning in such a way that the listener does not need further clarification. Describing the speech as "fasl" is describing the verbal noun, meaning "decisive" (fa'il). Al-fasil is the one who separates between two things; it is the opposite of al-wasil (the connector). It is used metaphorically for that which distinguishes a thing from confusion with its opposite.

Its conjunction here with wisdom is evidence that it is used in its metaphorical meaning, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision (yawm al-fasl) was an appointed time﴾ [al-Naba': 17].

The meaning is: Dawud was given, from soundness of judgment and eloquence of speech, what made his speech, when he spoke, a discourse separating truth from falsehood, like the speech of prophets and wise men. It is enough to consider his book, the Psalms, called by the Jews the Mazamir; it is a model of eloquence of speech in their language.

It is related from Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali: "Fasl al-khitab is his saying in his sermons: 'Amma ba'du' (as for what follows)." He said: "Dawud was the first to say that." I do not think this is correct, because it is an Arabic word, and it is not known that David said in the Hebrew language anything with its meaning. That phrase was called fasl al-khitab among the Arabs because it falls between the introduction of the subject and the subject itself. So "fasl" in it is in its literal sense, and it is from the description by the verbal noun, and the genitive construction is literal. The first to say "amma ba'du" was Suhban Wa'il, orator of the Arabs. It has also been said: fasl al-khitab is judgment between disputants, but this is far-fetched, since there is no basis for its being attributed to "khitab" (discourse).

Know that Muhammad ﷺ was given of everything that Dawud was given. He was an awwab, and he said: "Indeed, my heart is veiled, so I seek the forgiveness of Allah seventy times a day." He had the mountain of Hira subjected to him despite the difficulty of its paths, and he would seclude himself in it (yatahannath) until revelation descended upon him while he was in the cave of that mountain. The mountains of Makkah were offered to him to become gold for him, but he refused and chose servanthood. The pigeons were subjected to him, and they built their nest over the cave of Thawr during his concealment in it with al-Siddiq during their journey in the migration. Allah strengthened the kingdom of Islam for him, and He sufficed him against his enemies among his kin, such as Abu Lahab and his son 'Utbah, and against his enemies such as Abu Jahl. He gave him wisdom and gave him fasl al-khitab. He said: "I was given jawami' al-kalim (comprehensive words), and speech was condensed for me into brevity." Beyond what he was given, the Book that is miraculous, rendering the eloquent Arabs unable to oppose it. He, the Exalted, said in describing the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word, and it is not jest﴾ [al-Tariq: 13].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verses 17–20:

﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength. Indeed, he was constantly turning back (awwab) to Allah.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him, in the evening and at sunrise.﴾ ﴿And the birds, gathered; each was constantly turning back to him.﴾ ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom and gave him wisdom (hikmah) and decisive speech (fasl al-khitab).﴾

The narration of their statements of denial, from His saying ﴿And the disbelievers say, "This is a magician, a liar"﴾ [Sad: 4] up to here, has been followed by Allah's command to His Messenger ﷺ to be patient over their statements, since all of them were a harm: some explicit, as when they said, "a magician, a liar," and said ﴿This is nothing but an invention﴾ [Sad: 7] and ﴿Indeed, this is a thing intended﴾ [Sad: 6]; and some implicit, which is found in the rest of their statements denying what the Messenger ﷺ brought, and in their mockery when they said ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our share﴾ [Sad: 16], and in their affirmation that the God is one. It includes what they say that was not related at the beginning of this surah.

His saying ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud﴾ up to the end may be a conjunction with His saying ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾, by following His command to be patient with the example of some of the earlier prophets in what they encountered from the people, and then they had the outcome of victory and the removal of distress. It may also be a conjunction with the whole of what preceded, as a conjunction of narrative, and the purpose is the same.

Dawud is mentioned first because Allah gave him a kingdom and authority that his forefathers did not have. So in mentioning him there is an allusion that the condition of Muhammad ﷺ would come to honour and authority, though he had no predecessor and no army. Thus the condition of the Prophet ﷺ was more similar to the condition of Dawud (peace be upon him).

Woven into this is an allusion to a warning against impatience regarding the essence of Allah the Exalted, and to guarding against considering the desires of the self in governing the community, so as to keep His Messenger ﷺ far from the precipices of error and slipping, and to discipline him at the beginning and the end of his affair, lest he receive blame. Dawud also had been patient over what he suffered from the envy of Sha'ul (Talut), king of Israel, toward him for his victory over Jalut (Goliath), king of Palestine.

Yet both aims are achieved incidentally at the time of conveying the revealed text concerning Dawud to them and reciting it to them.

The meaning of the command to remember this is to recall what the Prophet ﷺ was previously informed of concerning his virtues, and to remind him of what he may not have known of what is made known in this verse.

[Page 231]

The clause "Has the report of the litigants reached you" through to the end of the passage is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the clause "Indeed We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him" [Sad: 18]. The interrogative form here carries the sense of a declarative statement, since this clause recounts an aspect of Dawud's (David's) relationship with his Lord, and so it is similar to what precedes it.

The interrogative is used either to express wonder (ta'ajjub) or to seek knowledge. If the story was already known to the Prophet ﷺ, the interrogative is used for wonder. If this was the first time he had learned of it, the interrogative serves to urge attention, as in "Has the report of the Overwhelming reached you?" [al-Ghashiyah: 1].

The address may be to every listener, and the first two meanings both still apply.

"Naba'" means report or news.

The definiteness of "al-khasm" (the litigant) is the mental definite (al-'ahd al-dhihni), meaning a specific but unnamed individual of its kind: the report of a particular litigant whose account is being given. This is like the definiteness in "enter the market" (udkhul al-suq).

Khisam and ikhtisam mean disputing and contending with one another. This was discussed earlier in His words "These two are disputants" [al-Hajj: 19] in Surat al-Hajj.

Khasm is a term applied to one person or to more than one. Here it refers to two, as shown by the following words "two disputants." Calling them "the disputant" is a figurative usage (majaz) based on the relationship of form (ʿalaqat al-sura). It belongs to the category of resemblance in essence, not in a quality of the essence. The rhetoricians usually illustrate this with someone who sees the image of a lion and says, "This is a lion."

The plural pronoun is used to refer to the dual. The meaning is "when they two climbed over the prayer chamber." The Arabs shift from the dual to the plural when there is a clear indication, because the dual form is heavy in use since it is rarely employed. Allah the Exalted said, "Your hearts have certainly swerved" [al-Tahrim: 4], meaning "your two hearts."

If "idh" (when) is taken as a temporal adverb of past time, it is connected to an omitted element indicated by "the litigants." The sense would be: "The litigants pleaded before Dawud at the time they climbed over the prayer chamber."

It cannot be connected to the verb "has reached you" or to "naba'," because a report dated to the time the litigants climbed Dawud's prayer chamber cannot reach the Prophet ﷺ.

You may take "idh" as a noun for past time, stripped of the adverbial function, and make it a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "the litigant." This is based on His words, "And mention in the Book Maryam, when she withdrew from her family" [Maryam: 16]. Thus "the litigant" includes the time of their climbing over the prayer chamber. The removal of "idh" from adverbial use is not restricted to its being an object. Rather, the point is that it is flexible: it can be an adverb and also a non-adverb.

[Page 232]

Tasawwur means climbing over a wall, derived from sur, which is the wall surrounding a place or town. One says "tasawwara" when one rises up over the wall. Similar are the expressions "tasannama jamalahu" (he mounted his camel's hump) when he climbed its hump, and "tadhdhara'ahu" when he reached its peak. Close to this in derivation is the saying "sahha," meaning he mounted the saddle of his horse.

The meaning is that the house of worship of Dawud, peace be upon him, was enclosed by a wall so that no one could enter except with permission from the guard of the wall.

Mihrab means the place built for worship. It was discussed earlier in His words "They made for him whatever he willed of sanctuaries (mahareeb)" [Saba': 13] in Surat Saba'.

"When they entered" is a substitute for "when they climbed," because they climbed over the prayer chamber in order to enter upon Dawud.

Al-fazaʿ means alarm (al-dhu'r). It is an emotional state that shows agitation in the person who feels it, arising from anticipating severity or from being surprised. It was discussed earlier in His words "The greatest terror will not grieve them" [al-Anbiya': 103] in Surat al-Anbiya'. Ibn al-'Arabi said in his book Ahkam al-Qur'an: If it is asked, why was Dawud alarmed when his soul was strengthened by prophethood? He answered that Allah had not guaranteed him protection from harm or from being killed, and he feared these things. Allah had said to Musa, "Do not fear" [al-Qasas: 31], and before that it had been said to Lut. They were given security against fears which had not been declared to them as things from which they were protected. End of quote.

The essence of his answer is that such things happened to the prophets, since they were not protected from suffering harm, until Allah granted one of them security so that he would be at peace. Allah had not granted Dawud security, and therefore he was alarmed. This answer is not fully convincing, because the question contained the questioner's statement that his soul was strengthened by prophethood, and so the questioner based his question on the premise that fear could not reach the souls of the prophets at all. The answer, however, denied that security had been given, and so it did not match the questioner's question.

The proper course would have been to deny in the answer that the prophets were free from the approach of fear. The better answer is as follows.

First: fear is a natural emotion which Allah placed in human nature when confronted with something disagreeable. The souls of human beings are not free from its first signs, so that emotion comes upon them at the very beginning. Then the steadfastness of courage follows and overcomes it through self-control. People's souls differ in how long fear lasts and how quickly it clears. But when Allah grants a prophet security, that is another state, as in His words to Musa, "Do not fear" [al-Qasas: 31], and His words to the Prophet ﷺ, "So Allah will suffice you against them" [al-Baqarah: 137].

Second: what befell Dawud, peace be upon him, was alarm, not fear. Alarm is more general than fear, since it is agitation arising from sensing something whose nature is that one can be freed from it. It has been reported in the hadith of the solar eclipse that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out alarmed (fazi'an)," meaning hastening and rushing to prayer, anticipating that the eclipse might be a warning of punishment. For this reason the Qur'an said "So he was alarmed by them" and did not say "he feared." Concerning Ibrahim, peace be upon him, it said "So he felt a little fear of them" [al-Dhariyat: 28], meaning a sense of apprehension that did not reach the level of fear. As for the litigant's words to Dawud, "Do not fear," this is a statement made by someone arriving in an unfamiliar state which is by nature likely to disturb the observer.

Third: the prophets are commanded to preserve their lives, because their lives are good for the community. A prophet may be alarmed by anticipating a danger, fearing that it might cause his destruction, which would end the benefit of him to his community. It has been reported in the hadith of 'A'ishah that "the Prophet ﷺ could not sleep one night, and he said, 'I wish a righteous man from my companions would guard me tonight.' Then we heard the sound of weapons, and he said, 'Who is this?' He said, 'Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas; I have come to guard you.' She said: The Prophet ﷺ slept until we heard his snoring." It is also narrated by al-Tirmidhi that "al-'Abbas used to guard the Prophet ﷺ until the verse was revealed, 'And Allah will protect you from the people' [al-Ma'idah: 67], and then the guarding was abandoned."

The meaning of "Some of us have wronged some of us" (baghā ba'duna 'ala ba'd) is that he transgressed and oppressed. Al-baghy means injustice. The clause is a qualifier (sifah) of "two disputants," and the connecting element (al-rabit) is the pronoun in "some of us." The pronoun of the speaker is used together with another, in consideration of the meaning of "two disputants."

They did not specify which of the two was the aggressor, because the situation of calming Dawud's fear calls for brevity through generality, followed afterward by detail. It also displays proper manners toward the judge, so that the two do not appoint themselves to identify the aggressor, but leave that to the judge, who identifies the aggressor in his ruling when he says to one of them: "He has certainly wronged you by asking for your ewe to be added to his ewes" [Sad: 24].

The fa' in "So judge between us with truth" is a consequence (tafri') of "two disputants," because Dawud, peace be upon him, was a king, and since the two who came to him were litigants, their request for judgment between them follows from that.

The ba' in "with truth" is for accompaniment (mulabasah) and is connected to "judge." This is a simple request from them for the truth, like the statement of the man to the Prophet ﷺ, whose son had committed adultery with his wife, which was: "Judge between us according to the Book of Allah."

The prohibition in "Do not be unjust" is used for reminding and guidance.

"Tushittu" is the present form of ashatta. One says "ashatta 'alayhi" when he acted unjustly toward him. It is derived from shatat, which means exceeding the limit and the customary measure.

The litigant's address to Dawud in these words is by way of eagerness to make the truth clear. It has the sense of reminding him of what is obligatory. For this reason such words are not counted as rudeness toward the judge or the magistrate. It belongs to the category of "Fear Allah concerning my case." Saying it before the judgment is closer to the sense of reminding and further from rudeness. If it comes after the judgment, it is closer to rudeness, like the man who said to the Prophet ﷺ regarding a division he had made, "Be just!" The Messenger said to him, "Woe to you! Who would be just if I am not just?"

Our scholars have said regarding the litigant's saying to the judge, "Fear Allah concerning my case," that it is not considered rudeness toward the judge, and the judge may not punish him for it as he would punish someone who wronged him. Malik gave a legal opinion to imprison a young man. The young man's father said to Malik, "Fear Allah, O Malik! By Allah, Hell was not created in vain." Malik said, "Among what is vain is what your son has done." This contains an added allusion in response to his words, "By Allah, Hell was not created in vain."

Their words "And guide us to the even path" turn away from the sense of rudeness in their words "and do not be unjust," because they knew that he would say nothing except the truth, and that they were seeking guidance from him.

Guidance here is used metaphorically to mean clarification and making the right course clear.

The "even path" (sawa' al-sirat) is used metaphorically for the truth that is not mixed with falsehood, because the sirat is the broad road, and its sawa' is the one with no twists in it and no branches splitting off from it. It is therefore the quickest in delivering one to the intended goal by its evenness, and furthest from confusion by its freedom from branching.

The whole of "And guide us to the even path" is a parable for the situation of the judge who rules with justice, likened to the situation of a guide who points out the route that leads to the destination. It is therefore among parables whose comparison can be divided into parts. From this it is understood that a just judge's ruling is to be taken as following the truth, and that the ruling must be according to the truth in the sense of the Law, because it is guidance. Thus it and the legal opinion (fatwa) are alike in being guidance, except that a ruling carries obligation.

The meaning of "Make it my charge" (akfilniha) is: place it in my custody, that is, in my keeping. It is a metonymy for giving and gifting, that is, give it to me.

The clause "Indeed this is my brother" through to the end is an explanation of the clause "two disputants, some of us have wronged some of us." Its apparent meaning is that by "brother" they meant brotherhood by lineage. They supposed themselves to be two brothers and posited the dispute as occurring within the dealings of kinship, the bond of blood, and the preservation of ties. Further, "my brother" may be a substitute for the demonstrative, or it may be the predicate of "indeed," and the latter is better because it adds to the enormity of his aggression against him.

"'Azzani" means he overpowered me in speech, that is, he displayed through his words a haughty might against me and an arrogance.

The address is made a container for the might, figuratively, because the address indicated might and dominance. Thus the indicated is placed in the position of what is contained. This is common in usage.

The meaning is: he asked him to give him his ewe, and when he saw resistance from him he pressed him harshly with words and threatened him. The complaining litigant then showed that he was guarding the bonds of kinship, so he complained to the king to restrain him from treating his brother with harshness and arrogance, so that he would take the ewe without goodwill.

Through this it becomes clear that the purpose of this litigation was to seek fairness in the treatment of kinsfolk, lest the disagreement between them lead to attack and thus sever the bonds of kindness and mercy between them.

Dawud knew, from the consecutive sequence of their dispute and from the silence of one of the two litigants, that they were close to what the narrator described of them, or that the defendant had acknowledged it.

So Dawud ruled that the brother's request of his brother for his ewe was an injustice, because the one who asked was in no need of it, while the one asked had no other. The asker's desire for what was in his brother's hand was from excessive greed for wealth.

[Page 236]

and the seeking of benefit for oneself without concern for the other's benefit. This is not the way of mutual affection and fairness between two brothers, so it is injustice. And it is not right that he should ask that: whether he gives it or refuses. Moreover, he was arrogant toward him in speech and rebuked him for not allowing himself to give up the ewe, and this too is injustice.

The genitive in His saying "﴿بِسُؤالِ نَعْجَتِكَ﴾ [Sad: 24]" is for specification, i.e., this particular request concerning a known ewe. That is, this request in its entirety contains injustice. The construction "the asking of [your] ewe" is an idafah of the verbal noun (al-masdar) to its object.

The attaching of "إلى نِعاجِهِ" (to his ewes) to "سُؤالِ" (asking) is by way of implying (tadmin) the meaning of "adding" (ḍamm) to "suʾāl," as if it were said: by requesting the adding of your ewe to his ewes.

This is the answer to their words "﴿فاحْكم بَيْنَنا بِالحَقِّ ولا تُشْطِطْ﴾" (judge between us with truth and do not exceed the bounds), and then he followed it with the answer to their words "﴿واهْدِنا إلى سَواءِ الصِّراطِ﴾" (guide us to the right path), when he said "﴿وإنَّ كَثِيرًا مِنَ الخُلَطاءِ لَيَبْغِي بَعْضُهم عَلى بَعْضٍ إلّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ﴾" [Sad: 24], which indicates that the transgression of one of two associates against the other is widespread among people who are not righteous believers. This is a metaphor for ordering them both to be among the righteous believers, and that what one of them did is not the way of the righteous.

Mentioning the general conditions of associates is intended as an admonition to them both after the judgment between them, in keeping with the practice of people of goodness of seizing opportunities for guidance. So David (peace be upon him) wished to encourage them to adopt the custom of righteous associates and to make injustice and transgression hateful to them.

It is inferred from the context that he (David) grieved over their condition, and that he meant to console the wronged one for what had befallen him from his associate, and that he has an example in most associates.

In concluding his speech with His saying "وقَلِيلٌ ما هم" (and few are they), there is an urging for them both to be among the righteous, because of what is firmly established in souls regarding the preciousness of anything rare. He, the Exalted, said: "﴿قُلْ لا يَسْتَوِي الخَبِيثُ والطَّيِّبُ ولَوْ أعْجَبَكَ كَثْرَةُ الخَبِيثِ﴾" [al-Ma'idah: 100]. The reason for this, from the side of wisdom, is that the motives toward worldly pleasures are many, following desire is loved, and striving against the self is hard to achieve. So a human being is surrounded by attractions to evil deeds, whereas the motives toward truth and perfection are religion and wisdom. Among the means of perfection is turning away from the stimulants of desires, and this turning away is difficult, and none follows it except one who raises his religion and aspiration to spiritual nobility and turns away from the appetitive motive. That is the cause of this judgment of fewness.

The addition of "ما" after "قَلِيلٌ" is for the purpose of vagueness, as was mentioned earlier in His saying "﴿جُنْدٌ ما هُنالِكَ﴾" [Sad: 11]. In this vagueness there is an indication of wonder at that, aided by context and situation, just as its addition conveyed the sense of longing and yearning in the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"And the talk of the riding party on the day of Hunā, and talk, though brief..."

The commentators differed about the identity of these two adversaries. Al-Suddi, al-Hasan, and Wahb ibn Munabbih said: they were two angels whom God sent in the form of two men to David (peace be upon him) to convey this parable to him as a rebuke. al-Tabari narrated it from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

It was also said: they were two full brothers from the Children of Israel; that is, God inspired them to deliver this admonition.

Know that placing this account immediately after the praise of David (peace be upon him) is only a completion of the praise of him, to repel what might be supposed to contradict what has been mentioned of his virtues, from what came in the Second Book of Samuel among the books of the Jews concerning this story, with false errors that contradict the station of prophethood. So the true portion of it is made clear, and its conclusion is that what proceeded from David (peace be upon him) merits reproach but does not entail punishment. For this reason the passage ends with His saying, the Exalted: "﴿وإنَّ لَهُ عِنْدَنا لَزُلْفى وحُسْنَ مَآبٍ﴾" [Sad: 25].

By this you know that this account has no connection with the purpose for which the mention of David and those linked with him among the prophets was brought.

This account which the verse contains refers to the story of David (peace be upon him) marrying the wife of (Uriah the Hittite), one of the men of his army. David had seen her, inclined toward her, and desired to marry her, so he asked him to cede her to him. In their law it was permissible for a man to cede his wife to another out of friendship between them, so he divorces her and the other marries her after the completion of her waiting period and the certainty of the cleanness of her womb, as was the case in early Islam. Uriah went out on the campaign against the city of (Rabbah) of the Ammonites, and it was said against Amman, the capital of al-Balqa' in Palestine, and he was killed in the battle. The woman's name was (Bathsheba daughter of Eliam), and she was the mother of Solomon. The Qur'an recounted it only in passing, since the account of the two adversaries indicates it, because the lesson lies in what the account of the two adversaries produced in David's own soul. God therefore rebuked David for having made this permissible thing his own, so He admonished him with this embodied parable. He sent to him two angels who descended from the top of the wall of the prayer niche in the form of two adversaries, related the story to him, and asked for his judgment and guidance. He judged between them and guided them by what its interpretation has already passed, so that this image would be an admonition to him. It also indicates that it would have been most fitting for his station not to undertake this marriage, even though it was permissible, because it involved preferring himself with what belongs to another, even in a permissible way; for the sense of the goodness or ugliness of an act may not arise in the one who does it at the time, so when he sees or hears that someone else has done it, he perceives its character.

In the Second Book of Samuel among the books of the Jews, this story is related in a manner contrary to this.

There is nothing in the words of the two adversaries, "this is my brother," nor in their supposing the dispute, which is not an actual occurrence, that involves lying; for this is one of the reports contrary to reality, which the informant does not intend the informed (al-mukhbar bihi, with fatḥ) to believe as actually occurring except for the time needed to achieve the lesson from it, after which its inner reality is revealed to him and he knows that it did not happen.

Whatever attributes and relations that run through it which did not occur are only by way of supposition and estimation, and with the intention of resemblance.

In this is a legal proof for the permissibility of composing illustrative tales that aim at education and admonition, and whose composer does not bear the blemish of lying, contrary to those who charged al-Hariri with lying in composing the Maqamat, as he himself indicated in its preface. And in it is a legal proof for the permissibility of representing those tales through bodies, provided they do not contradict the Shari'ah, and of this is the dramatization of narratives and stories in theaters of drama; for what occurs in the law of those before us serves as a proof for us in our law when the Qur'an or the Sunnah of the Prophet (ﷺ) relates it and nothing in our law abrogates it.

From the verse is derived the legitimacy of judging in the mosque. They said: there is nothing in the Qur'an that indicates this except this verse, based on the principle that the law of those before us is law for us when the Book or the Sunnah relates it.

This story has been related in the Second Book of Samuel in chapter eleven, contrary to what is in the Qur'an and contrary to what the infallibility of David's prophethood requires, so beware of it.

What is in the Qur'an is the truth, and it is consistent with what is customary and it is the dominant standard over it. Had this been related by a solitary report (khabar ahad) among the Muslims, it would have been obligatory to reject it and to affirm definitively that it is fabricated, because it contradicts what is certain regarding the infallibility of the prophets from major sins according to all the People of the Sunnah, and from minor sins according to their verifying scholars, and this is the preferred view.

[Page 231]

The clause "Has the report of the litigants reached you" through to the end of the passage is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the clause "Indeed We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him" [Sad: 18]. The interrogative form here carries the sense of a declarative statement, since this clause recounts an aspect of Dawud's (David's) relationship with his Lord, and so it is similar to what precedes it.

The interrogative is used either to express wonder (ta'ajjub) or to seek knowledge. If the story was already known to the Prophet ﷺ, the interrogative is used for wonder. If this was the first time he had learned of it, the interrogative serves to urge attention, as in "Has the report of the Overwhelming reached you?" [al-Ghashiyah: 1].

The address may be to every listener, and the first two meanings both still apply.

"Naba'" means report or news.

The definiteness of "al-khasm" (the litigant) is the mental definite (al-'ahd al-dhihni), meaning a specific but unnamed individual of its kind: the report of a particular litigant whose account is being given. This is like the definiteness in "enter the market" (udkhul al-suq).

Khisam and ikhtisam mean disputing and contending with one another. This was discussed earlier in His words "These two are disputants" [al-Hajj: 19] in Surat al-Hajj.

Khasm is a term applied to one person or to more than one. Here it refers to two, as shown by the following words "two disputants." Calling them "the disputant" is a figurative usage (majaz) based on the relationship of form (ʿalaqat al-sura). It belongs to the category of resemblance in essence, not in a quality of the essence. The rhetoricians usually illustrate this with someone who sees the image of a lion and says, "This is a lion."

The plural pronoun is used to refer to the dual. The meaning is "when they two climbed over the prayer chamber." The Arabs shift from the dual to the plural when there is a clear indication, because the dual form is heavy in use since it is rarely employed. Allah the Exalted said, "Your hearts have certainly swerved" [al-Tahrim: 4], meaning "your two hearts."

If "idh" (when) is taken as a temporal adverb of past time, it is connected to an omitted element indicated by "the litigants." The sense would be: "The litigants pleaded before Dawud at the time they climbed over the prayer chamber."

It cannot be connected to the verb "has reached you" or to "naba'," because a report dated to the time the litigants climbed Dawud's prayer chamber cannot reach the Prophet ﷺ.

You may take "idh" as a noun for past time, stripped of the adverbial function, and make it a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "the litigant." This is based on His words, "And mention in the Book Maryam, when she withdrew from her family" [Maryam: 16]. Thus "the litigant" includes the time of their climbing over the prayer chamber. The removal of "idh" from adverbial use is not restricted to its being an object. Rather, the point is that it is flexible: it can be an adverb and also a non-adverb.

[Page 232]

Tasawwur means climbing over a wall, derived from sur, which is the wall surrounding a place or town. One says "tasawwara" when one rises up over the wall. Similar are the expressions "tasannama jamalahu" (he mounted his camel's hump) when he climbed its hump, and "tadhdhara'ahu" when he reached its peak. Close to this in derivation is the saying "sahha," meaning he mounted the saddle of his horse.

The meaning is that the house of worship of Dawud, peace be upon him, was enclosed by a wall so that no one could enter except with permission from the guard of the wall.

Mihrab means the place built for worship. It was discussed earlier in His words "They made for him whatever he willed of sanctuaries (mahareeb)" [Saba': 13] in Surat Saba'.

"When they entered" is a substitute for "when they climbed," because they climbed over the prayer chamber in order to enter upon Dawud.

Al-fazaʿ means alarm (al-dhu'r). It is an emotional state that shows agitation in the person who feels it, arising from anticipating severity or from being surprised. It was discussed earlier in His words "The greatest terror will not grieve them" [al-Anbiya': 103] in Surat al-Anbiya'. Ibn al-'Arabi said in his book Ahkam al-Qur'an: If it is asked, why was Dawud alarmed when his soul was strengthened by prophethood? He answered that Allah had not guaranteed him protection from harm or from being killed, and he feared these things. Allah had said to Musa, "Do not fear" [al-Qasas: 31], and before that it had been said to Lut. They were given security against fears which had not been declared to them as things from which they were protected. End of quote.

The essence of his answer is that such things happened to the prophets, since they were not protected from suffering harm, until Allah granted one of them security so that he would be at peace. Allah had not granted Dawud security, and therefore he was alarmed. This answer is not fully convincing, because the question contained the questioner's statement that his soul was strengthened by prophethood, and so the questioner based his question on the premise that fear could not reach the souls of the prophets at all. The answer, however, denied that security had been given, and so it did not match the questioner's question.

The proper course would have been to deny in the answer that the prophets were free from the approach of fear. The better answer is as follows.

First: fear is a natural emotion which Allah placed in human nature when confronted with something disagreeable. The souls of human beings are not free from its first signs, so that emotion comes upon them at the very beginning. Then the steadfastness of courage follows and overcomes it through self-control. People's souls differ in how long fear lasts and how quickly it clears. But when Allah grants a prophet security, that is another state, as in His words to Musa, "Do not fear" [al-Qasas: 31], and His words to the Prophet ﷺ, "So Allah will suffice you against them" [al-Baqarah: 137].

Second: what befell Dawud, peace be upon him, was alarm, not fear. Alarm is more general than fear, since it is agitation arising from sensing something whose nature is that one can be freed from it. It has been reported in the hadith of the solar eclipse that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out alarmed (fazi'an)," meaning hastening and rushing to prayer, anticipating that the eclipse might be a warning of punishment. For this reason the Qur'an said "So he was alarmed by them" and did not say "he feared." Concerning Ibrahim, peace be upon him, it said "So he felt a little fear of them" [al-Dhariyat: 28], meaning a sense of apprehension that did not reach the level of fear. As for the litigant's words to Dawud, "Do not fear," this is a statement made by someone arriving in an unfamiliar state which is by nature likely to disturb the observer.

Third: the prophets are commanded to preserve their lives, because their lives are good for the community. A prophet may be alarmed by anticipating a danger, fearing that it might cause his destruction, which would end the benefit of him to his community. It has been reported in the hadith of 'A'ishah that "the Prophet ﷺ could not sleep one night, and he said, 'I wish a righteous man from my companions would guard me tonight.' Then we heard the sound of weapons, and he said, 'Who is this?' He said, 'Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas; I have come to guard you.' She said: The Prophet ﷺ slept until we heard his snoring." It is also narrated by al-Tirmidhi that "al-'Abbas used to guard the Prophet ﷺ until the verse was revealed, 'And Allah will protect you from the people' [al-Ma'idah: 67], and then the guarding was abandoned."

The meaning of "Some of us have wronged some of us" (baghā ba'duna 'ala ba'd) is that he transgressed and oppressed. Al-baghy means injustice. The clause is a qualifier (sifah) of "two disputants," and the connecting element (al-rabit) is the pronoun in "some of us." The pronoun of the speaker is used together with another, in consideration of the meaning of "two disputants."

They did not specify which of the two was the aggressor, because the situation of calming Dawud's fear calls for brevity through generality, followed afterward by detail. It also displays proper manners toward the judge, so that the two do not appoint themselves to identify the aggressor, but leave that to the judge, who identifies the aggressor in his ruling when he says to one of them: "He has certainly wronged you by asking for your ewe to be added to his ewes" [Sad: 24].

The fa' in "So judge between us with truth" is a consequence (tafri') of "two disputants," because Dawud, peace be upon him, was a king, and since the two who came to him were litigants, their request for judgment between them follows from that.

The ba' in "with truth" is for accompaniment (mulabasah) and is connected to "judge." This is a simple request from them for the truth, like the statement of the man to the Prophet ﷺ, whose son had committed adultery with his wife, which was: "Judge between us according to the Book of Allah."

The prohibition in "Do not be unjust" is used for reminding and guidance.

"Tushittu" is the present form of ashatta. One says "ashatta 'alayhi" when he acted unjustly toward him. It is derived from shatat, which means exceeding the limit and the customary measure.

In this vagueness there is an indication of wonder at that, aided by context and situation, just as its addition conveyed the sense of longing and yearning in the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"And the talk of the riding party on the day of Hunā, and talk, though brief..."

The commentators differed about the identity of these two adversaries. Al-Suddi, al-Hasan, and Wahb ibn Munabbih said: they were two angels whom God sent in the form of two men to David (peace be upon him) to convey this parable to him as a rebuke. al-Tabari narrated it from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

It was also said: they were two full brothers from the Children of Israel; that is, God inspired them to deliver this admonition.

Know that placing this account immediately after the praise of David (peace be upon him) is only a completion of the praise of him, to repel what might be supposed to contradict what has been mentioned of his virtues, from what came in the Second Book of Samuel among the books of the Jews concerning this story, with false errors that contradict the station of prophethood. So the true portion of it is made clear, and its conclusion is that what proceeded from David (peace be upon him) merits reproach but does not entail punishment. For this reason the passage ends with His saying, the Exalted: "﴿وإنَّ لَهُ عِنْدَنا لَزُلْفى وحُسْنَ مَآبٍ﴾" [Sad: 25].

By this you know that this account has no connection with the purpose for which the mention of David and those linked with him among the prophets was brought.

This account which the verse contains refers to the story of David (peace be upon him) marrying the wife of (Uriah the Hittite), one of the men of his army. David had seen her, inclined toward her, and desired to marry her, so he asked him to cede her to him. In their law it was permissible for a man to cede his wife to another out of friendship between them, so he divorces her and the other marries her after the completion of her waiting period and the certainty of the cleanness of her womb, as was the case in early Islam. Uriah went out on the campaign against the city of (Rabbah) of the Ammonites, and it was said against Amman, the capital of al-Balqa' in Palestine, and he was killed in the battle. The woman's name was (Bathsheba daughter of Eliam), and she was the mother of Solomon. The Qur'an recounted it only in passing, since the account of the two adversaries indicates it, because the lesson lies in what the account of the two adversaries produced in David's own soul. God therefore rebuked David for having made this permissible thing his own, so He admonished him with this embodied parable. He sent to him two angels who descended from the top of the wall of the prayer niche in the form of two adversaries, related the story to him, and asked for his judgment and guidance. He judged between them and guided them by what its interpretation has already passed, so that this image would be an admonition to him. It also indicates that it would have been most fitting for his station not to undertake this marriage, even though it was permissible, because it involved preferring himself with what belongs to another, even in a permissible way; for the sense of the goodness or ugliness of an act may not arise in the one who does it at the time, so when he sees or hears that someone else has done it, he perceives its character.

In the Second Book of Samuel among the books of the Jews, this story is related in a manner contrary to this.

There is nothing in the words of the two adversaries, "this is my brother," nor in their supposing the dispute, which is not an actual occurrence, that involves lying; for this is one of the reports contrary to reality, which the informant does not intend the informed (al-mukhbar bihi, with fatḥ) to believe as actually occurring except for the time needed to achieve the lesson from it, after which its inner reality is revealed to him and he knows that it did not happen.

Whatever attributes and relations that run through it which did not occur are only by way of supposition and estimation, and with the intention of resemblance.

In this is a legal proof for the permissibility of composing illustrative tales that aim at education and admonition, and whose composer does not bear the blemish of lying, contrary to those who charged al-Hariri with lying in composing the Maqamat, as he himself indicated in its preface. And in it is a legal proof for the permissibility of representing those tales through bodies, provided they do not contradict the Shari'ah, and of this is the dramatization of narratives and stories in theaters of drama; for what occurs in the law of those before us serves as a proof for us in our law when the Qur'an or the Sunnah of the Prophet (ﷺ) relates it and nothing in our law abrogates it.

From the verse is derived the legitimacy of judging in the mosque. They said: there is nothing in the Qur'an that indicates this except this verse, based on the principle that the law of those before us is law for us when the Book or the Sunnah relates it.

This story has been related in the Second Book of Samuel in chapter eleven, contrary to what is in the Qur'an and contrary to what the infallibility of David's prophethood requires, so beware of it.

What is in the Qur'an is the truth, and it is consistent with what is customary and it is the dominant standard over it. Had this been related by a solitary report (khabar ahad) among the Muslims, it would have been obligatory to reject it and to affirm definitively that it is fabricated, because it contradicts what is certain regarding the infallibility of the prophets from major sins according to all the People of the Sunnah, and from minor sins according to their verifying scholars, and this is the preferred view.

[Page 231]

The clause "Has the report of the litigants reached you" through to the end of the passage is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the clause "Indeed We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him" [Sad: 18]. The interrogative form here carries the sense of a declarative statement, since this clause recounts an aspect of Dawud's (David's) relationship with his Lord, and so it is similar to what precedes it.

The interrogative is used either to express wonder (ta'ajjub) or to seek knowledge. If the story was already known to the Prophet ﷺ, the interrogative is used for wonder. If this was the first time he had learned of it, the interrogative serves to urge attention, as in "Has the report of the Overwhelming reached you?" [al-Ghashiyah: 1].

The address may be to every listener, and the first two meanings both still apply.

"Naba'" means report or news.

The definiteness of "al-khasm" (the litigant) is the mental definite (al-'ahd al-dhihni), meaning a specific but unnamed individual of its kind: the report of a particular litigant whose account is being given. This is like the definiteness in "enter the market" (udkhul al-suq).

Khisam and ikhtisam mean disputing and contending with one another. This was discussed earlier in His words "These two are disputants" [al-Hajj: 19] in Surat al-Hajj.

Khasm is a term applied to one person or to more than one. Here it refers to two, as shown by the following words "two disputants." Calling them "the disputant" is a figurative usage (majaz) based on the relationship of form (ʿalaqat al-sura). It belongs to the category of resemblance in essence, not in a quality of the essence. The rhetoricians usually illustrate this with someone who sees the image of a lion and says, "This is a lion."

The plural pronoun is used to refer to the dual. The meaning is "when they two climbed over the prayer chamber." The Arabs shift from the dual to the plural when there is a clear indication, because the dual form is heavy in use since it is rarely employed. Allah the Exalted said, "Your hearts have certainly swerved" [al-Tahrim: 4], meaning "your two hearts."

If "idh" (when) is taken as a temporal adverb of past time, it is connected to an omitted element indicated by "the litigants." The sense would be: "The litigants pleaded before Dawud at the time they climbed over the prayer chamber."

It cannot be connected to the verb "has reached you" or to "naba'," because a report dated to the time the litigants climbed Dawud's prayer chamber cannot reach the Prophet ﷺ.

You may take "idh" as a noun for past time, stripped of the adverbial function, and make it a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "the litigant." This is based on His words, "And mention in the Book Maryam, when she withdrew from her family" [Maryam: 16]. Thus "the litigant" includes the time of their climbing over the prayer chamber. The removal of "idh" from adverbial use is not restricted to its being an object. Rather, the point is that it is flexible: it can be an adverb and also a non-adverb.

[Page 232]

Tasawwur means climbing over a wall, derived from sur, which is the wall surrounding a place or town. One says "tasawwara" when one rises up over the wall. Similar are the expressions "tasannama jamalahu" (he mounted his camel's hump) when he climbed its hump, and "tadhdhara'ahu" when he reached its peak. Close to this in derivation is the saying "sahha," meaning he mounted the saddle of his horse.

The meaning is that the house of worship of Dawud, peace be upon him, was enclosed by a wall so that no one could enter except with permission from the guard of the wall.

Mihrab means the place built for worship. It was discussed earlier in His words "They made for him whatever he willed of sanctuaries (mahareeb)" [Saba': 13] in Surat Saba'.

"When they entered" is a substitute for "when they climbed," because they climbed over the prayer chamber in order to enter upon Dawud.

Al-fazaʿ means alarm (al-dhu'r). It is an emotional state that shows agitation in the person who feels it, arising from anticipating severity or from being surprised. It was discussed earlier in His words "The greatest terror will not grieve them" [al-Anbiya': 103] in Surat al-Anbiya'. Ibn al-'Arabi said in his book Ahkam al-Qur'an: If it is asked, why was Dawud alarmed when his soul was strengthened by prophethood? He answered that Allah had not guaranteed him protection from harm or from being killed, and he feared these things. Allah had said to Musa, "Do not fear" [al-Qasas: 31], and before that it had been said to Lut. They were given security against fears which had not been declared to them as things from which they were protected. End of quote.

The essence of his answer is that such things happened to the prophets, since they were not protected from suffering harm, until Allah granted one of them security so that he would be at peace. Allah had not granted Dawud security, and therefore he was alarmed. This answer is not fully convincing, because the question contained the questioner's statement that his soul was strengthened by prophethood, and so the questioner based his question on the premise that fear could not reach the souls of the prophets at all. The answer, however, denied that security had been given, and so it did not match the questioner's question.

The proper course would have been to deny in the answer that the prophets were free from the approach of fear. The better answer is as follows.

First: fear is a natural emotion which Allah placed in human nature when confronted with something disagreeable. The souls of human beings are not free from its first signs, so that emotion comes upon them at the very beginning. Then the steadfastness of courage follows and overcomes it through self-control. People's souls differ in how long fear lasts and how quickly it clears. But when Allah grants a prophet security, that is another state, as in His words to Musa, "Do not fear" [al-Qasas: 31], and His words to the Prophet ﷺ, "So Allah will suffice you against them" [al-Baqarah: 137].

Second: what befell Dawud, peace be upon him, was alarm, not fear. Alarm is more general than fear, since it is agitation arising from sensing something whose nature is that one can be freed from it. It has been reported in the hadith of the solar eclipse that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out alarmed (fazi'an)," meaning hastening and rushing to prayer, anticipating that the eclipse might be a warning of punishment. For this reason the Qur'an said "So he was alarmed by them" and did not say "he feared." Concerning Ibrahim, peace be upon him, it said "So he felt a little fear of them" [al-Dhariyat: 28], meaning a sense of apprehension that did not reach the level of fear. As for the litigant's words to Dawud, "Do not fear," this is a statement made by someone arriving in an unfamiliar state which is by nature likely to disturb the observer.

Third: the prophets are commanded to preserve their lives, because their lives are good for the community. A prophet may be alarmed by anticipating a danger, fearing that it might cause his destruction, which would end the benefit of him to his community. It has been reported in the hadith of 'A'ishah that "the Prophet ﷺ could not sleep one night, and he said, 'I wish a righteous man from my companions would guard me tonight.' Then we heard the sound of weapons, and he said, 'Who is this?' He said, 'Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas; I have come to guard you.' She said: The Prophet ﷺ slept until we heard his snoring." It is also narrated by al-Tirmidhi that "al-'Abbas used to guard the Prophet ﷺ until the verse was revealed, 'And Allah will protect you from the people' [al-Ma'idah: 67], and then the guarding was abandoned."

The meaning of "Some of us have wronged some of us" (baghā ba'duna 'ala ba'd) is that he transgressed and oppressed. Al-baghy means injustice. The clause is a qualifier (sifah) of "two disputants," and the connecting element (al-rabit) is the pronoun in "some of us." The pronoun of the speaker is used together with another, in consideration of the meaning of "two disputants."

They did not specify which of the two was the aggressor, because the situation of calming Dawud's fear calls for brevity through generality, followed afterward by detail. It also displays proper manners toward the judge, so that the two do not appoint themselves to identify the aggressor, but leave that to the judge, who identifies the aggressor in his ruling when he says to one of them: "He has certainly wronged you by asking for your ewe to be added to his ewes" [Sad: 24].

The fa' in "So judge between us with truth" is a consequence (tafri') of "two disputants," because Dawud, peace be upon him, was a king, and since the two who came to him were litigants, their request for judgment between them follows from that.

The ba' in "with truth" is for accompaniment (mulabasah) and is connected to "judge." This is a simple request from them for the truth, like the statement of the man to the Prophet ﷺ, whose son had committed adultery with his wife, which was: "Judge between us according to the Book of Allah."

The prohibition in "Do not be unjust" is used for reminding and guidance.

"Tushittu" is the present form of ashatta. One says "ashatta 'alayhi" when he acted unjustly toward him. It is derived from shatat, which means exceeding the limit and the customary measure.

The litigant's address to Dawud in these words is by way of eagerness to make the truth clear. It has the sense of reminding him of what is obligatory. For this reason such words are not counted as rudeness toward the judge or the magistrate. It belongs to the category of "Fear Allah concerning my case." Saying it before the judgment is closer to the sense of reminding and further from rudeness. If it comes after the judgment, it is closer to rudeness, like the man who said to the Prophet ﷺ regarding a division he had made, "Be just!" The Messenger said to him, "Woe to you! Who would be just if I am not just?"

Our scholars have said regarding the litigant's saying to the judge, "Fear Allah concerning my case," that it is not considered rudeness toward the judge, and the judge may not punish him for it as he would punish someone who wronged him. Malik gave a legal opinion to imprison a young man. The young man's father said to Malik, "Fear Allah, O Malik! By Allah, Hell was not created in vain." Malik said, "Among what is vain is what your son has done." This contains an added allusion in response to his words, "By Allah, Hell was not created in vain."

Their words "And guide us to the even path" turn away from the sense of rudeness in their words "and do not be unjust," because they knew that he would say nothing except the truth, and that they were seeking guidance from him.

Guidance here is used metaphorically to mean clarification and making the right course clear.

The "even path" (sawa' al-sirat) is used metaphorically for the truth that is not mixed with falsehood, because the sirat is the broad road, and its sawa' is the one with no twists in it and no branches splitting off from it. It is therefore the quickest in delivering one to the intended goal by its evenness, and furthest from confusion by its freedom from branching.

The whole of "And guide us to the even path" is a parable for the situation of the judge who rules with justice, likened to the situation of a guide who points out the route that leads to the destination. It is therefore among parables whose comparison can be divided into parts. From this it is understood that a just judge's ruling is to be taken as following the truth, and that the ruling must be according to the truth in the sense of the Law, because it is guidance. Thus it and the legal opinion (fatwa) are alike in being guidance, except that a ruling carries obligation.

The meaning of "Make it my charge" (akfilniha) is: place it in my custody, that is, in my keeping. It is a metonymy for giving and gifting, that is, give it to me.

The clause "Indeed this is my brother" through to the end is an explanation of the clause "two disputants, some of us have wronged some of us." Its apparent meaning is that by "brother" they meant brotherhood by lineage. They supposed themselves to be two brothers and posited the dispute as occurring within the dealings of kinship, the bond of blood, and the preservation of ties. Further, "my brother" may be a substitute for the demonstrative, or it may be the predicate of "indeed," and the latter is better because it adds to the enormity of his aggression against him.

"'Azzani" means he overpowered me in speech, that is, he displayed through his words a haughty might against me and an arrogance.

The address is made a container for the might, figuratively, because the address indicated might and dominance. Thus the indicated is placed in the position of what is contained. This is common in usage.

The meaning is: he asked him to give him his ewe, and when he saw resistance from him he pressed him harshly with words and threatened him. The complaining litigant then showed that he was guarding the bonds of kinship, so he complained to the king to restrain him from treating his brother with harshness and arrogance, so that he would take the ewe without goodwill.

Through this it becomes clear that the purpose of this litigation was to seek fairness in the treatment of kinsfolk, lest the disagreement between them lead to attack and thus sever the bonds of kindness and mercy between them.

Dawud knew, from the consecutive sequence of their dispute and from the silence of one of the two litigants, that they were close to what the narrator described of them, or that the defendant had acknowledged it.

So Dawud ruled that the brother's request of his brother for his ewe was an injustice, because the one who asked was in no need of it, while the one asked had no other. The asker's desire for what was in his brother's hand was from excessive greed for wealth.

[Page 236]

and the seeking of benefit for oneself without concern for the other's benefit. This is not the way of mutual affection and fairness between two brothers, so it is injustice. And it is not right that he should ask that: whether he gives it or refuses. Moreover, he was arrogant toward him in speech and rebuked him for not allowing himself to give up the ewe, and this too is injustice.

The genitive in His saying "﴿بِسُؤالِ نَعْجَتِكَ﴾ [Sad: 24]" is for specification, i.e., this particular request concerning a known ewe. That is, this request in its entirety contains injustice. The construction "the asking of [your] ewe" is an idafah of the verbal noun (al-masdar) to its object.

The attaching of "إلى نِعاجِهِ" (to his ewes) to "سُؤالِ" (asking) is by way of implying (tadmin) the meaning of "adding" (ḍamm) to "suʾāl," as if it were said: by requesting the adding of your ewe to his ewes.

This is the answer to their words "﴿فاحْكم بَيْنَنا بِالحَقِّ ولا تُشْطِطْ﴾" (judge between us with truth and do not exceed the bounds), and then he followed it with the answer to their words "﴿واهْدِنا إلى سَواءِ الصِّراطِ﴾" (guide us to the right path), when he said "﴿وإنَّ كَثِيرًا مِنَ الخُلَطاءِ لَيَبْغِي بَعْضُهم عَلى بَعْضٍ إلّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ﴾" [Sad: 24], which indicates that the transgression of one of two associates against the other is widespread among people who are not righteous believers. This is a metaphor for ordering them both to be among the righteous believers, and that what one of them did is not the way of the righteous.

Mentioning the general conditions of associates is intended as an admonition to them both after the judgment between them, in keeping with the practice of people of goodness of seizing opportunities for guidance. So David (peace be upon him) wished to encourage them to adopt the custom of righteous associates and to make injustice and transgression hateful to them.

It is inferred from the context that he (David) grieved over their condition, and that he meant to console the wronged one for what had befallen him from his associate, and that he has an example in most associates.

In concluding his speech with His saying "وقَلِيلٌ ما هم" (and few are they), there is an urging for them both to be among the righteous, because of what is firmly established in souls regarding the preciousness of anything rare. He, the Exalted, said: "﴿قُلْ لا يَسْتَوِي الخَبِيثُ والطَّيِّبُ ولَوْ أعْجَبَكَ كَثْرَةُ الخَبِيثِ﴾" [al-Ma'idah: 100]. The reason for this, from the side of wisdom, is that the motives toward worldly pleasures are many, following desire is loved, and striving against the self is hard to achieve. So a human being is surrounded by attractions to evil deeds, whereas the motives toward truth and perfection are religion and wisdom. Among the means of perfection is turning away from the stimulants of desires, and this turning away is difficult, and none follows it except one who raises his religion and aspiration to spiritual nobility and turns away from the appetitive motive. That is the cause of this judgment of fewness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verses 24–25:

﴿And David realised that We had only tested him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness, fell down bowing and turned in repentance.﴾ ﴿So We forgave him that, and indeed he has near access to Us and a good return.﴾ That is, David came to know, after the dispute had ended, that God had made it a trial for him, so that He would make him aware of the state of his act with Uriyya (Uriyya). What had made him aware of this was the way the two litigants departed in an unusual manner, which indicated to him that they were two angels and that the dispute was a pretence. So he knew that God had sent them to him as a rebuke for following his own desire regarding the wife of Uriyya and for seeking to have her transferred to him.

He expressed this knowledge with the word "realised" (zann) because it is a speculative knowledge (ʿilm naẓarī) that he acquired through discernment (tawassum) of the circumstances of the incident. The speculative knowledge is often expressed by zann, since it resembles zann in that it does not lack some hesitation at first consideration.

The particle "annamā" with an open hamza, a sister of "innamā", indicates restriction (ḥaṣr). That is, he thought that the dispute was nothing but a trial for him, or he thought that what had come from him in marrying the wife of Uriyya was nothing but a trial.

The meaning of "fatannāhu" ("We had tested him") is "We ordained for him a trial". The trial may be in the commonly known sense of devising a stratagem to kill Uriyya, and it was described as a trial because it caused David to act contrary to what was more fitting for him, namely restraining himself from what belonged to another and not following his carnal inclination, even though that was within the permissible sphere in their religion. The meaning then is: he knew that what had come from him was a trial arising from the self (nafs).

He came to know this only after he perceived in himself a dislike of something similar to what the two litigants had depicted for him.

It is also possible that "fatn" means trial and examination, as in His saying, exalted is He, to Moses: ﴿And We tested you with a severe testing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40]. That is, he thought that We had examined his uprightness by sending the two angels, who depicted for him a situation resembling his own act, and so he realised that what he had done was something unbefitting him.

The connection of ﴿so he asked his Lord for forgiveness﴾ to that supposition is evident on both possibilities. That is, when he knew this, he sought forgiveness from his Lord for what he had done.

"Kharra kharūran" means he fell, and it has been mentioned earlier in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the roof fell down on them from above them﴾ [al-Nahl: 26] in Surat al-Nahl.

Rukūʿ (bowing) is bending with the intention of glorification without reaching the ground. He, exalted is He, said ﴿you see them bowing and prostrating﴾ [al-Fath: 29], mentioning two things. It has been said: the Children of Israel did not have prostration upon the ground, but they had bowing (rukūʿ). On this view, restricting the verb "kharra" with the circumstance "rākiʿan" (bowing) is a metaphorical extension (tamajjuz) of the verb "kharra" through the relation of resemblance (ʿalāqat al-mushābaha) [metaphor, majāz: a word used in a non-literal sense because of a link to its literal meaning], to draw attention to the intensity of the bowing, to the point that it approached falling down. Whoever says that the Children of Israel did have prostration takes the application of "rukūʿ" here as a metaphor through the relation of generality (ʿalāqat al-iṭlāq).

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: there is no disagreement that the rukūʿ here is prostration. I say: the disagreement exists.

It is well known that the Children of Israel did not have prostration with the forehead upon the ground. It is possible that prostration was an act of worship of the prophets, just as many of the laws of Islam were specific to the prophets before it, as in the earlier saying of God, exalted is He, ﴿so do not die except as Muslims﴾ [al-Baqara: 132], and as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they fell down before him in prostration﴾ [Yusuf: 100] in Surat Yusuf, which has been mentioned earlier.

David's bowing (rukūʿ), peace be upon him, was an act of humble supplication to God, exalted is He, that He might accept his seeking forgiveness.

"Ināba" means repentance (tawba). It is said anāba and it is said nāba. It has been mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed Abraham was forbearing, plaintive, and turning back in repentance﴾ [Hud: 75] in Surat Hud, and at His saying ﴿turning in repentance to Him﴾ [al-Rum: 31] in Surat al-Rum.

Here is the place of one of the prostrations of the Qur'an, which Mālik counts among the obligatory ones (ʿazāʾim) [obligatory prostrations of recitation], on the basis of the Prophet's prostration there (ﷺ). In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, on the authority of Mujāhid: "I asked Ibn ʿAbbās about the prostration in Ṣād. He said: Do you not recite ﴿And of his offspring, David and Solomon﴾ [al-Anʿam: 84] up to His saying ﴿those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-Anʿam: 90]? David was among those whom your Prophet was commanded to follow. So David prostrated for it, and the Messenger of God prostrated for it." And in the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās: "Ṣād is not among the obligatory prostrations, but I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prostrate in it." And in it also, on the authority of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited while on the pulpit, Ṣād, and when he reached the prostration he descended and prostrated, and the people prostrated with him. Then on another day he recited it, and when he reached the prostration the people stirred to prostrate (i.e., they prepared themselves and moved for it). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "It is only the repentance of a prophet, but I see that you have stirred," so he descended and prostrated, and they prostrated.

Abū Ḥanīfa's view regarding it is the same as Mālik's. Al-Shāfiʿī did not see a prostration in this verse, either because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is only the repentance of a prophet", so its ruling reverted to being the law of those before us, and al-Shāfiʿī does not regard the law of those before us as evidence.

The basis for prostration in it according to those who hold it is that David's bowing is the prostration of their law, so when the Prophet (ﷺ) followed him, he performed in his following what equals the bowing in the law of Islam, which is prostration. Abū Ḥanīfa said: bowing takes the place of the prostration of recitation, deriving this from this verse.

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿So We forgave him that﴾ refers to what the dispute of the two litigants indicated, namely the representation of David's act in the form of the case of the two litigants. This is one of the subtleties of the Qur'an: it omitted the story in which the two litigants appeared to him, then pointed to the omitted matter with the demonstrative. God followed the report of His forgiveness of him with what is higher in rank, namely that he is among those brought near to God, those with whom He is well pleased, and that he was not halted at forgiveness alone.

"Zulfā" means nearness, and it is either a verbal noun or a noun in the place of a verbal noun.

The emphasis of the report (with "inna") serves to remove the suspicion that God became angry with him when He tested him, so the situation of astonishment is treated as the situation of denial.

"Maʾāb" is a noun of place or verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī) in the sense of return (awb), which is coming back. The intended meaning is return to the Hereafter. It is called a return because it is a return to God, that is, to the wisdom of pure truth, outwardly and inwardly. He, exalted is He, said ﴿To Him I call, and to Him is the return﴾ [al-Raʿd: 36].

"Ḥusn al-maʾāb" means a good place of return, that is, that he returns a good return in his own estimation and in the sight of people. That is, he has a good return with Us, and this is an honour with God on the Day of Recompense, namely Paradise, to which he returns.

What had made him aware of this was the way the two litigants departed in an unusual manner, which indicated to him that they were two angels and that the dispute was a pretence. So he knew that God had sent them to him as a rebuke for following his own desire regarding the wife of Uriyya and for seeking to have her transferred to him.

He expressed this knowledge with the word "realised" (zann) because it is a speculative knowledge (ʿilm naẓarī) that he acquired through discernment (tawassum) of the circumstances of the incident. The speculative knowledge is often expressed by zann, since it resembles zann in that it does not lack some hesitation at first consideration.

The particle "annamā" with an open hamza, a sister of "innamā", indicates restriction (ḥaṣr). That is, he thought that the dispute was nothing but a trial for him, or he thought that what had come from him in marrying the wife of Uriyya was nothing but a trial.

The meaning of "fatannāhu" ("We had tested him") is "We ordained for him a trial". The trial may be in the commonly known sense of devising a stratagem to kill Uriyya, and it was described as a trial because it caused David to act contrary to what was more fitting for him, namely restraining himself from what belonged to another and not following his carnal inclination, even though that was within the permissible sphere in their religion. The meaning then is: he knew that what had come from him was a trial arising from the self (nafs).

He came to know this only after he perceived in himself a dislike of something similar to what the two litigants had depicted for him.

It is also possible that "fatn" means trial and examination, as in His saying, exalted is He, to Moses: ﴿And We tested you with a severe testing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40].
