Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 26:

﴿O Dawud, indeed We have made you a khalifah (vicegerent) upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth, and do not follow desire, for it will lead you astray from the way of Allah. Indeed, those who stray from the way of Allah will have a severe punishment for having forgotten the Day of Reckoning.﴾ This is a continuation of a omitted speech ("qawl") coordinated with ﴿So We forgave him that﴾ [Sad: 25]; that is, We pardoned him, reminded him of the blessing of kingship, and admonished him. By this He combined for him an honouring of his station and guidance toward what is obligatory.

The opening of the address with the vocative is to capture his attention and his attentiveness to what will be said to him.

The khalifah (vicegerent) is one who succeeds another in a task, that is, stands in his place in it. If it occurs while the one succeeded is still present, it is said: "He is the khalifah of so-and-so"; and if it occurs after the one succeeded has passed away, it is said: "He is a khalifah from so-and-so." The meaning intended here is the first, as indicated by His saying ﴿so judge between the people in truth﴾.

So the meaning is: he is the vicegerent of Allah in executing His laws among the community to which he has been made a vicegerent, by what is revealed to him and by what of the earlier Law revealed to him he is to act upon. And he is a successor to Musa (peace be upon him) and to the earlier rabbis of the Children of Israel, who were called judges; or he is a successor to the one who preceded him in kingship, namely Saul.

And "the earth" is the earth of his known kingdom, that is, We made you a vicegerent over the land of Israel.

It is permissible to take "the earth" as meaning the whole earth, for Dawud in his time was the greatest of the kings of the earth; he disposed of his kingdom, and the kings of the earth feared his might, so he was the vicegerent of Allah on earth, since nothing escapes his grip. This is close to the sense of khilafah in His saying, ﴿Then We made you successors in the earth after them﴾ [Yunus: 14], and His saying ﴿and makes you successors of the earth﴾ [al-Naml: 62].

This meaning differs from the meaning of His saying, ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I will make upon the earth a khalifah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], for the earth there is this terrestrial globe. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The phrase khalifat Allah is not used except for His Messenger ﷺ. As for the khulafa', each one of them is the khalifah of the one before him." Do you not see that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, clarified this meaning, so they said to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "O khalifah of the Messenger of Allah," and by this he was called so during his lifetime. When 'Umar came to office they said: "O khalifah of the khalifah of the Messenger of Allah," and it grew long; and they saw that it would grow longer in the future if another khalifah came after 'Umar, so they called 'Umar "Amir al-Mu'minin" (Commander of the Faithful), and this was restricted to the caliphs. As for what comes in poetry of calling one of the caliphs "khalifat Allah," that is a figurative usage, as Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

"The khalifah of Allah among His creatures; the pens have dried and the books [have been completed] with that."

And the consequence of making him a khalifah is his being commanded to judge between the people in truth, to indicate that this is his duty, and that he is the most entitled of people to judge with justice. That is because he is the one to whom the wronged return, and to whom the injustices of oppressive governors are brought. If he is just, the governors and commanders fear him, because he is accustomed to justice and dislikes injustice; so he does not permit what occurs from them among his subjects whenever it reaches him, and the people are wary lest what might come from them be raised to the khalifah and he exact retribution from the oppressor. But if the khalifah himself oppresses in his judgment, he becomes accustomed to injustice, so he is not angered when the grievance of any person is raised to him, and he does not strive to give the wronged his right.

In al-Kashshaf: that one of the Umayyad caliphs said to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, or to al-Zuhri: "Have you heard what has reached us?" He said: "And what is it?" He said: "It has reached us that the khalifah is not subject to the pen, and no disobedience is recorded for him." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, are the caliphs more excellent or the prophets?" Then he recited this verse.

By "the people" is meant the people of his kingdom, so the definite article is for a known reference or for customary generality.

And "the truth" is what the lawful justice requires regarding the dealings of people with one another and their conduct in their private and public affairs; the truth is determined by the determination of the Law.

The ba' in "bil-haqq" is the ba' of instrumentality: truth is made like the tool with which the agent works, as in your saying: "He cut it with the knife," and "He struck him with the staff."

His saying ﴿and do not follow desire﴾ is coordinated with the consequence, and perhaps this is the intended purpose of the consequence. The command to judge with truth precedes it so that it serves as a preparation for the prohibition against following desire, blocking the means to falling into error regarding the truth; for Dawud was among those who judged with truth, so he was commanded with it in view of the future.

The definite article in "al-hawa" (desire) is the definite article of the genus, which conveys generality, so the prohibition encompasses everything that is desire, whether it is the desire of the addressee or the desire of others, such as the desire of his wife, his child, his master, his friend, or the desire of the masses: ﴿They said, "O Musa, make for us a god just as they have gods." He said, "Indeed you are a people who are ignorant"﴾ [al-A'raf: 138].

The meaning of hawa is love, and it is applied to the beloved thing by way of hyperbole, that is, even if it is a strong desire to which the soul clings.

Hawa is a metaphor (kinayah) for falsehood, deviation and injustice, because of what is commonly known of the close connection between these matters and the desires of souls; for justice and equity are heavy upon souls, so they generally do not desire them; and whoever has the love of truth as a disposition has been given knowledge and wisdom and been supported with preservation or infallibility.

The prohibition against following desire is a warning to him and an awakening, so that he may be wary of the consequences of desire, suspect his own desire, scrutinize it, and not yield to it except after reflection and verification. Sahl ibn Hunayf, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Suspect opinion." That is because the desire of the soul is in matters that are easy for it and agreeable to it, whereas most perfections are difficult for the soul, because they return to refining the soul and elevating it from the lowliness of animality to the summit of angelic nature. So in all of them, or most of them, there is a turning of the soul away from the physical appetites that have clung to it, most of which return to the nature of animality, because the soul is either summoned by the call of appetite or the call of anger; so indulging in following them is generally a fall into vices. For this reason, here, straying from the way of Allah is made the consequence of following desire, and this is a customary, predominant causation. He likened desire to a traveller on a path of destruction by way of metaphorical comparison (makniyyah), and he indicated it by its necessary concomitant, namely misguidance from the path of rectitude, expressed as the way of Allah; for one who follows a traveller without knowing the path to beneficial stations will soon find himself and his companion in a place of ruin or a cut-off road.

Following desire may be by choice, and it may be under compulsion. The prohibition against it requires the prohibition against all its kinds. As for choosing to follow it, caution against it is evident; as for following it under compulsion, deliverance from it is by withdrawing from what led to the compulsion. For this reason the scholars stipulated conditions for the khalifah, all of which revolve around preventing him from following desire and what is equivalent to it of falling into falsehood; these are: legal responsibility (taklif), freedom, justice, being male; and as for the condition that he be of Quraysh according to the majority, it is so that he not be weakened before the tribes by disparagement.

The phrase ﴿fa-yudillaka﴾ is in the subjunctive after the fa' of causation, in response to the prohibition. The meaning of the response to a prohibition is the response of the thing forbidden; so it is the cause of misguidance, and the prohibition is not itself the cause of misguidance. This differs from the method of the jussive in response to a prohibition.

The way of Allah: the actions through which His pleasure is obtained, which are the actions Allah commanded and promised reward for, likened to the path that leads to Allah, that is, to His pleasure. The clause ﴿Indeed those who stray from the way of Allah﴾ to its end appears to be part of what Allah addressed to Dawud; according to those who count verses, it is one verse from His saying ﴿O Dawud, indeed We have made you a khalifah upon the earth﴾ up to "the Day of Reckoning." It is thus in the position of the reason for the prohibition, so the particle "inna" served in place of the fa' of causation and consequence. Whatever leads to severe punishment is worthy of being forbidden. If the clause is a statement separate from the address to Dawud, then it is parenthetical and resumptive, a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) to explain the gravity of straying from the way of Allah.

The generality in His saying ﴿those who stray from the way of Allah﴾ gives the clause the character of a concluding generalization (tadhyil) as well, and both considerations require that it not be coordinated.

The relative pronoun is used to indicate that the relative clause is the cause for deserving punishment. The lam in "lahum adhab" is for specification, and the ba' in ﴿bima nasu yawm al-hisab﴾ is causal.

The ma is verbal-masdarial, that is, "because of their forgetting the Day of Reckoning," and the ba' is attached to the stability (istiqrar) that the prepositional phrase in "lahum adhab" stands in for.

Forgetting (nisyan) is used metaphorically for severe aversion, because it resembles the forgetting of one who turns away from something, as in His saying ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67]. It has degrees, the most severe of which is denying the resurrection and recompense, as He said: ﴿So taste [the punishment] for having forgotten the meeting of this your day; indeed We have forgotten you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 14]. Below it are many degrees, corresponding to the degrees of punishment, for when the cause has degrees, the consequences follow accordingly.

The Day of Reckoning here means what occurs on it of recompense for good and evil; so it is, in meaning, with an implied genitive: the recompense of the Day of Reckoning, in the manner of His saying ﴿and forgets what his hands have sent forward﴾ [al-Kahf: 57], that is, he does not reflect on the outcome of the deeds he sends forward.

In making straying from the way of Allah and forgetting the Day of Reckoning two causes for deserving severe punishment, there is an indication of their mutual connection, for straying from the way of Allah leads to turning away from heeding the recompense.

The biography of Dawud has already been given at His saying ﴿and of his offspring, Dawud﴾ [al-An'am: 84] in al-An'am, and at His saying ﴿and We gave Dawud the Psalms﴾ [al-Nisa': 163] in al-Nisa'.

﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire.﴾ When mention of forgetting the Day of Reckoning had occurred in the address to Dawud, and the most extreme form of that forgetting is denying that it will occur, since that leads to never observing or being mindful of it, three verses were inserted between the two stories to explain the wisdom of God, exalted is He, in establishing recompense and its Day, as an argument against the polytheists who deny it.

"Al-batil" is the opposite of "al-haqq" (truth). Everything that is not true is "al-batil." For this reason, God, exalted is He, says in another verse: ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ (Surah al-Dukhan 44:39).

The meaning of "al-haqq," derived from the negation of "al-batil" here, is that those creatures were created in a state that does not depart from the truth. This is either in their present state, as with the creation of the angels, the messengers, and the righteous, or in their final outcome, as with the creation of the devils and the corrupters, because establishing recompense for them comes after a corrective response to what truth requires.

This argument is built on reasoning from observable matters, namely the conditions of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. The polytheists know that God is the Creator of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. So the proof is established on the basis of a premise that is not disputed: that God created that, and that if they reflect even slightly, they find in the order of these worlds a clear indication, obtained with minimal reflection, that it is an order of the utmost precision, consistently maintained. This is what God alerted them to with His words: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in vain.﴾

The point of the negation is the circumstantial phrase, His words "in vain" ("batilan"), and it is general because it falls within the context of negation. Deep reflection makes the observer aware that their Creator is wise and just, and that the actions of an agent can be used to infer from the apparent what is hidden. Those who have become accustomed to judging only by what is observed, and not going beyond it, have a duty to reason from what is hidden to them by analogy with what is observed to them. Since it is established that the order of the heavens and the earth and what is between them proceeds according to the requirements of wisdom and perfect order, they must reflect on what is hidden from them, namely the occurrence of resurrection and recompense. All that is on earth proceeds according to a wondrous order, except the deeds of humans. It is known by observation that among people there are righteous and beneficial ones, and among them are those lower than that, down to the category of criminals and corrupters. Also, many of the righteous have obtained little or none of the worldly goods of pleasure, or only a small amount, less than what their righteousness deserves and less than what they strove for in elevating themselves toward the heights of perfection. And among the corrupters are some who are the opposite of this.

Corruption (al-fasad) is a disorder that a person brings upon himself by following his desires, through the choice God placed within him, and through his inner faculties. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature, then We reduced him to the lowest of the low, except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ (Surah al-Tin 95:4). Through these levels, people draw near either gradually to the ranks of the angels, or hang down toward the abodes of the devils. Divine wisdom therefore requires that each group be joined with its like in eternal bliss or everlasting Hellfire.

Had it not been that the wisdom of the order of creation required that a barrier be placed between the transient worlds and the everlasting worlds for the period determined for the survival of the latter, God would have lifted the righteous to the summit of everlasting bliss and thrust the criminals into the depths of perpetual blaze. This is for many reasons, the sum of which requires preserving the properties of created beings until they fulfil the functions for which they were created. These properties may conflict, so if one of them were given preference over another for survival, the other would perish. Thus God enabled each kind and each category to strive for what suits it, guided all of them to good, commanded and forbade, explained and set limits.

And He made, after this transient world, another eternal world in which the existence of the categories is surrounded by what their perfections and their opposites deserve, whether good or evil. Had God not made the eternal world, the righteousness of the righteous would be lost in vain, since they strove with their souls and lost, in attaining it, a great deal of their transient pleasures without any return. The corruption of the corrupters would turn into a gain by which they satisfied their desires and attained their aims, so what they inflicted on people of harms would be lost in vain. Therefore, without the eternal recompense, the creation of the earth would indeed become vain, and the one who goes astray would triumph in his misguidance.

Once this premise is established, it becomes clear that denying resurrection and recompense entails that the denier must hold that the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them is some part of vanity. Other proofs have shown that there is no vanity at all in the creation of these things, by analogizing the hidden to the apparent. Thus what leads to the claim that there is some vanity in the creation of some of what has been mentioned is refuted.

Although the polytheists did not themselves say this, nor believe it, they are bound to it by way of implicit implication (dalalat al-iltizam), because whoever denies resurrection and recompense has thereby committed himself to the view that what proceeds in human affairs is vain. Humans are part of God's creation, so their vanity, if their Creator does not hold them accountable for it, is among what their Creator has permitted. Thus there would be some vanity in the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and the universal statement of His words ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ would be contradicted. This is what His words ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾ impose upon them. The demonstrative refers to the proposition that was negated, not to its negation. That is, the creation of the things mentioned as vain is the assumption of those who disbelieve, meaning their belief. "Assumption" (zann) is applied to knowledge, because their assumption is a knowledge that contradicts reality, so the term "assumption" is more appropriate for it, since the word "assumption" covers types of knowledge that are similar to it and are false.

In this verse is evidence that the implication of a statement is considered a statement, and that the implication of a doctrine is a doctrine. This is the principle that the Maliki jurists (fuqaha' al-Malikiyya) adopted regarding the grounds of apostasy (riddah), in the form of statements and actions.

He based on this argument, and on the polytheists' failure to act according to its requirement, His words ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾, that is, the Fire of Hell. They are referred to by the relative pronoun because the relative clause indicates that they deserved punishment for their bad belief and bad deeds, and that this too is one of the consequences of the negation of vanity from the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. For they were in error by turning away from reasoning from the order of the heavens and the earth, and by committing the corruptions of the customs and creed of polytheism. They enjoyed the life of this world more than the righteous did, so they rightly deserved the recompense of their deeds.

The word "woe" (waylun) denotes the utmost evil. The expression "woe to him" is used to express amazement at the severity of the bad condition of the one spoken of, and here it is a metaphor for the severity of their punishment in the Fire. The "min" (from) is initial (ibtida'iyya), as in His words ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah 2:79), and as in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Ibn al-Zubayr when he drank the blood of his cupping: "Woe to you from people, and woe to people from you."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 28:

﴿Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds as equal to those who spread corruption in the earth? Or shall We treat the God-conscious as equal to the wicked?﴾ (Am) here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), indicating a transitional turn (idrab intiqali), which is an escalation in the argument for the establishment of the Resurrection and an explanation of what follows from the creation of the heavens and the earth with truth, after this had been presented in the form of a general (jumli) argument. This transition was based on what was implied by His saying ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾ [Sad: 27]. Therefore, an implied interrogative was constructed after (am), which is a necessary consequence of its usage, and it is a rejecting (inkari) interrogative.

The meaning: If the Resurrection and recompense were absent, as you claim, then the conditions of the righteous and the conditions of the corruptors would be equal in the sight of God.

The comparison in His saying "as the corruptors" is for equalization. The meaning: a denial that they would be equal in God's making, that is, if He does not recompense each group according to what it deserves for its deeds. What is witnessed in this worldly life is contrary to that, so it is determined that the recompense must be in another world, which is the one people will enter after the Resurrection.

The argument has addressed the aspect of equality between those who believe and do righteous deeds and the corruptors in the earth, because many of both groups are equal in the state of worldly life, in blessing, in moderation, or in misery and poverty. Thus the state of equality is sufficient to be the basis of the argument for nullifying the assumption of those who disbelieve, setting aside another state that is more indicative, namely the contrast between the corruptors who enjoy blessing and the righteous who suffer misery, and setting aside a state below that, namely the corruptors who are in misery and poverty and the righteous who enjoy blessing, because it does not draw the attention of the observer.

Page 250

The second (am) is also disjunctive, and its implication is a second transitional turn (idrab intiqali) for escalation in the argument that the divine wisdom, by considering truth and the absence of falsehood in creation, requires recompense and resurrection for its sake.

The meaning of the interrogative required by the second (am) is rejection, like that required by the first (am).

This escalation in the argument aims to increase the reproach against those who deny the Resurrection and recompense, on the grounds that their assumption requires that God has made the God-conscious equal to the wicked in the conditions of the existence of both groups, and it confirms this in the same way as the first argument was established.

The God-conscious (al-muttaqun) are those whose emblem was God-consciousness (taqwa). Taqwa is the constant adherence to carrying out what is commanded and avoiding what is prohibited, outwardly and inwardly, and it has been discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

The wicked (al-fujjar) are those whose emblem is wickedness (fujur), which is the most severe disobedience. What is meant by it is disbelief and its deeds, which do not restrain their doers from God-consciousness, as in His saying ﴿Those are the disbelievers, the wicked﴾ [Abasa: 42]. A detailed explanation of this has preceded at His saying ﴿Indeed, He originates creation and then repeats it that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice; but those who disbelieved will have a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment for what they used to deny﴾ [Yunus: 4], ﴿It is He who made the sun a shining light﴾ [Yunus: 5] up to His saying ﴿God did not create that except in truth﴾ [Yunus: 5].

The purpose of this elaboration is to increase the terror and severity directed at those who assumed an assumption that leads to the claim that God created something of the heavens and the earth and what is between them in vain. In moving from the evidence of the weaker to the evidence of the stronger, and in repeating the particle of denial, there is a great matter of exposing the affair of the astray.

A Book We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may ponder its verses, and that those of understanding may take heed. (Q. 38:29)

Following the intensified warning to the polytheists and the charge of ignorance against them for turning away from reflection, with the wisdom of recompense and the Day of Reckoning, and the argument against them, God turned away from addressing them and directed the address to the Prophet ﷺ, praising the Book revealed to him. This Qur'an had already made clear to them what is in it: for them a source of persuasion, and an argument that uproots their doubts. And if the polytheists deprived themselves of benefiting from it, those of understanding have benefited from it, namely the believers. In this there is an incidental (idmaj) expression of pride in this Book for the one to whom it was sent down, and for those among the believers who hold fast to it and are guided by its guidance.

This is similar to His saying, Exalted is He, after the mention of the creation of the sun and the moon: ﴿God did not create that except with truth﴾ [Yunus: 5], ﴿We detail the signs for a people who know﴾, at the beginning of Surat Yunus.

The sentence is an intervening resumptive clause (isti'naf mu'taridh), and in this resumption there is a reference back to His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ [Sad: 1], a renewed emphasis on the status of the Qur'an, as this will be repeated in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿This is a reminder﴾.

Regarding His saying "Kitab" (a Book): it may be the predicate of an omitted subject, the sense being: "This is a Book," and the clause "anzalnahu" (We have sent it down) is an attributive description of "kitab," and it may be a subject, with the clause "anzalnahu" as a description of "kitab," and "mubarak" (blessed) as the predicate about "kitab."

The indefiniteness of "kitab" is for magnification, because the Book is known; its being indefinite is only to magnify its status. It is a subject, and what permitted its being a subject is its being described by the clause "anzalnahu," and "mubarak" is the predicate. You may also make the sense of magnification in the indefiniteness the justification for its being a subject, and make the clause "anzalnahu" a first predicate, "mubarak" a second predicate, and "li-yaddabbaru" (that they may ponder) connected to "anzalnahu." But "kitab" should not be made the predicate of an omitted subject, so that you would estimate "This is a Book," since this is not a significant point of eloquence (balaghah).

The "mubarak" (blessed) is that in which blessing (barakah) is diffused, and barakah is abundant good. Every verse of the Qur'an is blessed, because they are either guiding to good or turning away from evil and corruption, and that is the cause of good in this world and the next, and there is no blessing greater than that.

الصفحة ٢٥٢
Tadabbur (pondering) is reflection and contemplation by which its doer reaches knowledge of the intended meanings. This occurs only in speech that is brief in wording but rich in the meanings deposited within it, such that whenever the one pondering reflects further, meanings are unveiled to him that were not evident at first glance. The closest example of tadabbur here is what passed a moment ago of the meanings of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ up to His saying ﴿Shall We make those who are mindful like the wicked?﴾, and it was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Do they not ponder the Qur'an?﴾ [An-Nisa: 82] in Surat an-Nisa.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "﴿li-yaddabbaru﴾" with the ya' of the third person and the doubling of the dal.

The original form of "yaddabbaru" is "yatadabbaru," the ta' was changed to dal because their articulation points are close, so that assimilation (idgham) could take place for lightness; it is a form of effort (tukallaf) derived from the verb dabara, on the pattern of darabe, meaning "to follow," so "tadabbarahu" is equivalent to "tatabba'ahu." Its meaning is that one pursues the outward forms of the words to know what their outward forms lead to of hidden meanings and fitting interpretations. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Have they not pondered the word?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 68] in Surat al-Mu'minun.

Abu Ja'far read "﴿li-tadabbaru﴾" with the ta' of address and lightening of the dal; its original form is "litatadabbaru," and one of the two ta's was deleted for brevity. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ and those Muslims with him.

Tadhakkur (remembrance) is the mind's recalling what it already knew, whether by recalling what has been forgotten or by recalling what should not be neglected and what matters to knowledge. So the Qur'an was given to people that they might ponder its meanings and uncover its obscurities to the extent of their capacity, for across successive generations of its scholars they never reach an end of its hidden contents; and so that they might remember the verse by its parallel and what is close to it, and that they might remember what is an admonition to them and a waker from their heedlessness.

On the reading of the majority, the pronoun in "yaddabbaru" refers to "ulu al-albab" (people of understanding), by way of the omitted verb which is left unsatisfied by the operation of the verb in the construction of dependence (tanazu'), and the sense is: "that the people of understanding may ponder its verses and remember." As for the reading of Abu Ja'far, attributing "yatadhakkara" to "ulu al-albab" is sufficient in place of describing the ones who ponder as "ulu al-albab," because pondering leads to remembrance, and remembrance is among the effects of pondering, so describing the doer of one of the two verbs suffices in place of describing the doer of the other.

الصفحة ٢٥٣
Ulu al-albab are the people of intellects. In it there is an allusion that those who do not remember through the Qur'an are not among the people of intellect, and that remembrance is a trait of the Muslims who listen to speech and follow the best of it. They are among those who ponder its verses and derive from it meanings they did not know, and whoever reads it and is reminded by it of what he already knew, and is reminded by it of a truth he is obliged to uphold. The disbelievers turned away from pondering, so inevitably remembrance escaped them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 30:

﴿And We bestowed upon David Solomon. How excellent a servant! Indeed, he was ever oft-turning (to Allah).﴾ The transition to the virtues of Solomon (peace be upon him) is made on the basis that he was among the favours of Allah upon David (peace be upon him), so the story of Solomon serves as a complement to the story of David. The state of Solomon (peace be upon him) bears no resemblance to the state of Muhammad (ﷺ); therefore we affirm that the mention of his story here is not an example for the state of Muhammad (ﷺ), but rather a completion of what Allah bestowed upon David, when He gave him Solomon as a son, a delight to him in his lifetime and an heir to his kingdom after his death, as His saying the Exalted indicates: ﴿And We bestowed upon David Solomon﴾, and so on.

For this reason the story of Solomon was not introduced with the phrase "and mention" (wadhkur), as the stories of David and then Job were introduced, while the narratives that follow them, detailed and summarized, are, nonetheless, not devoid of places of exemplary conduct, lessons and warning, in accordance with the Qur'an's habit of presenting guidance.

It is a fitting connection to mention the gift of Solomon that he was born to David from the woman about whom David was rebuked for seeking to take her husband Uriah (Uriyya) from her, as has been previously mentioned. Thus Solomon's being given to David from her was a great honour, the result of Allah's forgiveness to David for that transgression, which his station required him to avoid even though it was permissible. This is confirmed by the report about his forgiveness being followed by His saying: ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a nearness and a good return﴾ [Sad: 25]. So Allah was pleased with him, and bestowed upon him from that wife a prophet and a great king.

The clause ﴿And We bestowed upon David Solomon﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to the clause "Indeed, We subjected the mountains to exalt with him" and the clauses that follow it.

The clause "how excellent a servant" (ni'ma al-'abd) is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to Solomon, and it is a praise and commendation of him from among those who merited the title of "servant of Allah." This is the title intended for proximity through context, as previously mentioned in His saying the Exalted: ﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ [As-Saffat: 40] ﴿For them is a known provision﴾ [As-Saffat: 41] in Surat As-Saffat.

The one specified for praise is omitted, because of the indication of what precedes it, namely His saying "Solomon," and the estimate is: "How excellent a servant is Solomon."

The clause "indeed, he was ever oft-turning" (innahu awwab) is a justification for the praise of him with "how excellent a servant." Awwab is an intensive form of aayib, meaning one who returns much, i.e., returns to Allah, as indicated by the context that he is the one praising him. What is meant by returning to Allah is returning to His commands and prohibitions: whenever something occurs that would distance him from that, he remembers and returns (fa-ab), i.e., repents (fa-tab), and this was previously mentioned in the discussion of David.

[Page 255]

﴿When there were displayed before him at evening the poised, swift-footed, noble steeds﴾ ﴿he said, "Indeed, I have loved the good things [of this world] over the remembrance of my Lord, until they were hidden behind the veil."﴾ ﴿"Bring them back to me." Then he began to pass his hand over their shins and necks.﴾

"When there was displayed" (idh ʿuriḍa) is attached to "one who turns back constantly" (awwāb). Attaching this adverbial phrase (ẓarf) to awwāb is a attachment of causation (taʿlīl), because adverbial phrases are often used to express causation. It is evident that the intended meaning is not that he turned back constantly only in this story, since the form awwāb implies intensity (mubālagha), whose basic sense is abundance. Therefore it is determined that the mention of this story, one of the incidents of his turning back, was because in it the greatness of his turning back becomes clear.

"Displayed" (al-ʿarḍ) means passing [the horses] and bringing them forward before the one who sees them, i.e., he reviewed his horse-handlers' horses before him.

"Evening" (al-ʿashiyy) is from the afternoon until sunset. It was mentioned in His words "in the morning and the evening" in Surat al-Anʿam. It is the time for inspecting horses and livestock after they return from their pastures and grazing grounds. The mention of evening here is not merely for specifying time, but so that His words "until they were hidden behind the veil" may be built upon it. So the mention of evening in this verse does not have the same effect as it has in the words of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

"Kings from the Banu Jusham ibn Bakr, who are driven at evening and killed."

"The poised" (al-ṣāfināt) is a description of an omitted noun that has been dispensed with, because the attribute indicates it, since the ṣāfin (one who stands poised) is only found among horses and steeds. It is the one that stands on three legs, with the tip of the hoof of the fourth leg touching the ground without putting weight on it. This is one of the signs of its lightness, which indicates the nobility of the horse's stock and the goodness of its qualities. It is said: "The horse stood poised" (ṣafana al-furs ṣufūnan). Ibn al-Aʿrabi and al-Zajjaj recited, in describing a horse:

"It has become accustomed to standing poised, so that it seems ∗∗∗ as if, from what it does standing on three [legs], it is lame."

"The swift" (al-jiyād) is the plural of jawād (with a fatḥa on the wāw), which is a horse of excellence, i.e., of nobility. Sulayman was devoted to increasing the number of horses and horsemen, so his horses were counted in the thousands.

The original structure of "I have loved the love of the good" was "I have loved the good, a love," and the structure was changed to "I have loved the love of the good," so "the love of the good" became a specification (tamyīz) for attributing the relation of love to himself, for the purpose of generality followed by detail, like His words, exalted is He, "and We caused the earth to burst forth with springs" and the words of Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr:

"How excellent is she as a companion..."

and the saying: "How excellent is his horsemanship!"

"I have loved" (aḥbabtu) is used with the implied meaning of "I have exchanged" (ʿawwaḍtu), so it takes "from" (ʿan) in His words "from the remembrance of my Lord." So the meaning becomes: "I have loved the good, a love, so I have passed beyond the remembrance of my Lord."

By "the remembrance of the Lord" is meant the prayer. Perhaps it was a prayer that he had established for himself, since in the evening time there is no obligatory prayer in the law of Musa except the maghrib (sunset prayer).

"The good" (al-khayr) means precious wealth, as in His words, exalted is He, "if he leaves behind good" [al-Baqara: 180], and horses are among precious wealth. Al-Farraʾ said: "The good with the letter rāʾ is one of the names of horses." The Arabs interchange the letters lām and rāʾ, as they say: "the eye poured forth" (inhamalat) and "flowed" (inhamarat). Also "khatala" and "khatara" when one deceives.

[Page 256]

I say: It is among the habits of the Arabs to seek omens (tafāʾul), and they had a great concern with horses, to the extent that they described their markings and believed they indicated good fortune or misfortune. Perhaps they called them "the good" as an omen, so that they would be purely associated with happiness and good fortune.

The pronoun in "they were hidden" (tawārat) refers to the sun, by the indication of the mention of evening, the particle of limit, and the word "veil," and also because the pronoun referring to the sun in mentioning times is frequent in their speech, as Labid said:

"Until, when it cast a hand into the unbeliever [i.e., the darkness], and its darkness concealed the nakedness of the frontiers..."

That is, the sun cast its hand into the darkness, i.e., it cast itself into it. This is an expression of the self by one of its parts.

"Hiding" (tawārī) is concealment. "Veil" (ḥijāb) is a screen in the house behind which a woman and others hide. From this is the saying of Anas ibn Malik: "So God revealed the verse of the veil."

The statement is an allegory (tamthīl) for the state of the sun's setting by the hiding of a woman behind a veil, and each part of this allegory is metaphorical. For the sun, a woman is borrowed in the manner of an implicit metaphor (makniyya); for its disappearance from sight, the word "hiding" is borrowed; and for the horizon of the sun's setting, the word "veil" is borrowed.

The meaning: his horses, the poised and swift, were displayed before him, and he occupied himself with their conditions out of love for them, until the sun set, and so he missed a prayer that he used to perform in the evening before sunset. So after the horses were displayed and had gone away, he said: "I have loved the horses and so I neglected my prayer to God."

His statement is a report used to express regret, like the words of the mother of Mary: "My Lord, I have given birth to her as a female" [Āl ʿImrān: 36].

The address in His words "Bring them back to me" is to the handlers of his horses. The pronoun in the accusative refers to the horses by indication, i.e., "return the horses to me." It was also said that it refers to the sun and the address is to the angels, but this is extremely remote, and were it not for its frequent mention in the books of the exegetes, it would be better for us not to address it. More preferable than this, according to this view regarding the referent of the third-person pronoun, is that the command is used to express incapacity, i.e., "Can you bring back the sun after its setting?", like the words of Muhalhil:

[Page 257]

"O Bakr, bring back Kulayb to me!"

and the words of al-Harith al-Dabbi, one of the companions of the Camel [battle]:

"Return to us our shaykh, then he will be honored."

He means ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may God be pleased with him. So there is no improbability in this interpretation.

The fāʾ in His words "then he began" (faṭafiqa) is consequential (taʿqībiyya), and ṭafiqa is one of the verbs of beginning, i.e., "then he began."

"Passing" (maswan) is a verbal noun standing in the place of the verb, i.e., he began to pass his hand (yamsaḥu maswan). The definite article in "the shins and the necks" is a replacement for the omitted genitive, i.e., "their shins and their necks," like His words, exalted is He, "for indeed the Garden is the refuge" [al-Nāziʿāt: 41].

The primary meaning of masḥ (passing) is passing the hand over a thing to remove what is upon it, such as dust, water, or dirt, or anything else whose presence is not desired on the thing. It is done with the hand or with a cloth or garment. The word masḥ is sometimes used metaphorically for other meanings, among which is striking with a sword; it is said: "he wiped him with the sword," and "he wiped the sword with it." Perhaps its original meaning is a metonymy for killing by the sword, because the sword is wiped of blood after striking with it.

"Shins" (al-sūq) is the plural of sāq. The majority of readers recited it with a silent wāw and in the pattern fuʿl, like dār and dūr, and the pattern fuʿl in the plural of a similar word is rare. Qunbul from Ibn Kathir and Abu Jaʿfar recited "al-suʾq" with a silent hamza after the sīn, the plural of sa'q with a hamza after the sīn, and this is a dialect of sāq.

"Necks" (al-aʿnāq) is the plural of ʿunuq, which is the neck.

The bāʾ in "with the shins" is superfluous (zāʾida) for emphasis, i.e., to emphasize the connection of the verb with its object, like that in His words, exalted is He, "and wipe your heads" [al-Māʾida: 6], and in the words of al-Nabigha:

"To you is the good, if the earth covers you, a single one, ∗∗∗ and the grandfather of the people is stumbling, straining [to rise]."

The exegetes have disagreed about the meaning intended by His words "then he began passing [his hand] over the shins and necks." According to Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Zuhri, Ibn Kaysan, and Qutrub: he began to pass his hand over the manes of the horses and their shins, out of love for them. This is the interpretation that accords with the station of a prophet and is most in keeping with the reality of [the word] masḥ, but it requires placing the sequence of the sentences contrary to what the apparent sense demands: namely, that His words "Bring them back to me, then he began passing [his hand] over the shins and necks" are connected to His words "when there were displayed before him at evening the poised..." — that is, after he had reviewed them and they had turned away with them to return to their stables, he said: "Bring them back to me," and then he began passing [his hand] over the shins and necks, honoring them and out of love for them. And His words "he said, 'Indeed, I have loved the love of the good over the remembrance of my Lord, until they were hidden behind the veil'" would be placed as an interjection between them. It was placed first only to hasten the mention of his regret over his neglect of the remembrance of God at a time of remembrance. That is, he did not become absorbed in forgetfulness; rather he hastened to remember as soon as the time of remembrance that he was accustomed to had passed. For it is not fitting, according to this interpretation, that His words "Bring them back to me, then he began" etc. be a consequence of his regret and grief. This indicates that the passing of the time of his remembrance resulted from that returning which he commanded by His words "Bring them back to me," for they were accustomed to display them before him and then depart while there remained enough time for remembrance. When his delight in them moved him to command their return and to busy himself with passing his hand over their necks and shins, the time of his remembrance went out, and so he regretted and grieved.

From al-Hasan, Qatada, and Malik ibn Anas, in the narration of Ibn Wahb, and from al-Farraʾ and Tha'lab: when Sulayman regretted his preoccupation with the horses, to the point that he neglected the remembrance of God at a time when he used to remember God, he commanded that the horses that had distracted him be returned to him. He then began to hamstring their shins and cut their necks, depriving himself of them despite his love for them, as repentance and as training for his soul. They sensed that this was corruption in the earth and a waste of wealth, so they answered: he intended to slaughter them so that the poor could eat them, since eating horses is permissible among them, and thus slaughtering them was not corruption in the earth.

Some avoided this view and made the masḥ a metaphor for branding the horses dedicated to the cause of God with a branding iron or by scraping the skin, because that removes the thin layer on the surface of the skin. That removal was likened to the removal done by wiping, which removes what is stuck to the surface of the thing wiped. This is safer from objection than the first view. It is attributed to some exegetes in Ibn al-ʿArabi's Aḥkām al-Qurʾān, and Ibn al-ʿArabi said: it is an error. This is a noble method of training the soul and a manifestation of the perfection of repentance regarding what was the cause of the lapse.

On these two interpretations, the statement "then he began" is a consequence of "Bring them back to me," and of an omitted element after it. The estimated sense is: "so they brought them back to him, and he began," like His words, "Strike the sea with your staff," [and] "so it split" [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 63]. Then he began to pass his hand over their shins and necks.﴾

It is evident that the intended meaning is not that he turned back constantly only in this story, since the form awwāb implies intensity (mubālagha), whose basic sense is abundance. Therefore it is determined that the mention of this story, one of the incidents of his turning back, was because in it the greatness of his turning back becomes clear.

"Displayed" (al-ʿarḍ) means passing [the horses] and bringing them forward before the one who sees them, i.e., he reviewed his horse-handlers' horses before him.

"Evening" (al-ʿashiyy) is from the afternoon until sunset. It was mentioned in His words "in the morning and the evening" in Surat al-Anʿam. It is the time for inspecting horses and livestock after they return from their pastures and grazing grounds. The mention of evening here is not merely for specifying time, but so that His words "until they were hidden behind the veil" may be built upon it. So the mention of evening in this verse does not have the same effect as it has in the words of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

"Kings from the Banu Jusham ibn Bakr, who are driven at evening and killed."

It is the one that stands on three legs, with the tip of the hoof of the fourth leg touching the ground without putting weight on it. This is one of the signs of its lightness, which indicates the nobility of the horse's stock and the goodness of its qualities. It is said: "The horse stood poised" (ṣafana al-furs ṣufūnan). Ibn al-Aʿrabi and al-Zajjaj recited, in describing a horse:

"It has become accustomed to standing poised, so that it seems ∗∗∗ as if, from what it does standing on three [legs], it is lame."

"The swift" (al-jiyād) is the plural of jawād (with a fatḥa on the wāw), which is a horse of excellence, i.e., of nobility. Sulayman was devoted to increasing the number of horses and horsemen, so his horses were counted in the thousands.

The original structure of "I have loved the love of the good" was "I have loved the good, a love," and the structure was changed to "I have loved the love of the good," so "the love of the good" became a specification (tamyīz) for attributing the relation of love to himself, for the purpose of generality followed by detail, like His words, exalted is He, "and We caused the earth to burst forth with springs" and the words of Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr:

"How excellent is she as a companion..."

and the saying: "How excellent is his horsemanship!"

"I have loved" (aḥbabtu) is used with the implied meaning of "I have exchanged" (ʿawwaḍtu), so it takes "from" (ʿan) in His words "from the remembrance of my Lord." So the meaning becomes: "I have loved the good, a love, so I have passed beyond the remembrance of my Lord."

By "the remembrance of the Lord" is meant the prayer. Perhaps it was a prayer that he had established for himself, since in the evening time there is no obligatory prayer in the law of Musa except the maghrib (sunset prayer).

"The good" (al-khayr) means precious wealth, as in His words, exalted is He, "if he leaves behind good" [al-Baqara: 180], and horses are among precious wealth. Al-Farraʾ said: "The good with the letter rāʾ is one of the names of horses." The Arabs interchange the letters lām and rāʾ, as they say: "the eye poured forth" (inhamalat) and "flowed" (inhamarat). Also "khatala" and "khatara" when one deceives.

[Page 256]

I say: It is among the habits of the Arabs to seek omens (tafāʾul), and they had a great concern with horses, to the extent that they described their markings and believed they indicated good fortune or misfortune. Perhaps they called them "the good" as an omen, so that they would be purely associated with happiness and good fortune.

The pronoun in "they were hidden" (tawārat) refers to the sun, by the indication of the mention of evening, the particle of limit, and the word "veil," and also because the pronoun referring to the sun in mentioning times is frequent in their speech, as Labid said:

"Until, when it cast a hand into the unbeliever [i.e., the darkness], and its darkness concealed the nakedness of the frontiers..."

That is, the sun cast its hand into the darkness, i.e., it cast itself into it. This is an expression of the self by one of its parts.

"Hiding" (tawārī) is concealment. "Veil" (ḥijāb) is a screen in the house behind which a woman and others hide. From this is the saying of Anas ibn Malik: "So God revealed the verse of the veil."

The statement is an allegory (tamthīl) for the state of the sun's setting by the hiding of a woman behind a veil, and each part of this allegory is metaphorical. For the sun, a woman is borrowed in the manner of an implicit metaphor (makniyya); for its disappearance from sight, the word "hiding" is borrowed; and for the horizon of the sun's setting, the word "veil" is borrowed.

The meaning: his horses, the poised and swift, were displayed before him, and he occupied himself with their conditions out of love for them, until the sun set, and so he missed a prayer that he used to perform in the evening before sunset. So after the horses were displayed and had gone away, he said: "I have loved the horses and so I neglected my prayer to God."

His statement is a report used to express regret, like the words of the mother of Mary: "My Lord, I have given birth to her as a female" [Āl ʿImrān: 36].

The address in His words "Bring them back to me" is to the handlers of his horses. The pronoun in the accusative refers to the horses by indication, i.e., "return the horses to me." It was also said that it refers to the sun and the address is to the angels, but this is extremely remote, and were it not for its frequent mention in the books of the exegetes, it would be better for us not to address it. More preferable than this, according to this view regarding the referent of the third-person pronoun, is that the command is used to express incapacity, i.e., "Can you bring back the sun after its setting?", like the words of Muhalhil:

[Page 257]

"O Bakr, bring back Kulayb to me!"

and the words of al-Harith al-Dabbi, one of the companions of the Camel [battle]:

"Return to us our shaykh, then he will be honored."

He means ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may God be pleased with him. So there is no improbability in this interpretation.

The fāʾ in His words "then he began" (faṭafiqa) is consequential (taʿqībiyya), and ṭafiqa is one of the verbs of beginning, i.e., "then he began."

"Passing" (maswan) is a verbal noun standing in the place of the verb, i.e., he began to pass his hand (yamsaḥu maswan). The definite article in "the shins and the necks" is a replacement for the omitted genitive, i.e., "their shins and their necks," like His words, exalted is He, "for indeed the Garden is the refuge" [al-Nāziʿāt: 41].

The primary meaning of masḥ (passing) is passing the hand over a thing to remove what is upon it, such as dust, water, or dirt, or anything else whose presence is not desired on the thing. It is done with the hand or with a cloth or garment. The word masḥ is sometimes used metaphorically for other meanings, among which is striking with a sword; it is said: "he wiped him with the sword," and "he wiped the sword with it." Perhaps its original meaning is a metonymy for killing by the sword, because the sword is wiped of blood after striking with it.

"Shins" (al-sūq) is the plural of sāq. The majority of readers recited it with a silent wāw and in the pattern fuʿl, like dār and dūr, and the pattern fuʿl in the plural of a similar word is rare. Qunbul from Ibn Kathir and Abu Jaʿfar recited "al-suʾq" with a silent hamza after the sīn, the plural of sa'q with a hamza after the sīn, and this is a dialect of sāq.

"Necks" (al-aʿnāq) is the plural of ʿunuq, which is the neck.

The bāʾ in "with the shins" is superfluous (zāʾida) for emphasis, i.e., to emphasize the connection of the verb with its object, like that in His words, exalted is He, "and wipe your heads" [al-Māʾida: 6], and in the words of al-Nabigha:

"To you is the good, if the earth covers you, a single one, ∗∗∗ and the grandfather of the people is stumbling, straining [to rise]."

The exegetes have disagreed about the meaning intended by His words "then he began passing [his hand] over the shins and necks." According to Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Zuhri, Ibn Kaysan, and Qutrub: he began to pass his hand over the manes of the horses and their shins, out of love for them. This is the interpretation that accords with the station of a prophet and is most in keeping with the reality of [the word] masḥ, but it requires placing the sequence of the sentences contrary to what the apparent sense demands: namely, that His words "Bring them back to me, then he began passing [his hand] over the shins and necks" are connected to His words "when there were displayed before him at evening the poised..." — that is, after he had reviewed them and they had turned away with them to return to their stables, he said: "Bring them back to me," and then he began passing [his hand] over the shins and necks, honoring them and out of love for them. And His words "he said, 'Indeed, I have loved the love of the good over the remembrance of my Lord, until they were hidden behind the veil'" would be placed as an interjection between them. It was placed first only to hasten the mention of his regret over his neglect of the remembrance of God at a time of remembrance. That is, he did not become absorbed in forgetfulness; rather he hastened to remember as soon as the time of remembrance that he was accustomed to had passed. For it is not fitting, according to this interpretation, that His words "Bring them back to me, then he began" etc. be a consequence of his regret and grief. This indicates that the passing of the time of his remembrance resulted from that returning which he commanded by His words "Bring them back to me," for they were accustomed to display them before him and then depart while there remained enough time for remembrance. When his delight in them moved him to command their return and to busy himself with passing his hand over their necks and shins, the time of his remembrance went out, and so he regretted and grieved.

From al-Hasan, Qatada, and Malik ibn Anas, in the narration of Ibn Wahb, and from al-Farraʾ and Tha'lab: when Sulayman regretted his preoccupation with the horses, to the point that he neglected the remembrance of God at a time when he used to remember God, he commanded that the horses that had distracted him be returned to him. He then began to hamstring their shins and cut their necks, depriving himself of them despite his love for them, as repentance and as training for his soul. They sensed that this was corruption in the earth and a waste of wealth, so they answered: he intended to slaughter them so that the poor could eat them, since eating horses is permissible among them, and thus slaughtering them was not corruption in the earth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verses 34–35:

﴿Indeed, We tested Solomon and placed upon his throne a body; then he turned back in repentance.﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me. Indeed, You are the Bestower."﴾ I have already said, when discussing His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And We gave to David Solomon﴾ [Sad: 30], that what was mentioned of the virtues of Solomon was not free of purposes of exemplary conduct, lesson and warning, in keeping with the Qur'an's custom of beginning the means of guidance with encouragement and admonition. Likewise, the verses concerning his remorse for busying himself with the horses to the neglect of the remembrance of God were a model for him in hastening to repentance, and a warning against falling into a heedlessness like his. Likewise, these verses came pointing to a trial that befell Solomon, which was followed by repentance, and then followed by the outpouring of great blessings. It is therefore mentioned after the account of what he suffered of neglect in his worship, which is less than a trial.

"Fatn" (trial), "futun" and "fitnah" (affliction): an intense disturbance of condition by which the degree of patience and steadfastness of the one who undergoes it becomes manifest. This was discussed earlier at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿We are only a trial﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The verse has indicated a great event that befell Solomon, and the statements of the exegetes differed in specifying this trial. They mentioned narratives that are more akin to fables, while Solomon's station is far more exalted than such things.

Among the strangest of them is their saying: a son was born to him, and he feared that people would kill him, so he entrusted him to the wind so that it would nurse him and feed him the milk of the rain-cloud. But soon death befell him, and the wind cast him upon the throne of Solomon, so that he would know that there is no averting what is decreed as death. Al-Ma'arri versified this, following the illusions of people, and said, relating about Solomon:

*He feared the treachery of people, so he entrusted to the wind a scion, which the milk of the clouds would nourish,*

*And he sought safety, though he knew that death lies in wait.*

*So the wind cast him upon the side of the throne, the mother of Lahaym, sister of al-Nu'ad.*

What appears from the context is that His saying, ﴿And We placed upon his throne a body﴾, is an indication of something of this trial, so that His saying ﴿then he turned back in repentance﴾ is connected to that.

It is also possible that it is a separate story, other than the story of his trial. The most apparent of their statements is that the verse is an indication of what is in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from Abu Hurayrah: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: Solomon said: 'Tonight I shall go around to ninety women, each of whom will bear a horseman who fights in the way of God.' His companion said to him: 'Say, if God wills.' But he did not say: 'If God wills.' So he went around to them all, and none of them became pregnant except one woman, who bore half a man. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, if he had said, 'If God wills,' they would have fought in the way of God as horsemen, all of them." But there is nothing in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) that this is the interpretation of this verse, nor did al-Bukhari or al-Tirmidhi place the hadith in the chapter of tafsir in their two books. A group said: that half of a human being is the body placed upon his throne; the midwife brought it and placed it for him while he was on his throne. So the trial, according to this, is the failure of his hope and the contradiction of what his companion had informed him of.

The application of the term "body" to that newborn is either because he was born dead, as is apparent in his saying "half a man," or because he was an unusual creation and so was merely a body. This is a remote interpretation, because the report does not require that the half that the woman bore was alive, nor that it sat upon Solomon's throne. And the construction of this verse according to that report is forced.

Wahb ibn Munabbih and Shahr ibn Hawshab said: Solomon married the daughter of the king of Sidon after he had attacked her father and killed him. She was grieved over her father, and Solomon had become infatuated with her love. So she asked him, to be pleased, to order the image-makers to make an image of her father, and it was made for her. She would go out and return with her female servants, prostrating to that image. When Solomon learned of this, he ordered that the statue be broken. It was also said: she used to worship an idol of hers made of ruby secretly, and when Solomon became aware, or the woman embraced Islam, that idol was abandoned.

On this interpretation, the meaning of "body" is an idol, since it is an image without a spirit, just as God named the calf that the Children of Israel worshipped a "body" in His saying: ﴿So He brought forth for them a calf, a body that had a lowing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88].

The meaning of placing it upon his throne would be setting it in the houses of his idolatrous wives near the places where he sat, since he would have a throne in each of their houses on which he sat.

Solomon was at that time in a great kingdom. So the request for the bestowal of kingdom means the continuation of that kingdom. The form of the imperative comes to request permanence, like ﴿O you who have believed, believe in God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa: 136].

The indefinite "mulkan" (a kingdom) is for magnification.

Solomon, in progressing in his request, reached the point of describing the kingdom as one that will not befit anyone after him, meaning it will not be attainable for anyone after him, that is, God will not give it to anyone who seeks it after him. So "will not befit" is a metonymy for "will not be given to anyone," i.e., you will not give it to anyone after me.

The verb "yanbaghi" (befits) is the reflexive of "baghahu" (sought). It is said: "baghahu fa-nbaghā lahu" (he sought it and it became suitable for him). The kingdom has no choice, no seeking; rather God is the Giver and the Facilitator. So attributing the "befitting" to the kingdom is an intellectual metaphor, and its reality is the befitting of its cause. This is from the courtesy in his supplication, since he did not say: "Do not give it to anyone after me."

He asked God that He not raise up for him a rival in his kingdom, and that He keep that kingdom for him until his death, and He responded. Solomon feared the rise of his servant (Jeroboam son of Nebat) of the tribe of Ephraim against him, for he had openly plotted against Solomon, so Solomon sought him to kill him, and he fled to (Shishaq), the Pharaoh of Egypt, and remained in Egypt until Solomon's death. This too is among the things that moved Solomon to ask God to confirm his kingdom and not to give it to anyone other than him.

Solomon also had two other enemies: (Hadad) the Edomite and (Rezon) of the people of Zarephath, who were residing at the borders of the kingdom of Israel. So he feared that God had prepared them to remove his kingdom.

"Min ba'di" (after me) is used with the meaning of "min duni" (other than me), as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Who then can guide him apart from God?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23]. So the meaning of "will not befit" would be that it will not befit anyone other than me, that is, during my lifetime. Thus this is a supplication that He not empower anyone over his kingdom for the duration of his life.

On this interpretation, there is nothing in his request for this kingdom of concern that others should not attain what he himself attained, so it is not objected to that such a thing is counted as envy.

It is also permissible for "min ba'di" to remain on its literal sense, i.e., after my life. The meaning of "will not befit" is: such a thing will not befit anyone after my death. The explanation of this is that he intended by his request to be apprehensive lest there come after him someone who holds such a kingdom who lacks the prophethood, wisdom and infallibility that would enable him to bear the burdens of such a kingdom, and who lacks the authority over his nation that Solomon had over his nation. Then he would soon be envied for the kingdom, and rivals to the king would arise among the nation over his kingdom. So on this interpretation too, the implication is removed that he asked this out of jealousy for himself, that anyone else should be given a kingdom like his, which would carry a whiff of envy.

His supplication contained two things: that he be given a great kingdom, and that no one else be given the like of it in its greatness.

God related Solomon's supplication, while it was a secret between him and his Lord, to indicate that He inspired him with it, and that He answered his prayer, to make known His good pleasure with him, and that He made its answering a favour of his repentance.

The meaning of that is that no king will come after him who has of authority all that Solomon had. End of quotation.

In the Sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed a powerful jinn (ifrit) from the jinn slipped away yesterday in order to cut off my prayer, but God enabled me to overcome him, and I seized him, and I wanted to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque so that all of you might look at him. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verses 34–35:

Indeed, You are the Bestower."﴾ I have already said, when discussing His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And We gave to David Solomon﴾ [Sad: 30], that what was mentioned of the virtues of Solomon was not free of purposes of exemplary conduct, lesson and warning, in keeping with the Qur'an's custom of beginning the means of guidance with encouragement and admonition. Likewise, the verses concerning his remorse for busying himself with the horses to the neglect of the remembrance of God were a model for him in hastening to repentance, and a warning against falling into a heedlessness like his. Likewise, these verses came pointing to a trial that befell Solomon, which was followed by repentance, and then followed by the outpouring of great blessings. It is therefore mentioned after the account of what he suffered of neglect in his worship, which is less than a trial.

"Fatn" (trial), "futun" and "fitnah" (affliction): an intense disturbance of condition by which the degree of patience and steadfastness of the one who undergoes it becomes manifest. This was discussed earlier at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿We are only a trial﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The verse has indicated a great event that befell Solomon, and the statements of the exegetes differed in specifying this trial. They mentioned narratives that are more akin to fables, while Solomon's station is far more exalted than such things.

Among the strangest of them is their saying: a son was born to him, and he feared that people would kill him, so he entrusted him to the wind so that it would nurse him and feed him the milk of the rain-cloud. But soon death befell him, and the wind cast him upon the throne of Solomon, so that he would know that there is no averting what is decreed as death. Al-Ma'arri versified this, following the illusions of people, and said, relating about Solomon:

*He feared the treachery of people, so he entrusted to the wind a scion, which the milk of the clouds would nourish,*

*And he sought safety, though he knew that death lies in wait.*

*So the wind cast him upon the side of the throne, the mother of Lahaym, sister of al-Nu'ad.*

What appears from the context is that His saying, ﴿And We placed upon his throne a body﴾, is an indication of something of this trial, so that His saying ﴿then he turned back in repentance﴾ is connected to that.

It is also possible that it is a separate story, other than the story of his trial. The most apparent of their statements is that the verse is an indication of what is in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from Abu Hurayrah: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: Solomon said: 'Tonight I shall go around to ninety women, each of whom will bear a horseman who fights in the way of God.' His companion said to him: 'Say, if God wills.' But he did not say: 'If God wills.' So he went around to them all, and none of them became pregnant except one woman, who bore half a man. ﴿So We subjected the wind to him, running gently by his command wherever he intended﴾ ﴿and the devils, every builder and diver﴾ ﴿and others bound together in chains﴾. The conjunction "fa" (so) and the order of the clauses indicate that the subjection of the wind and the subjection of the devils came after Solomon asked God for a kingdom that would not be fitting for anyone after him. God granted him these two gifts as an increase in the strength of his kingdom and as a fulfilment of the answer to his supplication, because he had asked only for a kingdom not fitting for anyone other than himself, and had not asked for an increase in what he had been given of kingship.

It may be that God intended to give him these two gifts and not to give them to anyone after him. Then, if He gave someone after him a kingdom like his in respects other than these two gifts, He would not have failed to answer his supplication.

Taskhir (subjection, here meaning compulsion to act without choice) is used here metaphorically for arranging the causes that direct the wind's movement toward the directions in which Solomon wished to steer his ships, so that the wind would help the speed of their sailing and would not oppose their course. This was mentioned earlier in God's words: ﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind: its morning course was a month's journey and its evening course a month's journey﴾ [Saba': 12], in Sūrat al-Naml.

Abu Ja'far (a reciter) read "al-riyāḥa" (the winds) in the plural.

What was mentioned earlier in His words "running by his command" concerns the land "which We had blessed" in Sūrat al-Anbiyā'.

The lam in "lahu" (for him) indicates cause, meaning: for his sake. That is, this subjection was an honour from God to him, in that He made the directing of the winds conform to his wishes.

The word "amr" (command) in "bi-amrihi" is used metaphorically for desire, or for supplication, in that he would ask God that the wind blow toward such-and-such a direction according to the plan of his ships' voyages; or that he would desire it in himself, and God would then direct the wind to what suits his desire, and He is the All-Knowing of hidden things.

Al-rukhā' (gentle) means the soft wind whose blowing is not violent. Rukhā' is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in tajrī (it runs), meaning: it runs by his command, gentle, assisting the sailing of the ships. This is part of the subjection, because the nature of the wind is to change its manner of blowing, and it most often blows fiercely and stormily. God said in Sūrat al-Anbiyā': ﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, blowing strongly﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 81]. Its meaning is: We subjected to Solomon the wind whose nature is to be violent, so the meaning of "fa-sakhkharnā lahu" (so We subjected it to him) is: We made it gentle for him. Thus ʿāṣifa (strongly) in the verse of Sūrat al-Anbiyā' is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from "the wind", and it is a changing circumstance (ḥāl muntaqila). Since He followed it with His words "running by his command", it is understood that its violence turns into gentleness by Solomon's command, that is, by his supplication, or by his resolve, or by his desire, because it is not appropriate for it to be violent under any circumstances for him. This is the way the apparent conflict between the two circumstances in the two verses is removed.

Aṣāba (to hit, to reach) in meaning means "intended", and it is derived from ṣawb, that is, the direction. That is: it runs to wherever in any direction he intended to travel. Al-Aṣma'ī reported from the Arabs: "aṣāba al-ṣawāba fa-akhṭa'a al-jawāb" (he hit the right answer but missed the reply), meaning he intended the right answer but did not hit it.

It was said: this usage of it is in the dialect of Ḥimyar, and it was said: in the dialect of Hajar.

Al-shayāṭīn (the devils) is the plural of shayṭān, and its literal meaning is a jinn. It is used figuratively for one who reaches the utmost ability and skill in the work he does. From this is God's words: ﴿And thus We appointed for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind and jinn﴾. So God subjected the first kind to Solomon in a subjection that breaks habit, as a miracle. So they were subjected to him in spiritual matters and hidden dealings, and it is not in the nature of their kind to produce skilled crafts such as building. He subjected the second kind to him in a subjection of humiliation and subjugation, because of the greatness of his authority and because he cast awe of him into the hearts of nations, so they came willingly to submit to his rule, as Bilqīs did; this was mentioned earlier in Sūrat Saba'. So it is permissible that "al-shayāṭīn" is used in both its literal and figurative senses.

Kulla bannā' (every builder): it is a substitute (badal) for "al-shayāṭīn": a partial substitute from a whole (badal al-ba'ḍ min al-kull, partial apposition), meaning: every builder and diver among them, that is, among the devils.

Kulla (every) is used here in the sense of "many". This usage occurs in the Qur'an and in eloquent speech. God said: ﴿But even if every sign came to them﴾ [Yūnus: 97], and He said: ﴿Then eat from all the fruits﴾ [al-Naḥl: 69], and al-Nābigha said:

In it is every long-tailed [creature], and a flat-nosed cow that grazes.

It was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾ [al-An'ām: 25] in Sūrat al-An'ām.

[p. 266]

Al-bannā' is the one who builds. It is an active participle formed on the intensive pattern (ṣīgat al-mubālagha, the form of intensity) to indicate the meaning of a craft, like najjār (carpenter), qaṣṣār (launderer), and ḥaddād (blacksmith).

Al-ghawwāṣ is the one who dives into the sea to extract pearl oysters. It is also among what is formed on the intensive pattern to indicate a craft. Al-Nābigha said:

Or a Ṣadafī pearl whose diver is joyful; whenever he sees it he exclaims and prostrates.

God said: ﴿And among the devils were those who dived for him and did other work besides that﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 82].

The craft in Solomon's kingdom reached a level of perfection, excellence and grandeur. Consider the building of the Temple of Jerusalem, which was called in Islam al-Masjid al-Aqṣā, and what was brought to it of building materials from the neighbouring kingdoms. Likewise the palace (ṣarḥ) that he built, into which the kingdom of Saba' was admitted.

Wa-ākharīna (and others) is coordinated with "kulla bannā' wa-ghawwāṣ", so it is part of the partial substitute. The plural of ākhar (other) is used in the sense of "different", so the difference may be in kind, being other than the kind of jinn, and the difference may be in attribute, meaning: not builders and divers. There was brought from the neighbouring kingdoms, and from those who came under the shadow of his rule, whatever he needed for building palaces, fortresses and cities. His kingdom was great, and all kings feared his might and courted him.

Al-muqarran is a passive participle from qarana-hu, in intensive form for "qarnihi", meaning: making him a companion of another, so that neither of the two is separated from the other.

Al-aṣfād is the plural of ṣafad, with two fatḥas, and it means fetter. It is said: ṣaffada-hu, when he fettered him.

This is a category of those who are referred to as devils, of fierce disposition, feared to escape, and it is desired that they remain. They do work that others cannot do well, so they are fettered in chains so that they work under the guard of guards. The wise kings used to confine those who had special skills in crafts, where they would not be in contact with anyone, lest the spies of other kings should lure them away to produce for them, so that the people of that kingdom would specialise in the special skills of those crafts and no other kingdom would share them in them. This was especially so in making instruments of war: swords, arrows, bows, shields, targes, helmets, skull caps and coats of mail. So it is possible that the meaning of "muqarranīna fī al-aṣfād" (bound together in chains) is literal, and it is possible that it is a figure of speech for preventing the devils from escaping.

[p. 267]

Solomon's kingdom was famous for making excellent, well-crafted coats of mail. They say: "Sulaymānī coats of mail." al-Nābigha said:

And every smooth-linked coat of Tubba'ī mail, and the weaving of Sulaym, every flowing qamṣā'.

He meant the weaving of Sulaymān, that is, the weaving of his craftsmen.
