The lam in "lahu" (for him) indicates cause, meaning: for his sake. That is, this subjection was an honour from God to him, in that He made the directing of the winds conform to his wishes.

The word "amr" (command) in "bi-amrihi" is used metaphorically for desire, or for supplication, in that he would ask God that the wind blow toward such-and-such a direction according to the plan of his ships' voyages; or that he would desire it in himself, and God would then direct the wind to what suits his desire, and He is the All-Knowing of hidden things.

Al-rukhā' (gentle) means the soft wind whose blowing is not violent. Rukhā' is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in tajrī (it runs), meaning: it runs by his command, gentle, assisting the sailing of the ships. This is part of the subjection, because the nature of the wind is to change its manner of blowing, and it most often blows fiercely and stormily. God said in Sūrat al-Anbiyā': ﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, blowing strongly﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 81]. Its meaning is: We subjected to Solomon the wind whose nature is to be violent, so the meaning of "fa-sakhkharnā lahu" (so We subjected it to him) is: We made it gentle for him. Thus ʿāṣifa (strongly) in the verse of Sūrat al-Anbiyā' is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from "the wind", and it is a changing circumstance (ḥāl muntaqila). Since He followed it with His words "running by his command", it is understood that its violence turns into gentleness by Solomon's command, that is, by his supplication, or by his resolve, or by his desire, because it is not appropriate for it to be violent under any circumstances for him. This is the way the apparent conflict between the two circumstances in the two verses is removed.

Aṣāba (to hit, to reach) in meaning means "intended", and it is derived from ṣawb, that is, the direction. That is: it runs to wherever in any direction he intended to travel. Al-Aṣma'ī reported from the Arabs: "aṣāba al-ṣawāba fa-akhṭa'a al-jawāb" (he hit the right answer but missed the reply), meaning he intended the right answer but did not hit it.

It was said: this usage of it is in the dialect of Ḥimyar, and it was said: in the dialect of Hajar.

Al-shayāṭīn (the devils) is the plural of shayṭān, and its literal meaning is a jinn. It is used figuratively for one who reaches the utmost ability and skill in the work he does. From this is God's words: ﴿And thus We appointed for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind and jinn﴾. So God subjected the first kind to Solomon in a subjection that breaks habit, as a miracle. So they were subjected to him in spiritual matters and hidden dealings, and it is not in the nature of their kind to produce skilled crafts such as building. He subjected the second kind to him in a subjection of humiliation and subjugation, because of the greatness of his authority and because he cast awe of him into the hearts of nations, so they came willingly to submit to his rule, as Bilqīs did; this was mentioned earlier in Sūrat Saba'. So it is permissible that "al-shayāṭīn" is used in both its literal and figurative senses.

Kulla bannā' (every builder): it is a substitute (badal) for "al-shayāṭīn": a partial substitute from a whole (badal al-ba'ḍ min al-kull, partial apposition), meaning: every builder and diver among them, that is, among the devils.

Kulla (every) is used here in the sense of "many". This usage occurs in the Qur'an and in eloquent speech. God said: ﴿But even if every sign came to them﴾ [Yūnus: 97], and He said: ﴿Then eat from all the fruits﴾ [al-Naḥl: 69], and al-Nābigha said:

In it is every long-tailed [creature], and a flat-nosed cow that grazes.

It was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾ [al-An'ām: 25] in Sūrat al-An'ām.

[p. 266]

Al-bannā' is the one who builds. It is an active participle formed on the intensive pattern (ṣīgat al-mubālagha, the form of intensity) to indicate the meaning of a craft, like najjār (carpenter), qaṣṣār (launderer), and ḥaddād (blacksmith).

Al-ghawwāṣ is the one who dives into the sea to extract pearl oysters. It is also among what is formed on the intensive pattern to indicate a craft. Al-Nābigha said:

Or a Ṣadafī pearl whose diver is joyful; whenever he sees it he exclaims and prostrates.

God said: ﴿And among the devils were those who dived for him and did other work besides that﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 82].

The craft in Solomon's kingdom reached a level of perfection, excellence and grandeur. Consider the building of the Temple of Jerusalem, which was called in Islam al-Masjid al-Aqṣā, and what was brought to it of building materials from the neighbouring kingdoms. Likewise the palace (ṣarḥ) that he built, into which the kingdom of Saba' was admitted.

Wa-ākharīna (and others) is coordinated with "kulla bannā' wa-ghawwāṣ", so it is part of the partial substitute. The plural of ākhar (other) is used in the sense of "different", so the difference may be in kind, being other than the kind of jinn, and the difference may be in attribute, meaning: not builders and divers. There was brought from the neighbouring kingdoms, and from those who came under the shadow of his rule, whatever he needed for building palaces, fortresses and cities. His kingdom was great, and all kings feared his might and courted him.

Al-muqarran is a passive participle from qarana-hu, in intensive form for "qarnihi", meaning: making him a companion of another, so that neither of the two is separated from the other.

Al-aṣfād is the plural of ṣafad, with two fatḥas, and it means fetter. It is said: ṣaffada-hu, when he fettered him.

This is a category of those who are referred to as devils, of fierce disposition, feared to escape, and it is desired that they remain. They do work that others cannot do well, so they are fettered in chains so that they work under the guard of guards. The wise kings used to confine those who had special skills in crafts, where they would not be in contact with anyone, lest the spies of other kings should lure them away to produce for them, so that the people of that kingdom would specialise in the special skills of those crafts and no other kingdom would share them in them. This was especially so in making instruments of war: swords, arrows, bows, shields, targes, helmets, skull caps and coats of mail. So it is possible that the meaning of "muqarranīna fī al-aṣfād" (bound together in chains) is literal, and it is possible that it is a figure of speech for preventing the devils from escaping.

[p. 267]

And every smooth-linked coat of Tubba'ī mail, and the weaving of Sulaym, every flowing qamṣā'.

He meant the weaving of Sulaymān, that is, the weaving of his craftsmen.

﴿So We subjected the wind to him, running gently by his command wherever he intended﴾ ﴿and the devils, every builder and diver﴾ ﴿and others bound together in chains﴾. God granted him these two gifts as an increase in the strength of his kingdom and as a fulfilment of the answer to his supplication, because he had asked only for a kingdom not fitting for anyone other than himself, and had not asked for an increase in what he had been given of kingship.

It may be that God intended to give him these two gifts and not to give them to anyone after him. Then, if He gave someone after him a kingdom like his in respects other than these two gifts, He would not have failed to answer his supplication.

And every smooth-linked coat of Tubba'ī mail, and the weaving of Sulaym, every flowing qamṣā'.

This is Our gift, so bestow [favor] or withhold, without account. The reference is to the subjugation derived from ﴿We subjected the wind to him﴾ [Sad: 36] up to His saying, Exalted is He, "and the devils." That is, this subjugation is Our gift.

The idafa (genitive construction) serves to magnify the status of the first term by its attachment to the second, as if it were said: "This is a great gift that We have given you." Here ʿaṭāʾ (gift) is a verbal noun used in the sense of the thing given, like khalq (creation) in the sense of the thing created.

Famnun (bestow) is an imperative used to express permission and allowance. It is derived from al-mann (bestowing favor), which is used as a metonym for granting benefits. That is: "Bestow favor upon whomever you wish by releasing him, or hold back from service whomever you wish."

So al-mann is a kinaya (metonymy) for release, through a concomitant of a concomitant, like His saying, ﴿Then either release [them] with favor or with ransom﴾ [Muhammad: 4].

The two clauses famnun aw amsik (bestow or withhold) are parenthetical (iʿtirād) between His saying "our gift" and His saying "without account," and this is a fronted resultant clause (tafrīʿ muqaddam min taʾkhīr), i.e., a consequence placed before its position.

The fronting serves to hasten the joy of the blessing. Its parallel is His saying later on, ﴿This, so let them taste it: boiling water and dark pus﴾ [Sad: 57], and the saying of ʿAntara:

"Indeed you have descended, so do not suppose otherwise of me; from me you stand in the position of the beloved, honored one."

And the saying of Bashshar:

"Like one who says, 'Indeed the donkey, so turn it away from the fodder, [O] people of sesame, the refined.'"

Metaphorically and metonymically, it denotes limitlessness and lack of restriction: that is, this gift is not bounded or constrained. That is, Our gift is broad and abundant, with no narrowing upon you in it.

Page 268

It is also permissible for "without account" (bi-ghayri ḥisāb) to be a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in famnun or amsik, and for ḥisāb to mean "calling to account," used as a metonym for punishment. The meaning would then be: "Bestow or withhold, with no punishment upon you regarding those whom you have released by bestowing favor, if he was corrupt, nor regarding those whom you have held back in service, if he was righteous."

Verse 40: ﴿And indeed, for him with Us is nearness and a good return﴾. Its parallel has already been mentioned just before, in the story of Dawud, along with an explanation of the rhetorical purpose of emphasis through the particle inna.

[p. 269]

These are another example that the Prophet (ﷺ) was reminded of, as a model for himself in patience under the harm of his people and in turning to God to remove affliction. It is coordinated with "Remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength" (Q. 38:17). Because he is the intended subject of the example, the verb "remember" (udhkur) is repeated with him, as we pointed out in the commentary on ﴿Remember Our servant Dawud﴾ (Q. 38:17). The discussion of the opening of this verse has already been given in Surat al-Anbiya'.

The biography of Ayyub (peace be upon him) has been given in Surat al-An'am.

Since the verb "remember" is transitive to the name Ayyub through an elided noun, meaning that the intended object is the remembrance of the particular state connected with him, the phrase "when he called out to his Lord" is a badal ishtimal (a substitute of inclusion) for "Ayyub," because the time of his calling to his Lord is among the states that Ayyub's circumstances encompass. This particular state was singled out from among his conditions because it shows his trust in God and God's answering his supplication by removing the harm from him.

The "nida'" (calling out) here is a nida' of supplication (nida' du'a'), because supplication begins with "O my Lord" or similar words.

The phrase ﴿that the Satan has touched me﴾ is connected to "called out" with the deletion of the preposition "bi" before "anni" (that), so that it means "called out: that the Satan has touched me." Originally it is a clause explaining the clause "called out to his Lord." Were it not for the presence of the opening "anna," which makes the clause occupy the position of a single noun, it would have been an explanatory clause for "called out," and the verb "called out" would not have needed the elided preposition to take it as its object, especially since the clause has no vocative particle. Thus the grammarians' statement that it is governed by an assumed "bi" follows the grammatical considerations, in order to distinguish the position of "anna" with a fatha from the position of "inna" with a kasra. For this distinction between fatha and kasra, both readings of the hamza are permitted in phrases such as "khayru al-qawli anni ahmadu" (the best speech is that I praise [God]).

We discussed in the commentary on ﴿So He answered you: I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another﴾ (Q. 8:9) in Surat al-Anfal that "anna," with a fatha on the hamza and a doubled nun, is composed of "an" (the explanatory "that") and the "inna" of affirmation.

The statement is used in the sense of supplication and complaint, as in His saying ﴿My Lord, I have given birth to a female﴾ (Q. 3:36). In the verse of Surat al-Anbiya' He said ﴿Harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful﴾ (Q. 21:83).

"Nusb," with a damma on the nun and a sukun on the sad, means hardship and fatigue. It is a dialectal variant of "nasab" with two fathas. "Nasab" was discussed in Surat al-Kahf.

Abu Ja'far read "bi-nusubin," with a damma on the sad, which is an assimilative damma following the damma of the nun.

"Adhab" means pain. Its intended sense here is sickness, that is, the Satan afflicted me with weariness and pain. This is harm that came upon his body, and a need that befell him in his property, as in the other verse ﴿Harm has touched me.﴾

The apparent sense of attributing the touching with "nusb" and "adhab" to the Satan is that the Satan actually touched Ayyub with them, that is, afflicted him with them. Yet "nusb" and "adhab" are what actually touched Ayyub, since in Surat al-Anbiya' it says ﴿Harm has touched me﴾; there the touching is attributed to "harm," and harm is the "nusb" and "adhab." The commentators have been perplexed about the meaning of attributing the touching of "nusb" and "adhab" to the Satan, since the Satan has no influence over the children of Adam except through whispering, as is established from the repeated verses of the Qur'an, and "nusb" and "adhab" are neither whispering nor among its effects.

They interpreted this in more than ten opinions, most of which are weak, and all of them rest on taking the "ba'" in "bi-nusubin" as the ba' of transitivity, making the verb "touched me" transitive, or as the ba' of instrument, as in "he struck him with a stick," or on understanding "nusb" and "adhab" as the second object in the pattern of "a'ta" (to give).

In my view, the correct reading is to take the "ba'" as expressing causation, so that "nusb" and "adhab" are the causes of the Satan's touching him. The meaning is: he touched me with a whisper whose cause was hardship and pain. So the Satan began to whisper to Ayyub, magnifying the hardship and pain in his sight and suggesting to him that he did not deserve that pain, in order to cast into Ayyub's soul ill thoughts about God or displeasure at that.

Or the "ba'" may be taken as accompaniment, meaning: he touched me with a whisper accompanied by harm and pain. In this case, Ayyub's saying ﴿that the Satan has touched me with hardship and pain﴾ is a subtle allusion to seeking God's gentleness toward him, and to the removal of the hardship and pain from him, since they had become an entry point for the Satan into his soul. So asking for protection from this is like the saying of Yusuf (peace be upon him): ﴿And unless You turn away from me their plotting, I would incline toward them and be among the ignorant﴾ (Q. 12:33).

The tanwin (indefiniteness marking) of "nusb" and "adhab" is for magnification or for generality (nau'iyya). He left them indefinite rather than definite because they are known to God.

The clause "Strike with your foot" and what follows is a quoted speech of an elided saying, meaning: We said to him, "Strike with your foot." This indicates that this was a response to his supplication.

"Rakd" means striking the earth with the foot. The phrase "with your foot" is an explanatory addition to clarify the meaning of the verb, like ﴿nor a bird that flies with its wings﴾ (Q. 6:38). God called this a response in Surat al-Anbiya' when He said ﴿So We responded to him and removed what harm was upon him﴾ (Q. 21:84).

The clause "this is a cool bath" is a quoted speech of an elided saying, indicated by the preceding quoted speech. There is an ellipsis in the statement, indicated by the pointing word. The sense is: So he struck the earth, and water gushed forth, and We said to him, "This is a cool bath and drink." The pointing word refers to water, because it is what one bathes in and drinks.

The description of the water in this way, in the context of praise, indicates that in it is his cure if he bathes in it and drinks from it, so that God's words to him correspond to his calling to his Lord, since it is evident that the speech following the calling is the speech of response to supplication from the one supplicated.

"Mughtasal" is a passive participle from the verb "ightasala" (to bathe), meaning "a place to bathe with" (mughtasal bihi). It is a case of dropping the preposition and making the intransitive "mughtasal" reach its object, like the verse:

"You pass by the abodes and do not turn aside."

Describing it as "cool" hints that by it the fever and the sores that Ayyub had are removed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Fever is from the heat of Hell, so extinguish it with water." Its meaning is that it is beneficial and healing. By the tanwin of "sharab" (drink) one is spared from describing it as a drink, since it is known that water is a drink. Had the tanwin not been meant to magnify, the statement that the water is a drink would have been an informing about a known matter. The magnification of "sharab" refers to its being great for Ayyub, which is the cure of the illness he had.

"Adhab" means pain. Its intended sense here is sickness, that is, the Satan afflicted me with weariness and pain. This is harm that came upon his body, and a need that befell him in his property, as in the other verse ﴿Harm has touched me.﴾

The apparent sense of attributing the touching with "nusb" and "adhab" to the Satan is that the Satan actually touched Ayyub with them, that is, afflicted him with them. Yet "nusb" and "adhab" are what actually touched Ayyub, since in Surat al-Anbiya' it says ﴿Harm has touched me﴾; there the touching is attributed to "harm," and harm is the "nusb" and "adhab." The commentators have been perplexed about the meaning of attributing the touching of "nusb" and "adhab" to the Satan, since the Satan has no influence over the children of Adam except through whispering, as is established from the repeated verses of the Qur'an, and "nusb" and "adhab" are neither whispering nor among its effects.

They interpreted this in more than ten opinions, most of which are weak, and all of them rest on taking the "ba'" in "bi-nusubin" as the ba' of transitivity, making the verb "touched me" transitive, or as the ba' of instrument, as in "he struck him with a stick," or on understanding "nusb" and "adhab" as the second object in the pattern of "a'ta" (to give).

In my view, the correct reading is to take the "ba'" as expressing causation, so that "nusb" and "adhab" are the causes of the Satan's touching him. The meaning is: he touched me with a whisper whose cause was hardship and pain. So the Satan began to whisper to Ayyub, magnifying the hardship and pain in his sight and suggesting to him that he did not deserve that pain, in order to cast into Ayyub's soul ill thoughts about God or displeasure at that.

Or the "ba'" may be taken as accompaniment, meaning: he touched me with a whisper accompanied by harm and pain. In this case, Ayyub's saying ﴿that the Satan has touched me with hardship and pain﴾ is a subtle allusion to seeking God's gentleness toward him, and to the removal of the hardship and pain from him, since they had become an entry point for the Satan into his soul. So asking for protection from this is like the saying of Yusuf (peace be upon him): ﴿And unless You turn away from me their plotting, I would incline toward them and be among the ignorant﴾ (Q. 12:33).

The tanwin (indefiniteness marking) of "nusb" and "adhab" is for magnification or for generality (nau'iyya). He left them indefinite rather than definite because they are known to God.

The clause "Strike with your foot" and what follows is a quoted speech of an elided saying, meaning: We said to him, "Strike with your foot." This indicates that this was a response to his supplication.

"Rakd" means striking the earth with the foot. The phrase "with your foot" is an explanatory addition to clarify the meaning of the verb, like ﴿nor a bird that flies with its wings﴾ (Q. 6:38). God called this a response in Surat al-Anbiya' when He said ﴿So We responded to him and removed what harm was upon him﴾ (Q. 21:84).

The clause "this is a cool bath" is a quoted speech of an elided saying, indicated by the preceding quoted speech. There is an ellipsis in the statement, indicated by the pointing word. The sense is: So he struck the earth, and water gushed forth, and We said to him, "This is a cool bath and drink." The pointing word refers to water, because it is what one bathes in and drinks.

The description of the water in this way, in the context of praise, indicates that in it is his cure if he bathes in it and drinks from it, so that God's words to him correspond to his calling to his Lord, since it is evident that the speech following the calling is the speech of response to supplication from the one supplicated.

"Mughtasal" is a passive participle from the verb "ightasala" (to bathe), meaning "a place to bathe with" (mughtasal bihi). It is a case of dropping the preposition and making the intransitive "mughtasal" reach its object, like the verse:

"You pass by the abodes and do not turn aside."

Describing it as "cool" hints that by it the fever and the sores that Ayyub had are removed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Fever is from the heat of Hell, so extinguish it with water." Its meaning is that it is beneficial and healing. By the tanwin of "sharab" (drink) one is spared from describing it as a drink, since it is known that water is a drink. Had the tanwin not been meant to magnify, the statement that the water is a drink would have been an informing about a known matter. The magnification of "sharab" refers to its being great for Ayyub, which is the cure of the illness he had.

[p. 270]

[Page 272]

The phrasing of Ayyub's supplication, in which he limited himself to alluding to the removal of hardship and torment, suggests that he was afflicted only with harm to his body. It is also possible that he suffered the loss of his property and the death of his dependents, as is reported in the Book of Job among the books of the Jews. In that case, his limiting of his supplication to hardship and torment would be because the loss of family and property is itself hardship and torment for the soul.

Nothing in this verse, nor in the verse in Surah al-Anbiya', states that Ayyub lost his family. Therefore, the meaning of ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾ may be that God preserved his family for him, so that he was not afflicted through them with what he disliked, and He increased him with sons and grandchildren.

In this case, the verb "wahabna" (We gave) is used in both its literal and figurative senses. The word "ma'ahum" (with them) placed right after "mithlahum" (the like of them) supports this interpretation, for "ma'" indicates that the thing given is joined to his family and added to them. Therefore, the verse does not require an implied noun in the phrase "We gave him his family."

There is nothing in the authentic reports that contradicts this, except some statements from the exegetes (mufassirun) arising from differing understandings.

It is also possible that among what afflicted him was that he, together with his children, perished during the period of his affliction, as is reported in the Book of Job among the books of the Jews, and in the sayings of some of the early generations (al-salaf) of exegetes. In that case, an implied noun must be supposed, meaning: "We gave him in place of his family."

But the wording of the verse runs counter to this second view.

The meaning of "mithlahum" (the like of them) is "their equivalent." The intended sense is "equivalent in number," that is, double the number of his family, consisting of sons and grandchildren.

A similar verse occurred earlier, in the words of Him, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:84], in Surah al-Anbiya'. The slight variation between the two verses is merely a variety of expression and does not imply any difference in eloquence. As for the difference between them in His words here, ﴿and a reminder for those of understanding﴾, and His words in Surah al-Anbiya', ﴿and a reminder for the worshippers﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:84]: His words here, ﴿a reminder for those of understanding﴾, are because "dhikra" (reminder) means reminding of what is hidden or what is concealed, and "ulu al-albab" (those of understanding) are the people of intellect, that is, a reminder for people of reflection and inference. In the story of Ayyub, both its summary and its detail contain what, if heard by sensible people who take lessons from events and who reason from analogies, would lead them to conclude that his patience is an exemplar for everyone who is in distress and awaits relief. Since the stories of the prophets in this surah are presented for taking lessons from the outcomes of those who are patient, and since the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims were commanded to take lessons from them, from His words ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength﴾ [Sad 38:17], as mentioned earlier, it was fitting that they be referred to as "ulu al-albab."

As for the verse in Surah al-Anbiya', it was brought as evidence that prophethood does not contradict humanity, and that prophets are subject to the events that befall human beings, which do not diminish them in the view of reason and wisdom, and that they only act by the command of God. This begins from His words, exalted is He: ﴿We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:7], and that they are exposed to the harm of people, which does not violate their true dignity, and the ultimate of that is death. From His words: ﴿We did not grant to any human before you eternity. So if you die, will they be eternal?﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:34].

Since the polytheists were saying, "We await for him the vicissitudes of fate (rayb al-manun)," and they attempted to kill him more than once, but God protected him, then from His words: ﴿Messengers were mocked before you, but those who mocked them were enveloped by what they used to mock﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:41]. Then He said: ﴿And We certainly gave Musa and Harun the criterion and a light and a reminder for the righteous who fear their Lord unseen and are apprehensive of the Hour﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:48]. He mentioned among the prophets those who were tested by their people and were patient, and how the outcome of their patience was one and the same despite the differing causes that prompted it. Thus there were signs in that for the worshippers, that is, those who comply with the command of God and avoid His prohibitions, for among what God commanded is patience over harm that a person cannot repel, because repelling it lies beyond his capacity. Therefore the passage concludes with the conclusion: ﴿Indeed, in this is a message for a people who worship﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:105].

﴿And take in your hand a bundle of grass, and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾ is a statement attached to an omitted utterance that the structure of the speech indicates. The intended meaning is: "We said: take in your hand a bundle of grass, and strike with it, and do not break your oath." This statement differs from the omitted utterance in His words, ﴿Strike with your foot﴾, because that was an answer to a supplication, whereas this is a legal pronouncement permitting a concession. That incident has its own story, and this one has another story, which the verse alludes to in general terms. No authentic report specifies it. In summary, Job's wife undertook an action, and this caused Job to lose his patience, through seeking help from some people to console him. When he learned of this, he became angry and swore that he would strike her a number of blows. Then he regretted it, for he loved her, and she had been devoted to him during his illness. When his affliction was lifted, he feared for his wife because of this. In their religion there was no expiation (kaffarah) for an oath, so God revealed to him that he should strike her with a bundle containing a number of twigs equal to the number of blows he had sworn to inflict. This was a concession toward his wife, for his sake, and a preservation of his oath from being broken, since breaking an oath does not befit the station of prophethood. This matter has no bearing on the purpose for which the story of Job was related, which is exemplarity. It is mentioned here only as a completion of the manifestation of God's kindness toward Job as a reward for his patience.

The meanings of the verse make clear that this permission was a kindness toward Job, and that such a provision was not known in the religion that Job followed, out of consideration for his piety, honouring him for his love of his wife, and showing mercy to his wife for her goodness toward him. It is therefore a concession with certainty regarding the ruling on breaking an oath.

Our scholars then examined the established principle relevant to the question in the discipline of legal theory (usul al-fiqh), namely: is the law of those before us (shar' man qablana) a law for us when the Qur'an or an authentic Sunnah relates it, provided that our own law contains nothing abrogating it, whether a text or a principle of the Islamic legal system?

As for those who did not hold that the law of those before us is law for us, namely Abu Bakr al-Baqillani from the Malikis, the majority of the Shafi'is, and all of the Zahiris, their position on this is clear. As for those who affirmed the principle of following the law of those before us under the conditions mentioned, namely Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i,

Page 274

they then went beyond the discussion of whether this ruling in this verse is to be established in the jurisprudence of Islam regarding fatwas on oaths, and whether it may be extended to make it a basis for analogy (qiyas) in every type of striking that is prescribed in the law with a fixed number, when a cause exists in the one struck that calls for a concession, after building on the affirmation of analogy from concessions. They also considered whether it may be extended to make it a basis for analogy to establish a similar principle, namely evading a required legal obligation by a lawful device (tahayyul) in order to escape a required legal duty. They ventured into this, despite the summary nature of the narration of Job's story, which does not allow the observer to discern the nature of his oath, its wording, or his intention, since that is not the purpose of the story.

As for oaths, God has spared us the burden of such speculation by prescribing for us the expiations of oaths. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By God, if I swear an oath and then see something other than it to be better, I will make expiation for my oath and do what is better." Thus what is in our law has abrogated (nasikh) what was prescribed for Job, so there is no need to delve into it. The position of the Hanafis is to act upon this, relying on its being a law for those before us, and this is also the view of al-Shafi'i.

Malik said: this is specific to Job, whom God permitted to act in this way as a prophet. Al-Qurtubi relates from al-Shafi'i that he restricted it to the case where a person swears and has no intention, as if he took it to the least that would truly be called striking and a number.

As for analogy from Job's fatwa to every fixed striking with a number outside oaths, that is, in the domain of the hudud (fixed penalties) and the ta'zirat (discretionary penalties), it is an extravagance in analogy, because the genus of the original and the derivative differ, and because the purpose of the Law in expiations differs from its purpose in the hudud and ta'zirat, and because harm results from neglecting the hudud and ta'zirat but not from neglecting expiations. There is no doubt that such leniency in the hudud leads to their neglect and their becoming futile.

As for what occurred in the Sunan of Abu Dawud from the hadith of Abu Umamah: "From one of the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from the Ansar, that a man among them was ill and wasted away, and a slave girl entered upon him and he was aroused by her and had intercourse with her. They asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for a fatwa regarding him and said: 'If we were to carry him to you, his bones would break apart, for he is nothing but skin over bone.' So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded that they take for him one hundred palm-fronds and strike him with them in a single blow."

Others besides Abu Dawud related it through different chains and different wordings. It is but one story, and there is no proof in it, because it is subject to several possibilities.

The first of them: that man was ill and wasted away, and a hadd is not carried out upon someone like him.

The second: perhaps the illness had impaired his mind to such an extent that it led him to fornication, so the illness was a doubt that averts the hadd from him.

The third: it is a khabar al-wahid (report from a single transmitter), which does not override the tawatur ma'nawi (conceptual mass-transmission) established regarding the execution of the hudud.

The fourth: to interpret it as specific to that case. Al-Shafi'i's position is that this is acted upon in the hadd due to necessity, as with illness, but this is strange, because the hadiths of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the statements of the early generations (salaf) are unanimous that a sick person and a pregnant woman wait before the hadd is carried out upon them until they recover. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not command that a pregnant woman be struck with palm-fronds. What benefit is there in this striking, which deters no offender and averts no sin? In the Ahkam of al-Jassas, it is reported from Abu Hanifa that he held a view similar to al-Shafi'i's. Al-Khattabi relates that Abu Hanifa and Malik agreed that there is no hadd except the well-known hadd. Thus the transmission from Abu Hanifa has varied.

﴿Indeed, We found him patient; what an excellent servant! Indeed, he was ever turning back (to God)﴾ is a reason (ʿillah) for the clause "strike with your foot." The clause "and We gave him his family" means: We bestowed upon him favour by restoring his condition, because We found him patient in what befell him. He is therefore an exemplar for the one commanded by the words ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾ [Sad: 17] (ﷺ). Thus "inna" (indeed) serves in place of the particle of consequence (fa').

The meaning of "We found him" is that his patience manifested what was in God's knowledge concerning him.

His words ﴿what an excellent servant! Indeed, he was ever turning back﴾ are like His words about Solomon: ﴿what an excellent servant! Indeed, he was ever turning back﴾. Solomon was one who turned back to God from the trial of wealth and luxury, and Job was one who turned back to God from the trial of harm and need. The praise of both is equal, because they are alike in turning back, although their motives differ. Sufyan said: God praised two servants who were tested: one of them was patient, the other was grateful, with a single praise. Thus He said of Job and Solomon: "what an excellent servant! Indeed, he was ever turning back."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verses 45–47:

[Page 276]
﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, men of strength and vision.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality: the remembrance of the Abode.﴾ ﴿And indeed, they are with Us among the chosen and the excellent.﴾ The discussion of this is like the discussion of its counterparts linguistically and in meaning.

The mention of these three is a mention for the sake of emulation and following their example. As for Abraham, peace be upon him, it is due to what is known of his patience over the harm of his people, his being thrown into the fire, and his being tested by being commanded to slaughter his son. As for the mention of Isaac and Jacob, it is a digression occasioned by the mention of Abraham, and because of the virtues they shared with their father, which are gathered in their shared meaning of His words ﴿men of strength and vision﴾, so that the Prophet ﷺ might emulate all three in strength in establishing the religion and insight into the realities of affairs.

Abraham is mentioned first because of his preeminence in the station of messengerhood and the sharia; the mention of his son is joined to him, and his son's son Jacob is joined to his son.

The majority recited ﴿And remember Our servants﴾ in the plural form, with Abraham and those joined to him all in apposition (ʿatf bayan). Ibn Kathir recited "ʿabdana" in the singular, with "Ibrahim" in apposition to "ʿabdana." The outcome of the two readings is one.

Al-Aydi (the hands) is the plural of yad in the sense of strength in religion, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the heaven We built with might (bi-aydin)﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 47] in Surat al-Dhariyat.

Al-Absar (the sight) is the plural of basar in a figurative sense, namely reflective contemplation known as insight (basirah), that is, looking carefully into observing the rulings of God, exalted is He, and seeking His pleasure.

The clause ﴿Indeed, We purified them﴾ is the reason for the command to remember them, because their remembrance brings the one who remembers to emulate them in their sincerity and the hope of attaining what they attained of election and preeminence in goodness.

Akhlasnahum (We purified them): We made them sincere (khalisin), so the hamza is for transitivity, meaning: We cleansed them from the filth of souls, so their souls became pure of the defects that befall humans. This sincerity is the meaning of the infallibility (ʿis-mah) necessary for prophethood.

ʿIsmah (infallibility): a power that God places in the soul of the Prophet, which turns him away from doing what is sinful in his religion against God, exalted is He, whether deliberately or inadvertently, and from what would incur aversion and contempt among people of sound intellect in his community's era.

The pillars of infallibility are four. The first: a property of the soul that God creates, which requires a faculty preventing disobedience.

The second: the attainment of knowledge of the blameworthiness of sins and the praiseworthiness of acts of obedience.

The third: the confirmation of that knowledge through the successive revelation and clarification from God, exalted is He.

The fourth: reproach from God for leaving the better course and for forgetfulness.

The attribution of sincerity to God, exalted is He, is because it is a matter that does not arise in the human soul except through a special placement from God, exalted is He, and a divine providence, such that the dominance of desire is removed from the soul in every state, and the soul is directed to pure good. Nothing remains in the soul except slight impulses, which the soul quickly abandons as soon as they occur. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, my heart is veiled, so I seek forgiveness from God seventy times a day."

The "ba'" in "bi-khalisah" denotes cause, alerting to the cause of their infallibility. This cause is expressed in a general way, to alert that it is a great and subtle matter that cannot be conceived in its essence but is known in its aspect. For this reason, this cause is evoked by a derived descriptor from the verb akhlasnahum, in the manner of the Prophet's ﷺ saying to one who asked him about his abstention from eating the lizard: "There comes to me from God a presence (hadirah)," meaning a presence that cannot be described. Then this sincerity is explained by the furthest that language can express, namely that it is ﴿the remembrance of the Abode﴾.

Dhikra (remembrance) is a noun of verbal action indicating the intensity of the meaning of the verbal noun, like ruj'a and buqya, because an increase in the form entails an increase in meaning. The Abode known to people like them is the Hereafter, that is:

[Page 278]
such that they do not forget the Hereafter and do not turn to this world. So the Abode that is the object of their concern is the Hereafter. The Prophet ﷺ said: "So I say: what have I to do with this world?"

The words of God, exalted is He, ﴿with the sincere remembrance of the Abode﴾ point out that the origin of infallibility is divine revelation, warning against what does not please God, warning of the punishment of the Hereafter, and making its bliss beloved, so that it produces in the soul of the Prophet ﷺ intense caution against disobedience and love of obedience. Then revelation continually attends to him, awakens him, and keeps him away from falling into what he has been forbidden, so that infallibility soon becomes a faculty in the Prophet by which he dislikes sins. Thus the root of infallibility is the furthest limit of piety, which is the fruit of obligation. With this, the statement of our companions can be reconciled: "Infallibility is the non-creation of sin while the capacity to sin remains," with the statement of the Mu'tazila: "It is a faculty that prevents the will toward sins." The former looked at the origin, and the latter looked at the end. By this it also becomes clear that infallibility does not negate obligation or the merit earned by acts of obedience.

Nafi' and Hisham on the authority of Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far recited "khalisati" without tanwin, its being construed as a genitive construction with ﴿dhikra al-dar﴾. The construction is explicative (bayaniyyah), because "dhikra al-dar" is itself the sincere quality, as if it were said: "by the remembrance of the Abode." It is neither an adjective-noun construction nor a verbal noun construction with its object or its subject. The word "khalisah" was mentioned to occur in a general way, then specified by the genitive construction, to alert to the subtlety of this sincerity as indicated. The definiteness is by the genitive construction, because it is the furthest route to definiteness in this context.

The majority recited "khalisatin" with tanwin, so "dhikra al-dar" is in apposition (ʿatf bayan) or an identical substitution (badal mutabiq). The purpose of generality and specificity is evident.

The genitive construction of "khalisah" with "dhikra al-dar" in Nafi's reading is of the type of adjective to noun, and its substitution for it in the majority's reading is of the type of adjective substituted for the noun.

It is possible that "dhikra" is a synonym of "dhikr" with a kasra on the dhal, meaning good mention, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We gave them a tongue of truth, elevated﴾ [Maryam: 50], and then the Abode is the worldly abode.

[Page 279]
It is also possible that it is a synonym of "dhikr" with a damma on the dhal, meaning reflective remembrance and observance of the precepts of religion. Then "al-dar" is the Hereafter.

Joined to it is ﴿And indeed, they are with Us among the chosen and the excellent﴾, because it is among what prompts remembering them, that God chose them from among His creation, brought them near to Him, and made them excellent.

Al-akhyar is the plural of khayyir with the yaa shaddah, or the plural of khayr without the shaddah, like al-amwat as plural of mayyit and mayt. Both forms indicate intensity of the attribute in the one described.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verses 45–47:

[Page 276]
﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, men of strength and vision.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality: the remembrance of the Abode.﴾ ﴿And indeed, they are with Us among the chosen and the excellent.﴾ The discussion of this is like the discussion of its counterparts linguistically and in meaning.

The mention of these three is a mention for the sake of emulation and following their example. As for Abraham, peace be upon him, it is due to what is known of his patience over the harm of his people, his being thrown into the fire, and his being tested by being commanded to slaughter his son. As for the mention of Isaac and Jacob, it is a digression occasioned by the mention of Abraham, and because of the virtues they shared with their father, which are gathered in their shared meaning of His words ﴿men of strength and vision﴾, so that the Prophet ﷺ might emulate all three in strength in establishing the religion and insight into the realities of affairs.

Abraham is mentioned first because of his preeminence in the station of messengerhood and the sharia; the mention of his son is joined to him, and his son's son Jacob is joined to his son.

The majority recited ﴿And remember Our servants﴾ in the plural form, with Abraham and those joined to him all in apposition (ʿatf bayan). Ibn Kathir recited "ʿabdana" in the singular, with "Ibrahim" in apposition to "ʿabdana." The outcome of the two readings is one.

Al-Aydi (the hands) is the plural of yad in the sense of strength in religion, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the heaven We built with might (bi-aydin)﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 47] in Surat al-Dhariyat.

Al-Absar (the sight) is the plural of basar in a figurative sense, namely reflective contemplation known as insight (basirah), that is, looking carefully into observing the rulings of God, exalted is He, and seeking His pleasure.

The clause ﴿Indeed, We purified them﴾ is the reason for the command to remember them, because their remembrance brings the one who remembers to emulate them in their sincerity and the hope of attaining what they attained of election and preeminence in goodness.

Akhlasnahum (We purified them): We made them sincere (khalisin), so the hamza is for transitivity, meaning: We cleansed them from the filth of souls, so their souls became pure of the defects that befall humans. This sincerity is the meaning of the infallibility (ʿis-mah) necessary for prophethood.

ʿIsmah (infallibility): a power that God places in the soul of the Prophet, which turns him away from doing what is sinful in his religion against God, exalted is He, whether deliberately or inadvertently, and from what would incur aversion and contempt among people of sound intellect in his community's era.

The pillars of infallibility are four. The first: a property of the soul that God creates, which requires a faculty preventing disobedience.

The second: the attainment of knowledge of the blameworthiness of sins and the praiseworthiness of acts of obedience.

The third: the confirmation of that knowledge through the successive revelation and clarification from God, exalted is He.

The fourth: reproach from God for leaving the better course and for forgetfulness.

The attribution of sincerity to God, exalted is He, is because it is a matter that does not arise in the human soul except through a special placement from God, exalted is He, and a divine providence, such that the dominance of desire is removed from the soul in every state, and the soul is directed to pure good. Nothing remains in the soul except slight impulses, which the soul quickly abandons as soon as they occur. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, my heart is veiled, so I seek forgiveness from God seventy times a day."

The "ba'" in "bi-khalisah" denotes cause, alerting to the cause of their infallibility. This cause is expressed in a general way, to alert that it is a great and subtle matter that cannot be conceived in its essence but is known in its aspect. For this reason, this cause is evoked by a derived descriptor from the verb akhlasnahum, in the manner of the Prophet's ﷺ saying to one who asked him about his abstention from eating the lizard: "There comes to me from God a presence (hadirah)," meaning a presence that cannot be described. Then this sincerity is explained by the furthest that language can express, namely that it is ﴿the remembrance of the Abode﴾.

Dhikra (remembrance) is a noun of verbal action indicating the intensity of the meaning of the verbal noun, like ruj'a and buqya, because an increase in the form entails an increase in meaning. The Abode known to people like them is the Hereafter, that is:

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 48:

﴿And remember Isma'il, al-Yasa' and Dhu al-Kifl, each of them among the good.﴾ The mention of Isma'il is separated from his being counted together with his father Ibrahim and his brother Ishaq, because Isma'il was the grandfather of the Arab nation, that is, of most of it, for he is the father of the 'Adnanites; and he was a maternal grandfather to most of the Qahtanites, because Isma'il's wife was from Jurhum. For this reason, his mention was cut off from its coordination with the mention of Ibrahim, and the speech returns to him here.

As for his being joined in mention with al-Yasa' and Dhu al-Kifl by coordinating their names with his, the reason for this is subtle in eloquence, and it is not sufficient to explain it by what is contained in His saying ﴿each of them among the good﴾, because equality in goodness is established for all the prophets and messengers. So their mention after the mention of Isma'il is not more appropriate than the mention of others among those of goodness who are included by the word "the good" and "chosen." The condition for the acceptability of coordination with the particle waw (and) is that there be between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined a rational, imaginary, or conceptual connecting factor (jami'), as he said in al-Miftah. He said: "It is from here that they faulted Abu Tammam in his saying:

No, by He who knows that separation is bitterness, and that Abu al-Husayn is generous,

where he combined the bitterness of separation and the generosity of Abu al-Husayn, even though both are linked in the knowledge of God concerning them; and this is equivalent to the conjunction of Isma'il, al-Yasa' and Dhu al-Kifl in that they are among the good in this verse."

Page 280

So we must seek the subtle point which made the coordination of al-Yasa' and Dhu al-Kifl with Isma'il fitting in this verse.

As for the coordination of al-Yasa' with Isma'il, it is because al-Yasa's position among the Children of Israel was like Isma'il's position among the children of Ibrahim, for al-Yasa' was in the position of a son to the messenger Elijah (Ilyas, Ilya), and Elijah used to defend the kings of Judah and the kings of Israel against worshipping idols, and al-Yasa' was in supporting him as Isma'il was in supporting Ibrahim. When Elijah was raised up to heaven, al-Yasa' took his place, as is clarified in the Second Book of Kings, chapters 1–2.

As for the coordination of Dhu al-Kifl with Isma'il, it is because he resembles Isma'il in the attribute of patience. God the Exalted said in Surat al-Anbiya': ﴿And Isma'il and Idris and Dhu al-Kifl, each of them among the patient﴾ [al-Anbiya: 85].

The majority read al-Yasa' with a hamza of elision (hamzat wasl) and one lam, and it is from the original form of the name in the Hebrew language, and the Arabs Arabized it with the lam, and it is not the definite article lam; so leave aside what they have prolonged about it. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a hamzat wasl and two lams, with the second lam doubled, and this is closer to its Hebrew original. It is a non-Arabic name that has been Arabized, and the hamza and the lam, or the two lams, are original (radical) letters.

The tanwin on "kullun" in His saying ﴿and each of them among the good﴾ is a replacement for the genitive noun omitted, that is, "and each of those three is among the good." The mention of al-Yasa' has already occurred in Surat al-An'am, and the mention of Dhu al-Kifl in Surat al-Anbiya'.

This is a dense passage, so I will translate it as it stands, keeping Qur'anic quotations in ﴿ ﴾ markers.

﴿This is a reminder. Indeed, for the God-fearing is a good place of return.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual abode, their doors opened for them.﴾ ﴿Reclining therein, they call for abundant fruit and drink.﴾ ﴿And with them will be women restraining their gaze, of equal age.﴾

This "This is a reminder" is a sentence that separates the preceding discourse from the following discourse, intended to transition from one purpose to another, like the phrase: "As for what follows, so-and-so," and like the bare demonstrative such as ﴿This, and indeed for the transgressors is an evil place of return﴾ [Sad: 55], and his saying, "That," ﴿And whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 30] in Surat al-Hajj. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "It is as the writer says when he has finished a section of his book and wishes to begin another: 'This' — and such and such had happened."

Page 281

This style of transition is what the scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamaʾ al-adab) call "al-iqtiḍāb" (abrupt transition), and it is the practice of the Arabs and those who came after them among the Mukhadramun. For this type they have two methods: to mention the predicate, as in this verse and in the words of authors, "This is a chapter on such-and-such"; or to omit the predicate, the demonstrative indicating the intended meaning, as in His saying, exalted is He, "That, and whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah" [al-Hajj: 30], meaning: that is the condition of those who acted upon what Ibrahim called them to, mentioned the name of Allah over their sacrifices and did not mention the names of idols; and His saying, "That, and whoever honours the rites of Allah" [al-Hajj: 32], meaning: that is the example of those who associated others with Allah; and His saying, after verses, "This, and indeed for the transgressors is an evil place of return" [Sad: 55], meaning: this is the return of the God-fearing. From this is the writer's saying: "This, and such and such had happened." The predicate was stated in His saying "This is a reminder" for the sake of emphasis on specifying the predicate, and because the intended purpose of what is pointed to is remembrance and emulation. Thus the listener does not take the demonstrative in the manner of a bare separation and an abrupt transition, while the word "dhikr" also carries the sense of a good reputation, meaning: a reminder about those named among the later generations, and also a reminder for those who emulate them, in accordance with both meanings in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44] in Surat al-Zukhruf.

From here it is possible that the demonstrative "this" refers to the Qur'an, i.e., the Qur'an is a reminder, and then the sentence is a new independent statement glorifying the status of the Qur'an, returning to the purpose of His saying, ﴿A Book We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses and that those of understanding may be reminded﴾ [Sad: 29].

The waw in "wa-inna lil-muttaqina" etc. may be a conjunction of mention, i.e., the preceding speech ends with our saying "This," and we conjoin to it "Indeed, for the God-fearing" etc. It may also be the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal).

The meaning of "ḥusn maʾab" has already been discussed.

The lam in "lil-muttaqin" is the lam of specification, i.e., for them is a good place of return on the Day of Recompense.

"Jannāt ʿadn" is in the accusative as an explanation (bayan) of "ḥusn maʾab." ʿAdn means perpetuity.

"Mufattaḥatan" is a circumstantial clause (ḥal) of "jannāt ʿadn," and the element governing the ḥal is what is contained in "lil-muttaqin" of the sense of a verb, namely "istiqrār" (settling), so the "al" in "al-abwab" is a substitute for a pronoun.

Page 282

The estimate is: "abwābuhā" (its doors), according to the view of the Kufan grammarians. But according to the Basran grammarians, "al-abwab" is an apposition (badal) of the pronoun in "mufattaḥatan," being a badal of inclusion or part, and the connecting link between it and the element it replaces is omitted, its estimate being: "al-abwab minha" (the doors of it). The opening of the doors is a metaphor for the enabling of enjoying its bliss, because the opening of doors entails permission to enter, and that entails leaving the one entering free to benefit from what is behind the doors.

His saying "reclining therein" has been mentioned nearby in Surat Ya Sin.

"Yadʿūna": they command that it be brought to them. One says: "daʿā bi-kadhā," meaning he asked for it to be brought.

The bāʾ in their saying "daʿā bi-kadhā" is for accompaniment, and the estimate is: he called for someone accompanying him such-and-such. ʿAdī ibn Zayd said:

"And they called for the morning draught one day, and there came a maid with a jug in her right hand."

He, exalted is He, said in Surat Ya Sin: ﴿For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they ask for﴾ [Ya Sin: 57].

"Muttakiʾīn" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause of "al-muttaqin," and it is a future (muqaddara) circumstance. The clause "yadʿūna" is a second circumstance, also future.

"Al-sharāb" is a name for what is drunk, and its use became predominantly for wine when there is no mention of water in the speech, as in His saying just before, ﴿This is a cool bath and drink﴾ [Sad: 42]. The tanwin of "sharāb" here is for magnification, meaning: a drink precious in its kind, like the saying of Abu Khirash al-Hudhali:

"Indeed I have come upon meat..."

﴿And with them are women restraining the gaze﴾. "ʿInda" is a adverb of nearby place, and "qāṣirāt al-ṭarf" is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning: women restraining their gaze. The definiteness of "al-ṭarf" is the definiteness of the genus, which covers the many, meaning: restraining their glances. "Al-ṭarf" is the look of the eye, and restricting the glance is directing it to a single viewed object, so it may mean: they restrain their glances upon their husbands. Thus the restrained glances are their own glances.

The attribution of "qāṣirāt" to the pronoun "hunna" is a literal attribution, meaning: they do not direct their glances to others, and this is a metaphor for their love for their husbands.

It may also mean: they restrict the glances of their husbands to themselves, so the husbands' glances do not turn to others, being content with their beauty. This is a metaphor for the perfection of their beauty in the eyes of their husbands, such that their admiration does not attach to others. Thus the restrained glances are the glances of their husbands, and the attribution of "qāṣirāt" to them is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), since their beauty is the cause of restraining the husbands' glances, as they are the ones possessing the cause of restraint.

"Atrāb" is the plural of "tirb," with a kasra on the taʾ and a sukun on the rāʾ, and it is a name for one whose age is equal to the age of the one he is attributed to. One says: "he is the tirb of so-and-so," and "she is the tirb of so-and-so" (feminine), and the form "tirb" does not take the feminine marker.

The meaning intended is: they are of equal age to one another, and they are of equal age to their husbands, because affection is stronger among peers.

The apparent meaning is that "atrāb" is a description applying to all the women of Paradise, both the created beings of Paradise and the women who were wives in the world of the people of Paradise, so that none of them is younger in youth than another, and no inhabitant of Paradise is harmed by freshness being lacking when the women of another are more youthful, and so that the women of one of the God-fearing do not differ in the bloom of youth, such that the bliss with the less youthful would be less than the bliss with the more youthful among them.

The discussion of ﴿And with them are women restraining the gaze, with wide, beautiful eyes﴾ [al-Saffat: 48] has already been given in Surat al-Saffat.

This is the commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 53:

﴿This is what you are promised, for the Day of Reckoning.﴾ It is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), and it may be speech addressed to the God-fearing at the time the verse was revealed. In that case it emphasizes the content of the clause ﴿And indeed, for the God-fearing is a excellent place of return.﴾ [Sad: 49]. The demonstrative ("this") thus refers to what was mentioned earlier, namely the phrase "an excellent place of return." The demonstrative here differs from its earlier use in ﴿This is a reminder﴾. The near demonstrative is used, treating the referent as if it were a present, visible referent, which indicates that its occurrence is certain, and as good news to the God-fearing. The expression "you are promised" (tu'adun) in the present tense is to be taken at its apparent meaning.

It may also be speech said to the God-fearing in Paradise, in which case the clause is the object of an omitted verb (maqul qawl mahdhuf), standing in the position of a second circumstantial state (hal thaniyah) relating to the God-fearing. The implied sense is: "said to them: This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning." The speaking is either from the angels, like the verse ﴿Enter Paradise for what you used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 32], or from God Most High Himself, like His words to their opposites ﴿And We will say: Taste the punishment of the burning﴾ [Al 'Imran: 181].

The demonstrative then refers to the bliss they are witnessing.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "tu'adun" with the second-person pronoun of address. On the first possibility this is an iltifat (shift) from the third person to the second, to honor the God-fearing by the dignity of being present for God's address. On the second possibility, the address to them is on its apparent meaning. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr alone read "yu'adun" with the third-person prefix. On the first possibility this is a shift away from addressing them directly to addressing the transgressors, for greater humiliation of them. The demonstrative refers to what was mentioned of the excellent place of return. On the second possibility it is likewise: the speech is directed to the people of the gathering, in order to disgrace the transgressors and bring regret and grief upon them. The demonstrative refers to the bliss being witnessed.

The lam in "li-yawm al-hisab" is the lam of cause (lam al-'illah), meaning: you were promised it for the sake of the Day of Reckoning. The sense is: for the sake of the recompense on the Day of Reckoning. Since reckoning signals recompense, the day itself is made the cause. This lam also carries, secondarily, the sense of timing, as in God's words ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra': 78], treating the time as if it were a cause. For this reason the jurists said: "The times of the prayers are causes (asbab)."

Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 54:

﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end.﴾ The placement (mahmal) of the demonstrative noun "hadha" (this) follows the two possibilities mentioned in the preceding discourse.

The shift from the pronoun to the demonstrative noun is for the utmost care in distinguishing it and directing the listener's mind toward it.

The term "rizq" (provision) is applied to a blessing, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "If one of them, when he lies with his wife, were to say: 'O Allah, keep Satan away from us, and keep Satan away from what You have provided us,' and then a child were born to them, Satan would never harm that child." So he called the child "rizq."

The emphasis by "inna" (indeed) is for emphasis. And "nafad" means cessation and cessation of existence (zawal).

This is so. Indeed, for the transgressors is an evil return. ﴿Hell, they will burn in it, so wretched is the resting place.﴾ The demonstrative ﴿هَذا﴾ (this) is used here to move from one subject to another, as a closing of the subject that preceded it.

The discussion of it is the same as the discussion of ﴿This is a reminder. And indeed, for the righteous is an excellent return.﴾ [Sad: 49]. The implied meaning is: this is the condition of the righteous, or this is the matter, or this is as has been mentioned.

The clause ﴿يَصْلَوْنَها﴾ (they will burn in it) is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to ﴿جَهَنَّمَ﴾ (Hell). It is an emphatic circumstantial clause for the meaning of the preposition ﴿لِ﴾ (for), which governs ﴿الطّاغِينَ﴾ (the transgressors). The meaning of the preposition is that Hell is specifically for them, and its being specific to them is their experiencing its punishment, because punishment is intrinsic to Hell.

The ṭāghī (transgressor) is one who is characterized by ṭughyān (transgression), which is: exceeding the limit in pride and self-magnification. What is meant by them is the great leaders of the polytheists, because they were arrogant with their status against accepting Islam, turned away from the call of the Messenger (ﷺ) with pride and mockery, and ruled that the common people of their tribe should keep away from the Prophet (ﷺ), from the Muslims, and from listening to the Qur'an. They are: Abu Jahl, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, al-Walid ibn Utbah, al-'As ibn Wa'il, and their likes.

The fa' (the coordinating fa', al-fa' al-'atifah, "so") in ﴿فَبِئْسَ المِهادُ﴾ (so wretched is the resting place) indicates the sequential order of the report and its causation by what precedes it.
