﴿This is a host rushing in with you. No welcome to them! They are going to burn in the Fire.﴾ This is the beginning of a speech that relates the mutual disputing of the polytheists in the Fire among themselves when they enter it, as indicated by His words at the end of the passage: ﴿Indeed, that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad 38:64]. Qatadah and Ibn Zayd also interpreted it this way.

Their dispute among themselves takes place so that they may increase in hatred, by adding to their physical punishment the punishment of their own souls, through some of them blaming and mistreating others.

The style of the speech requires a speaker who utters it, and the style of the exchange requires that the speakers be the tyrants who will have the worst of the final return, because they are the root of this matter. The sense is: the tyrants say to one another, "This is a host rushing in with you," meaning they say, pointing to a group of the people of the Fire who have been forced in among them, who are not their equals or of their rank, and who are the group of followers among the polytheists who followed the tyrants in the worldly life. This is what His words indicate: ﴿You brought it upon us﴾ [Sad 38:60], meaning: you are the cause of bringing this punishment upon us. This agrees with the meaning of its parallels in the Qur'an, such as His words ﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾ [al-A'raf 7:38], up to His words ﴿for what you used to earn﴾ [al-A'raf 7:39], in Surat al-A'raf; His words ﴿when those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:166], in Surat al-Baqarah; and His words ﴿they turn to one another, questioning﴾ [al-Saffat 37:27] and the verses that follow in Surat al-Saffat. Most clear of all of this is His words at the end of this verse: ﴿Indeed, that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad 38:64].

The clause of the omitted speech is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the tyrants.

The clause "This is a host..." up to its end is the quoted content of the omitted speech.

The word fawj (host, group) means a large company of people; it was discussed earlier in His words ﴿and on the Day We gather from every nation a host﴾ [al-Naml 27:83], in Surat al-Naml.

Iqtiham (rushing in) means entering among people by force. The word ma'a ("with") indicates that the speakers are the ones followed, and that the group who rushed in are their followers, who have been placed among them in the manner of a follower with a leader, through signs that make this apparent.

The clause "No welcome to them!" is an interposed, resumptive clause, for the purpose of expressing disdain for the group.

"No welcome" (la marhaban) is a negation of a phrase that the one visited says to his visitor, and it is a performative expression of welcoming the arrival. Marhaban is a verbal noun in the form mafal, namely al-rahb (with a dammah on the ra'), and it is in the accusative governed by an omitted verb indicated by the meaning of rahb, meaning: you have come to a wide, spacious place, that is, a place of spaciousness. When they wish to express aversion to the arrival and to invoke a curse upon him, they say: "No welcome to him!" as if they intended negation by the whole phrase:

*No welcome to a morrow, nor family with it, if the separation of loved ones is to occur in that morrow.*

This is like what they say in praise, "How excellent!" (habbadha), and when they want to express blame they say "How not excellent!" (la habbadha). The verse of Kanzah, mother of Shamlah al-Minqari, satirizing the companion of Dhu al-Rummah, combines both:

*Ah, how excellent are the people of that gathering, except that when Mayy is mentioned, then how not excellent is the one named!*

The meaning of rahb in all of this is the figurative spaciousness, which is joy and meeting what is desired in that place. This is shown by the fact that mere spaciousness does not benefit the visitor. They only said this because they disliked being in one place together with their followers, acting according to the disposition of their pre-Islamic ignorance of arrogance and contempt for the weak.

The clause ﴿They are going to burn in the Fire﴾ is a second predicate of the demonstrative noun, and the predicate is used to express their irritation, meaning: they are crowding us in the narrowness of the Fire, as indicated by their words ﴿rushing in with you. No welcome to them!﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verse 60:

﴿They say: "Nay, it is you! No welcome to you! You have brought this upon us, so evil is the abode!"﴾ Then the followers hear them and say, ﴿Nay, it is you! No welcome to you!﴾ as a turning away from their speech. The quoted speech is presented in the manner of dialogue, which is why the conjunction has been dropped. The meaning is: you are more deserving of abuse and hatred, that it be said to you, "No welcome to you," because you are the ones who brought this on yourselves and on us, through your enticing us to deny and to persist in disbelief.

"Bal" (bal, here) is for the idrab ibtali (the annulling turn away), to reject the abuse directed at them and to affirm that they are more deserving of it than they are.

The mention of the pronoun of the addressees in their saying ﴿antum la marhaban bikum﴾ ("you, no welcome to you") serves to disclaim their abuse, meaning: you are the abused, that is, you are more deserving of abuse than we are. This meaning is derived from the particle of negation (of annulment), not from the pronoun, because the pronoun has no implied meaning of its own, and because its position here does not require restriction (hasr) or emphasis (taqwiyya), since it is the subject of a performative (insha'i) sentence, meaning: "you, it is said to you: no welcome to you."

Since "marhaban" is an utterance of supplication (insha' du'a') in the form of a report, and its negation is an utterance of supplication for its opposite, the phrase "bihim" (with them) is an explanation of those for whom the supplication is directed, that is, a clarification to the listener that the supplication is against the owners of the pronoun governed by the preposition "ba'," so the "ba'" here is for clarification (li al-tabyin). Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "Bihim" is an explanation of those against whom the supplication is made. Al-Hamadhani said in his commentary on al-Kashshaf: he means the technical bayan (explanation), as if someone were to say: "With whom does this welcome occur?" and it is answered: "With them." This is like "hayta laka" (come, I am ready for you), meaning that the "ba'" in it has the sense of the "lam" of clarification.

Ibn Hisham omitted this meaning in his discussion of the meanings of "ba'." Al-Hamadhani indicated that it derives from the sense of causation (sababiyya). In my opinion, the better view is that it derives from the sense of accompaniment (musahaba) by way of the subordinate metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya), and then the use of "ba'" in such a construction became common in their speech until it became like a literal usage, because when it became an utterance of supplication, the consideration of reporting the occurrence of welcome with them or because of them no longer remained, as becomes apparent upon reflection.

The clause ﴿antum qaddamtumuhu lana﴾ ("you brought it upon us") is the reason for transferring the cause of the abuse to them, meaning: because you brought the punishment upon us. The pronoun of the object in "qaddamtumuhu" refers to the punishment that is witnessed, which is present in the mind though not mentioned explicitly, like ﴿hatta tawarat bil-hijab﴾ [Sad: 32].

The placing of "antum" before the verbal predicate "qaddamtumuhu" conveys restriction (hasr), meaning: no one else misled us, so you are the ones deserving of the punishment.

Taqdim (advancing/bringing forward) means placing a thing in front of another. The Exalted said: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning. That is for what your hands have sent forward﴾ [al-Anfal: 50]. So bringing the punishment forward for them means placing it before them, that is, placing it where they will find it upon their arrival. The attribution of bringing forward the punishment to the addressees is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because the leaders were the cause of bringing the punishment upon their followers by misleading them, and the punishment was a recompense for the misguidance. The punishment was described as "brought forward," though what is actually brought forward is the deed that deserved the punishment; this is a rational metaphor in the object, so two rational metaphors are combined in the phrase "qaddamtumuhu."

The phrase ﴿fa-bi'sa al-qarar﴾ ("so evil is the abode") occupies the same position as the earlier phrase ﴿fa-bi'sa al-mihad﴾, and it is a condemnation of their dwelling in Hell, a reproach for what they brought upon themselves. The meaning is: "so evil is the abode is what you brought forward for us," that is, the punishment. "Qarar" means staying, remaining.

[Page 291]

﴿They will say: "Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, add to him a double punishment in the Fire."﴾ *Qalū* (they said), that is, the crowd that rushes in, which is the group of followers. This is from the speech of those who said, ﴿Rather, you—there is no welcome for you﴾ [38:60], because their words *"man qaddama lanā hādhā"* (whoever brought this upon us) specify this interpretation. For this reason, it is appropriate for the reader to ask about the reason for repeating the verb *qālū* and about the reason it is not joined by a conjunction to their first statement.

As for the repetition of the verb of saying, it serves to show that the speakers are the followers. The verb of saying is repeated as an emphasis of the first verb, in order to emphasize the subject of the saying, following on from the fact that it can refer to the speakers' pronoun.

The purpose of quoting their words is to warn the leaders of the polytheists about the consequences of their leadership and their authority, by which they bring calamities upon their followers, so that they throw them into the pit of evil. Thus the followers find no recompense after the escape except to seek a doubling of the punishment for them.

As for the verb *qālū* being stripped of the conjunction (*al-ʿāṭif*), it is because it is intended as a verbal emphasis (*al-tawkīd al-lafẓī*), and verbal emphasis is in the pattern of what it emphasizes.

The quoting of this statement in this manner should not be confused with the quoting of dialogues, so that one might suppose it is the speech of the other group. For the invocation under the heading *"man qaddama lanā hādhā"* (whoever brought this upon us) makes clear that its speakers are those who say, "You brought it upon us," and that those who brought it upon them are the tyrants. The meaning of this verse is found in the verse of Surat al-Aʿrāf: ﴿Its latter ones will say to its former ones, "Our Lord, these led us astray, so give them a double punishment from the Fire"﴾ [7:38].

In his words *"man qaddama lanā hādhā,"* *man* is a relative pronoun (*mawṣūla*), and the clause *"fazidhu"* (so add to him) is the predicate of *man*. The attaching of the predicate with *fa* (the particle *fāʾ*) follows the treatment of the relative pronoun as a conditional (*shart*) in attaching its predicate with *fa*, which is common. This was discussed earlier at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of God—give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [9:34], in Surat Barāʾa.

*Al-ḍiʿf* (the double), with a *kasra* on the *ḍād*, is used as the verbal noun of *ḍaʿʿafa* and *ḍāʿafa*. Both are nouns of multiplying (*ism al-taḍʿīf* and *ism al-muḍāʿafa*), meaning the repetition of a quantity and the repetition of strength. It is among the terms whose meanings are correlative, like "half" and "pair."

[Page 292]

It is also used as a noun meaning the thing that has been multiplied. This is the regular form of the pattern *fiʿl* with a *kasra* on the first letter and a sukūn on the middle letter, so it means "the thing that has been multiplied," because the pattern *fiʿl* indicates that which has been subjected to the action. It is like *dhiḥ*, meaning *madhūḥ* (slaughtered).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verses 62–63:

﴿And they will say, "What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the evil?"﴾ ﴿Did we take them in mockery, or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ This is coordinated with ﴿This is a host rushing in with you﴾ [Sad: 59], according to what was estimated in it of a deleted verb of saying, as has preceded. So this is from the speech of the tyrants, for they used to belittle the Muslims.

The interrogation in ﴿What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men﴾ is an interrogation that some of them direct to others, expressing dismay at not seeing those whom they knew to be among the Muslims. It is a figurative expression for the reproach of some of them to others for their belittling of the Muslims and their admission of error in their reckoning.

So the interrogation is not about their not seeing the Muslims in Hell as a genuine interrogation arising from a supposition that they would find the men of the Muslims with them, since it does not occur to the tyrants that the men of the Muslims would be with them; how could it, when they know that their state is the opposite of theirs, so they do not imagine them to be with them in punishment. It is possible that the interrogation is genuine: they ask about the fate of the Muslims because they do not see them that Day, since they know that people have gone to another realm, which is the one they were warned of. Their saying ﴿What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men﴾ etc. would then serve as a preface to their saying ﴿Did we take them in mockery﴾, according to both readings that will be mentioned below.

Al-ashrar: the plural of sharr, which has the meaning of ashirr (the wicked), like al-akhyar, the plural of khayr in the sense of akhyar (the better). Or it is the plural of shirrir, the opposite of good, i.e., those described by an evil state. That is: "We used to reckon them wretched, having lost the pleasure of life by following Islam and accepting the hardship of livelihood." They mean the likes of Bilal, 'Ammar ibn Yasir, Suhayb, Khabbab and Salman. The intended meaning is not that they count them as evil in the Hereafter, deserving punishment, for they did not believe in the Resurrection.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read ﴿atta-khadhnahum﴾ with a hamzat qat' which is the hamzat al-istifham (the interrogative hamza). The hamzat al-wasl of the verb "ittakhadhna" was deleted, because it does not remain with the interrogative hamza, owing to the impossibility of pausing on the interrogative hamza. So the clause ﴿atta-khadhnahum﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the clause ﴿What is [the matter] with us that we do not see men﴾.

And ﴿am﴾ is a particle of transition (idrab), and the estimate is: "Rather, our eyes have turned away from them."

Al-zaygh: the inclining away from a direction, i.e., our eyes inclined away from their direction, so we did not look at them.

The "al" in ﴿al-absar﴾ is a replacement for the genitive pronoun, i.e., "our eyes," so the meaning is: "Was our belittling of them in the world a mistake?" It is expressed by their being taken in mockery, because in the verb ﴿atta-khadhnahum﴾ there is an allusion that they were not fit for mockery. This is a regret on their part for having mocked them.

Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Khalaf read ﴿ittakhadhnahum﴾ with a hamzat wasl, on the basis that the clause is a second attribute (sifah) of ﴿rijalan﴾. In this case ﴿am﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'ah), for transition away from their saying ﴿we took them in mockery﴾, i.e., "rather, their eyes have turned away from them."

Al-sukhriyy: an verbal noun (ism masdar) from "sakhira minhu," meaning he mocked him; so al-sukhriyy means mockery. It indicates intensity of mockery, because its yā' is originally the yā' of nisbah (relative), and the yā' of nisbah comes for emphasis in description.

Nafi', Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read it with a dammah on the sin. The rest read it with a kasrah on the sin, as has preceded in Surat al-Mu'minun.

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 38, verse 64:

﴿Indeed, that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire.﴾ This is a *tadhyil* (a concluding statement that restates and completes what precedes it), bringing to an end the description of the state of the tyrants (*al-taghun*) and their followers, their punishment, and their disputing.

The emphasis of the statement by the particle of emphasis (*harf al-tawkid*) is considered in view of what the statement implies: an indirect warning to the polytheists, and an affirmation of their gathering (*hashr*) and recompense, that it is true, meaning established. This is like His saying: ﴿And indeed, the Religion will surely occur﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 6].

[Page 294]

The reference is to the exchange of speech related about them. The exchange is called "disputing" (*takhasum*), meaning mutual contention, even though no actual argument took place between them. The tyrants did not answer the group (*fawj*) when it said: ﴿Nay, you! No welcome for you﴾ [Sad: 60]. But since the exchange included something more severe than contention, namely each party's saying to the other, ﴿No welcome for you﴾ [Sad: 60], the reproach was more severe than mutual contention, so the name "disputing" was applied to it literally. The word *khisam* (contention) was already discussed at His saying, ﴿These are two disputants﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], in Surah al-Hajj.

This disputing is attributed to the people of the Fire as a whole, by reference to the majority of its people, because most of the people of the Fire are people of doctrinal misguidance (*al-dalalat al-i'tiqadiyya*), and they do not think it possible that they would be callers to misguidance or followers of its callers. Thus all of them engage in this disputing. As for those among the sinners in the Fire, many of them committed their sin only as followers of their own desires, while knowing that what they were doing was misguidance, and no one had enticed them to it.

The people of the Fire are those who abide in it eternally, like the saying "the people of such-and-such a town," which does not include the stranger among them. Moreover, at the time this verse was revealed, there were in Mecca none but righteous Muslims and polytheists. Therefore the description "people of the Fire" at that time applies only to the polytheists, not to Muslim sinners.

His saying, ﴿disputing of the people of the Fire﴾, is either the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated form being: "and it is the disputing of the people of the Fire," and the sentence is a resumption (*isti'naf*) to further clarify what the demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*) refers to; or it is in the nominative as a second predicate of *inna*; or it is in apposition (*badal*) to *haqq* ("true").

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verses 65–66:

﴿Say, "I am but a warner, and there is no god except Allah, the One, the Subduer."﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, the Mighty, the Forgiving.﴾ This refers back to His words ﴿And the disbelievers say, "This is a magician, a liar."﴾ [Sad: 4] up to His words ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ [Sad: 8]. When their denial was answered by likening their situation to that of the denying nations before them, and by likening the situation of the Messenger ﷺ to that of the prophets who were patient, and this was thoroughly covered in a manner that is convincing, the discourse returned to establishing the station of the Messenger ﷺ among his people. So Allah commanded him to say, "I am but a warner," in response to their saying ﴿This is a magician, a liar.﴾ [Sad: 4]

And to say, "There is no god except Allah," in response to their denial of monotheism, such as their saying ﴿Has he made the gods one God?﴾ [Sad: 5]. So the sentence is a fresh, independent resumption.

The mention of the attribute "the One" is an emphasis on the meaning of "there is no god except Allah," alluding to the refutation of their denial. The mention of the attribute "the Subduer" is an allusion that threatens the polytheists with the fact that Allah is able to subdue them, that is, to overpower them. The discussion of subjugation (al-qahr) was already presented at His words, exalted is He, ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am: 18] in Surah al-An'am.

Following this with the attribute ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ is an explicit statement of the generality of His lordship and that He has no partner in any of it.

The description "the Mighty" is a preparation for the description "the Forgiving," i.e., the Forgiving out of might and capability, not out of weakness, flattery, or regard for an equal party.

The purpose of the attribute "the Forgiving" here is to invite the polytheists to monotheism after threatening them with the import of the attribute "the Subduer," so that they do not despair of acceptance of repentance because of the abundance of the threats directed at them, following the Qur'an's usual practice of following intimidation with encouragement and vice versa.

**[Page 296]**

The repetition of the command to speak here is a new, resumptive statement (*isti'naf*, a sentence beginning a fresh point). The avoidance of a conjunction that would link the saying *"it is a momentous news"* to the earlier saying, *"I am only a warner"*, indicates concern for this saying, so that it is not presented as a dependent clause of another saying, which would weaken the listeners' attention to understanding it.

The sentence ﴿Say: It is a momentous news﴾ ﴿from which you turn away﴾ may be a fresh, initiating statement (*isti'naf ibtida'i*), shifting from the theme of describing the condition of the people of the gathering (*al-mahshar*) to the theme of the story of the creation of Adam and the wretchedness of Satan. In that case the pronoun *"huwa"* (it) is a pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr sha'n*), explained by what follows it, and what clarifies what follows it is His saying: ﴿When your Lord said to the angels: "I am creating a human from clay."﴾ [Sad: 71]. This is presented as a preface to the story, to arouse interest in receiving it. Thus the intended "news" is the news of the creation of Adam and what happened after it. The pronoun in *"yakhtaṣimūn"* (they dispute) refers to the *al-Mala' al-A'lā* (the Exalted Assembly), because *mala'* means a group.

By "dispute" (*ikhtiṣām*) is meant the disagreement that took place between Satan and those angels who received God's command to prostrate to Adam. The angels are the Exalted Assembly, and Satan was among them, so he was counted among them before he was expelled from the heaven.

It is also possible that the sentence ﴿Say: It is a momentous news﴾ etc. is a closing statement (*tadhyīl*) for what preceded from His saying ﴿And indeed for the righteous is a good return﴾ [Sad: 49] up to this point. It is a closing that signals the elevation of this matter and the call to attentive reflection upon it and to taking a lesson from it.

On this reading, the pronoun *"huwa"* is a pronoun referring back to the preceding speech, interpreted as "the thing mentioned." It is therefore expressed with the singular pronoun to define it.

By "the news" is meant the report of the Gathering (*ḥashr*) and what is prepared in it for the righteous of a good return, and for the tyrants of an evil return, and of the evil companionship of some of them with others, and their mutual reproach and dispute among themselves while they are in punishment, and their bewilderment about the reason why they did not find with them the believers whom they used to count among the wicked.

Describing the news as *"ʿaẓīm"* (momentous) is for emphasis (*tahwīl*), in the manner of His saying: ﴿About what are they asking one another? About the momentous news, about which they are in disagreement﴾ [An-Naba': 1–3]. The greatness of this news among the news of its kind (that is, news of evil) is like His saying: *"fasādun kabīr"* (great corruption). Thus the speech is complete at His saying: ﴿from which you turn away﴾.

Then the sentence ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly﴾ up to His saying *"a clear warner"* is a resumptive statement presenting proof of the truth of the news, that it is a revelation from God. Were it not a revelation, the Messenger (ﷺ) would have had no means of knowing these conditions, in the manner of His saying: ﴿You were not with them when they cast their pens, [to see] which of them would take charge of Mary, nor were you with them when they disputed﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 44]. Parallels to this kind of argument are numerous in the Qur'an.

**[Page 297]**

And the sentence ﴿When your Lord said to the angels: "I am creating a human"﴾ [Sad: 71] to its end is an initiating resumptive statement.

On this reading, the pronoun in *"yakhtaṣimūn"* refers to the people of the Fire, from His saying ﴿the dispute of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad: 64], since there is no dispute among the people of the Exalted Assembly.

The meaning is: I had no knowledge of the unseen world and what takes place in it, by way of reporting what will happen, when the people of the Fire dispute in the Fire on the Day of Resurrection.

On both interpretations, the meaning of *"antum ʿanhu muʿriḍūn"* (you turn away from it) is that they are heedless of knowing it. They were informed of the news in its first meaning, and they will soon come to know the news in its second meaning.

The nominal sentence in His saying *"antum ʿanhu muʿriḍūn"* is used to convey the affirmation of their turning away and its firm establishment in them. As for their turning away from the news in its first meaning, its firm establishment in their souls is evident, for he had long warned them of the punishment of the Hereafter and described it, yet they paid it no heed and did not desist from their disbelief.

As for their turning away from the news in its second meaning, its firm establishment in their souls is understood as their not being prepared to take a lesson from its implication, namely recognizing that what they are in is an insinuation from Satan intended to harm them.

Perhaps this verse in this surah is the first thing revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioning the story of the creation of Adam, the prostration of the angels, and Iblis's refusal to prostrate. For in the order of revelation of the surahs of the Qur'an, no mention of the story of Adam is found in any surah revealed before it.

This is the reason for the preparatory introduction (*tawṭi'a*) to the story through means of care and emphasis which are absent from other passages, and because it is a news from which they were turning away.

Whatever the case, His saying *"antum ʿanhu muʿriḍūn"* is a rebuke to them and a mockery of them.

The sentence ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they disputed﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraḍ*) of communication, within the rebuke for turning away from the momentous news, and a proof for the certainty of the news on the ground that it is revealed by God, and the Messenger (ﷺ) has no way to know it except by God's revelation to him. The use of the verb *"kāna"* (was) indicates that the knowledge negated is in the past, before it was revealed to him, as He said: ﴿You were not with them when they cast their pens…﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 44] and His saying: ﴿You were not on the western side when We decreed the command to Moses, nor were you among the witnesses﴾ [Al-Qasas: 44].

The preposition *"bi"* in His saying *"bil-mala' al-a'lā"* (about the Exalted Assembly) is, on both meanings of "news," used to make the verb "knowledge" transitive, by implying the sense of encompassing (*iḥāṭa*). This is a common usage with the verb "knowledge." An example is in the hadith of the questioning of the two angels in the Ṣaḥīḥ: *"Then it is said to him: What is your knowledge of this man?"*

On the second meaning of "news," the *"bi"* may also be locative (*ẓarfiyya*), meaning: "I had no knowledge existing in the Exalted Assembly," that is, "I was not present in the Exalted Assembly." It is then like the *"bi"* in His saying: ﴿You were not on the western side when We decreed the command to Moses﴾ [Al-Qasas: 44].

*Al-Mala'* means a group of people with standing, and describing it as *"al-a'lā"* (exalted) is because the intended meaning is the assembly of the heavens, namely the angels, who have both a literal elevation and a figurative elevation in the sense of nobility.

*"Idh yakhtaṣimūn"* (when they dispute) is an adverbial clause (*ẓarf*) connected to the verb of "I had no knowledge of," meaning: "at the time when the people of the Exalted Assembly dispute," on one of the two interpretations, that is, at the time of the dispute between the angels and Iblis in the heaven.

The use of the present tense in place of the past is to intend the vivid recollection of the situation (*istiḥḍār al-ḥāla*). Or it means: at the time when the tyrants and their followers dispute in the Fire before the Exalted Assembly, that is, the angels of the Fire or the angels of the Gathering. The present tense here retains its original sense of the future.

*Al-ikhtiṣām* (disputing) is a reflexive form (*iftiʿāl*) from *khaṣama*, meaning to contend with someone and oppose him; it is therefore an intensified form of *khaṣama*.

The sentence ﴿It is only revealed to me that I am a clear warner﴾ [Sad: 70] explains the sentence ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they disputed﴾, meaning: I knew of that news only by revelation from God, and God revealed it to me only so that I might be a clear warner.

This sentence is constructed by two means of restriction (*qaṣr*): one is the method of negation and exception (*nafy wa istithnā'*), and the other is the method of *annamā* with a *hamza* that is open (*anna-mā*), which is the sister of *innamā* with a *hamza* that is kasra, in its meanings, among which is the restriction of meaning. No attention is paid to the view of those who deny that it expresses restriction, for *anna* with an open *hamza* is composed of *anna* with an open *hamza* and the *kāffa* particle *mā*. Yet *anna* with an open *hamza* is nothing but *inna* with a kasra on the *hamza*, changed to a fatḥa so as to express a verbal-noun meaning (*ma-ṣdariyy*) imbued with the verbal particle *an* in an elegant blend, which is made its distinctive mark by opening its *hamza* so that it resembles the verbal particle *an* in the opening of the *hamza* and resembles *inna* in the doubling of the *nūn*. This is among the subtle features of the construction of the Arabic language.

*Annamā* takes an open *hamza* when it is made governed by a governing word in the sentence. What the context here requires is that the opening of the *hamza* in *annamā* is for the sake of a cause-marking *lām* (*lām ta'līl*) that is understood and governs *annamā* in the genitive. The estimate is: "except because I am a warner," that is, "except for the reason of warning," meaning: the news of the Exalted Assembly was revealed to me only so that I might warn you with it; it is not merely for narration.

Thus the exception is from causes, and the verb *"yūḥā"* (is revealed) is treated as intransitive, meaning: "nothing is revealed to me as a revelation," so no object is estimated for it, because its benefit is slight and the benefit of stating the cause of the revelation is preferred.

On this estimate, the relation between the position of this sentence and the position of the sentence ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they disputed﴾, which it explains, and the position of the sentence ﴿Say: It is a momentous news, from which you turn away﴾, is complete. Without this estimate there would be no relation, if *"innamā anā nadhīrun mubīn"* were made an exception from the deputy subject of the revelation, by estimating: "nothing is revealed to me except that I am a clear warner," meaning: nothing is revealed to me except my being a warner. Though that estimate may first come to mind, upon reflection the preponderance of the cause-marking estimate becomes clear.

Thus the sentence ﴿It is only revealed to me that I am a clear warner﴾ conveys the restriction of the wisdom of the revelation he receives to the achieving of warning, and restricts the attribute of the Messenger (ﷺ) to the attribute of warning. These two restrictions imply a third restriction, namely that the reporting of the Qur'an is a revelation from God, and it is not "fables of the ancients," as they claimed.

Thus three restrictions occur in this sentence: two of them by the explicit wording, and the third by implication of the speech (*kināyat al-kalām*). To this meaning His saying points: ﴿You were not at the side of the mount when We called, but it is a mercy from your Lord, that you might warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾ [Al-Qasas: 46]. Of these restrictions, two are relative (*iḍāfiyyān*): the restriction of what is revealed to him to the cause of warning, and the restriction of the Messenger (ﷺ) to the attribute of warning. Both are a reversal (*qalb*) of their belief that they hear the Qur'an in order to take it as a jest, and of their belief that the Messenger (ﷺ) is a sorcerer or a madman.

From this it is known that the mention of the news of the creation of Adam is intended for the purpose of warning against the plot of Satan.

Abu Ja'far read *"illā innamā"* with a kasra on the *hamza* of *"innamā,"* on the estimate of a saying, meaning: "nothing is revealed except this speech."

Commentary of Ibn ‘Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 38, verses 71–74:

﴿When your Lord said to the angels: "I am going to create a human being from clay."﴾ ﴿So when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down before him in prostration.﴾ ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together.﴾ ﴿Except Iblis; he was arrogant and was among the disbelievers.﴾

The position of ﴿When your Lord said to the angels﴾ may be a fresh sentence (isti'naf, a resumptive new clause). If the "news" (al-naba') is understood to mean the news of the Gathering that was promised, then ﴿when﴾ (idh) is linked to a verb that has been omitted, whose estimated form is "Remember," in the style of His words: ﴿And indeed you receive the Qur'an from One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Naml: 6] ﴿when Moses said to his family: "I have perceived a fire"﴾ [al-Naml: 7], and similar verses.

As for taking the "news" to mean the news of the creation of Adam, then the clause ﴿when your Lord said﴾ is a substitute (badal, a partial substitution, badal ba'd min kull) for ﴿when they dispute﴾. This is because the disputation of the Exalted Assembly (al-Mala' al-A'la), on both of the two interpretations mentioned above, is not restricted to the matter of the story of Iblis. Al-Tirmidhi related with his chain of narration from Malik ibn Yakhamur, from the Prophet ﷺ, a lengthy hadith concerning the Prophet's ﷺ vision, in which he saw his Lord, the Exalted, and He said to him: "O Muhammad, about what does the Exalted Assembly dispute?" I said: "I do not know." He said it three times. Then after the third time, after Allah had opened (the understanding) to him, he said: "I said: 'About the expiations (al-kaffarat).' He said: 'What are they?' I said: 'Walking on foot to the good deeds and sitting in the mosque.'" He mentioned other righteous deeds. He did not mention their disputing about the matter of the creation of Adam. Al-Tirmidhi said: "It is a hadith hasan sahih." Al-Bukhari said about it: "It is more authentic than others similar to it in meaning." Al-Bukhari did not include it in his Sahih. **Page 303**

That is: God addressed Iblis. There is no doubt that this address at that time was conveyed through one of the angels, because when Iblis became arrogant he had departed from the attribute of angelhood, so he was no longer fit to receive direct address from God. Nor was he of higher rank than the messengers, concerning whom God said: ﴿It is not for any human that God should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or that He send a messenger who reveals by His permission what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 51]. On this basis, the dialogue related here takes place through an angel, and the dispute between him and the angels is according to making the pronoun in *yakhtasimun* (they dispute) refer to the Exalted Assembly (*al-Mala' al-A'la*), as has already been explained.

The verb *qala* (he said) is used without a conjunction, following the manner of exchanged speech. A passage close to this verse has preceded in Surat al-Hijr, except that here he says *ma mana'aka an tasjud* ("what prevented you from prostrating"), meaning: what prevented you from prostration. In Surat al-A'raf, the phrasing is *an la tasjud* ("that you do not prostrate"), with *la* being extra (*za'ida*, i.e., a grammatical particle added for emphasis). Here it is related that God said to him ﴿for that which I created with My hands﴾, meaning: I created it by My power, that is, a special creation, direct and immediate, for the matter of bringing into being. Thus the connection of this creation was closer than the connection of the existence of beings that are brought about through causes which they directly undergo, such as gestation and birth, as is well known in the coming-into-being of creatures from their origins. There is no doubt that the creation of Adam contains extra care and a closer honour of connection. Thus "the two hands" is a figure for Adam's coming into being from the mere command of bringing into existence, applied to clay in the manner of a potter shaping a vessel from clay, as he shapes it with his hands. The early generations (*al-salaf*) affirmed that "the two hands" is a specific attribute of God, Exalted, because they occur in the Qur'an, while being firmly committed to declaring God free of resemblance to created things and of corporeality. Their intention was caution against subjecting the attributes of God to the judgement of opinions, or that deficient intellects should apply to God's attributes what they are familiar with, as in ﴿and that you may be brought up under My eye﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], and He said elsewhere ﴿indeed, you are under Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48]. The discussion of such analogous verses has preceded at the beginning of Surat Al 'Imran.

In addressing this question to Iblis there is a cutting off of any excuse for him. The meaning is: is it because you magnify yourself without right, or because you are among those of high station? By "high station" is meant nobility, that is, among those who are exalted over Adam, so he does not deserve that you should honour him. Iblis answered with something that is difficult for the second part of the question. It becomes clear that he considered himself more excellent than Adam, because he was created from fire while Adam was created from clay, meaning: fire is more excellent than clay, in his opinion.

He referred to Adam by the relative pronoun *ma* ("that which"), and at that point he was a human being, because the angels' prostration to Adam occurred after his creation and his being taught the names, as in Surat al-Baqarah. The view of the people of verification (*ahl al-tahqiq*) is supported by the fact that *ma* is not restricted to non-rational beings; there are many instances of this in the Qur'an and in other Arabic speech.

His saying "I am better than him" is a statement of Satan, related in the manner of dialogues.

The clause ﴿You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ explains the clause "I am better than him." Iblis based his excuse on the premise that fire is better than clay. The Qur'an does not mention that God refuted this premise, because it was too contemptible for that; so He cursed him and expelled him, because he claimed a falsehood and disobeyed his Lord out of arrogance. His total expulsion nullified his knowledge and refuted his argument. However, the light found in fire is an accidental light subsisting in the glowing bodies called fire, and fire has no self-subsistence; for this reason its existence cannot be separated from that which kindles it.

As for the meaning of Satan's being created from fire: the beginning of the formation of the primary atom that constitutes the essence of his being is from the element of fire, and then that atom mixes with other elements such as air. God knows best what that is.

**Page 304**

As for the meaning of Adam's being created from clay: the beginning of the formation of the particles of his body is from the element of earth, and there was introduced into those particles what they were mixed with, such as the elements of air, water and fire, and what arises from that composition of chemical elements and electrical force, by the totality of which the reality of the human being is constituted.

"From" (*min*) in both places is for the starting point (*ibtida'iyya*), not for partitive meaning (*tab'idiyya*).

The early philosophers and physicians have firmly held that the element of fire is more noble than the element of earth (which is also expressed as "the land"), because fire is subtle and luminous in colour, while earth is dense and dark in colour.

Al-Shirazi said in his commentary on *Kulliyyat al-Qanun* (Universal Principles of the Canon): Although fire is preferred over earth for what has been mentioned, earth is preferred over it in that it is good for animals and plants, and is not corrupting through its coldness, unlike fire, which is corrupting through its heat, for it is extreme in heat, and so on.

The truth is that the excellence of the elements does not entail the excellence of the beings produced from them, because the elements are simple bodies, and created beings are not formed from their mere components; rather, created beings are formed through composition among the elements. The human bodies are composed of all the elements. The human spirit is a subtle luminous entity, by which the human being excels over all composites, in that there is within him a angelic part in which he shares with the angels. For this reason, his Creator, exalted and sanctified be He, asked him to join himself to the angels, and this joining was fully realised in the prophets and messengers. On account of this we say that the prophets and messengers are more excellent than the angels, since both groups are equal in being purely luminous, and the group of prophets is distinguished by having attained those ranks through election and obedience. Therefore Iblis has no proof for preferring himself over Adam; he was merely struck by an errant doubt, and for this reason he was recompensed for his refusal to prostrate to him with expulsion from the Exalted Assembly.

We have expanded on this discussion here to refute the doubts of a group of heretics (*malahida*) who promote the doubt of Iblis as a way of attacking religion, not out of belief in the devils. Let them know that even if we concede that fire is nobler than clay, this would not require that what arises from fire be more excellent than what arises from clay, because the created being is a composite of elements and components of varying degrees, and composition may add nobility to the primary matter, and may add baseness to it. Excellence is established only by perfection in essence and in effects.

That is: God addressed Iblis. There is no doubt that this address at that time was conveyed through one of the angels, because when Iblis became arrogant he had departed from the attribute of angelhood, so he was no longer fit to receive direct address from God. Nor was he of higher rank than the messengers, concerning whom God said: ﴿It is not for any human that God should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or that He send a messenger who reveals by His permission what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 51]. On this basis, the dialogue related here takes place through an angel, and the dispute between him and the angels is according to making the pronoun in *yakhtasimun* (they dispute) refer to the Exalted Assembly (*al-Mala' al-A'la*), as has already been explained.

The verb *qala* (he said) is used without a conjunction, following the manner of exchanged speech. A passage close to this verse has preceded in Surat al-Hijr, except that here he says *ma mana'aka an tasjud* ("what prevented you from prostrating"), meaning: what prevented you from prostration. In Surat al-A'raf, the phrasing is *an la tasjud* ("that you do not prostrate"), with *la* being extra (*za'ida*, i.e., a grammatical particle added for emphasis). Here it is related that God said to him ﴿for that which I created with My hands﴾, meaning: I created it by My power, that is, a special creation, direct and immediate, for the matter of bringing into being. Thus the connection of this creation was closer than the connection of the existence of beings that are brought about through causes which they directly undergo, such as gestation and birth, as is well known in the coming-into-being of creatures from their origins. There is no doubt that the creation of Adam contains extra care and a closer honour of connection. Thus "the two hands" is a figure for Adam's coming into being from the mere command of bringing into existence, applied to clay in the manner of a potter shaping a vessel from clay, as he shapes it with his hands. The early generations (*al-salaf*) affirmed that "the two hands" is a specific attribute of God, Exalted, because they occur in the Qur'an, while being firmly committed to declaring God free of resemblance to created things and of corporeality. Their intention was caution against subjecting the attributes of God to the judgement of opinions, or that deficient intellects should apply to God's attributes what they are familiar with, as in ﴿and that you may be brought up under My eye﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], and He said elsewhere ﴿indeed, you are under Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48]. The discussion of such analogous verses has preceded at the beginning of Surat Al 'Imran.

In addressing this question to Iblis there is a cutting off of any excuse for him. The meaning is: is it because you magnify yourself without right, or because you are among those of high station? By "high station" is meant nobility, that is, among those who are exalted over Adam, so he does not deserve that you should honour him. Iblis answered with something that is difficult for the second part of the question. It becomes clear that he considered himself more excellent than Adam, because he was created from fire while Adam was created from clay, meaning: fire is more excellent than clay, in his opinion.

He referred to Adam by the relative pronoun *ma* ("that which"), and at that point he was a human being, because the angels' prostration to Adam occurred after his creation and his being taught the names, as in Surat al-Baqarah. The view of the people of verification (*ahl al-tahqiq*) is supported by the fact that *ma* is not restricted to non-rational beings; there are many instances of this in the Qur'an and in other Arabic speech.

His saying "I am better than him" is a statement of Satan, related in the manner of dialogues.

The clause ﴿You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ explains the clause "I am better than him." Iblis based his excuse on the premise that fire is better than clay. The Qur'an does not mention that God refuted this premise, because it was too contemptible for that; so He cursed him and expelled him, because he claimed a falsehood and disobeyed his Lord out of arrogance. His total expulsion nullified his knowledge and refuted his argument. However, the light found in fire is an accidental light subsisting in the glowing bodies called fire, and fire has no self-subsistence; for this reason its existence cannot be separated from that which kindles it.

As for the meaning of Satan's being created from fire: the beginning of the formation of the primary atom that constitutes the essence of his being is from the element of fire, and then that atom mixes with other elements such as air. God knows best what that is.

**Page 304**

As for the meaning of Adam's being created from clay: the beginning of the formation of the particles of his body is from the element of earth, and there was introduced into those particles what they were mixed with, such as the elements of air, water and fire, and what arises from that composition of chemical elements and electrical force, by the totality of which the reality of the human being is constituted.

"From" (*min*) in both places is for the starting point (*ibtida'iyya*), not for partitive meaning (*tab'idiyya*).

The early philosophers and physicians have firmly held that the element of fire is more noble than the element of earth (which is also expressed as "the land"), because fire is subtle and luminous in colour, while earth is dense and dark in colour.

Al-Shirazi said in his commentary on *Kulliyyat al-Qanun* (Universal Principles of the Canon): Although fire is preferred over earth for what has been mentioned, earth is preferred over it in that it is good for animals and plants, and is not corrupting through its coldness, unlike fire, which is corrupting through its heat, for it is extreme in heat, and so on.

The truth is that the excellence of the elements does not entail the excellence of the beings produced from them, because the elements are simple bodies, and created beings are not formed from their mere components; rather, created beings are formed through composition among the elements. The human bodies are composed of all the elements. The human spirit is a subtle luminous entity, by which the human being excels over all composites, in that there is within him a angelic part in which he shares with the angels. For this reason, his Creator, exalted and sanctified be He, asked him to join himself to the angels, and this joining was fully realised in the prophets and messengers. On account of this we say that the prophets and messengers are more excellent than the angels, since both groups are equal in being purely luminous, and the group of prophets is distinguished by having attained those ranks through election and obedience. Therefore Iblis has no proof for preferring himself over Adam; he was merely struck by an errant doubt, and for this reason he was recompensed for his refusal to prostrate to him with expulsion from the Exalted Assembly.

We have expanded on this discussion here to refute the doubts of a group of heretics (*malahida*) who promote the doubt of Iblis as a way of attacking religion, not out of belief in the devils. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 38, verses 77–78:

﴿He said, "Then get out of it, for indeed you are accursed."﴾ ﴿And indeed upon you is My curse until the Day of Recompense.﴾ God punished him for what emerged from his inner self, so that he opposed what had been his way, and He expelled him from the exalted assembly and from Paradise. The pronoun in "He said" refers to God, in the manner of relating exchanges of speech. His command to leave Paradise was linked by the particle fa' (then) to what preceded it of question and answer, because his response indicated that there was corruption in his self, whose effects had appeared in his action, so he was not fit to mix with the people of the exalted assembly. The explanation of the parallel of this verse has already passed in Surat al-Hijr.

Al-La'na (the curse) is removal from the mercy of God. It is attributed to God in order to make its object, namely the one cursed, appear more abominable, because the one cursed by God is the most abominable of the cursed.

"The Day of Recompense" is made the endpoint of the curse to indicate its continuance throughout the whole duration of this life, so that it encompasses all times. The intended meaning is not that the opposite of the curse, namely mercy, will be attained by him on the Day of Recompense; for the Day of Recompense is the day of requital for deeds, so the requital of the cursed one is painful punishment, as the expression "the Day of Recompense," rather than "the Day they will be raised" or "the Day of the Appointed Time," indicates.

The fa' here links his speech to God's command to him to leave the Garden and to His curse upon him, which remains in force.

This linking is a case of what is called a ruled pattern in which one speaker's words are built upon another speaker's words, known as ʿaṭf al-talqīn (the "instructive coupling" construction). It appears in the Qur'an in His saying, ﴿He said, "And [what of] my descendants?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Iblis swore by the might of God to affirm that he would carry out misleading without any failure. He swore to this while knowing the greatness of this oath, because he found within himself that God had empowered him to carry out misleading and whispering. "﴿He said: 'Then the truth, and the truth I speak﴾ ﴿that I will surely fill Hell with you and with those among them who follow you, all together.'﴾" That is, God Most High said this as a consequence (tafri'an), and this consequence is similar to the consequence in His saying ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82].

The emphasis of His resolve, indicated by His saying "By Your might", is answered with an emphasis of the same kind, namely the word al-haqq (the truth), which indicates that what follows it is a established truth that does not fail. In emphasizing the statement, He did not go beyond the word al-haqq, as a reminder that God's promise is true and needs no oath to confirm it, out of exaltation of God's majesty above matching the words of Satan with an oath of the same kind. For this reason, this meaning was further affirmed by the parenthetical clause "wal-haqqa aqulu" ("and the truth I speak"), which means: I say only the truth, and there is no need for an oath.

Ibn Kathir and others read "fa-al-haqqa" with the accusative (naṣb); its case is that of the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq), in place of a verb of the same root that is omitted; its implied form is: uhiqqu (I make it binding), i.e., I impose and establish it. Its original form is indefinite (tankir), so its definition with the article "al-" is the definition of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), like the definition in:

"Arsalaha al-'Irak" (the wind let it loose), so it is in the status of an indefinite noun.

The definition is merely a verbal embellishment (hilya lafziyya), indicating what the listener already knows about what the truth is. Its explanation was given at the beginning of al-Fatiha.

ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza read it in the nominative (raf'), on the basis that, since it has become definite by the article, the nominal character predominated over it, so its being a substitute for the verb was forgotten. This nominative is either as a subject (mubtada'), i.e., "fa-al-haqqu qawli" (so the truth is My word), or "fa-al-haqqu la-amla'anna jahannam" etc., so that the oath clause stands in the place of the predicate; or as a predicate, i.e., "fa-qawliya al-haqq" (so My word is the truth), and the clause "la-amla'anna jahannam" is then the explanation of the omitted saying. There is no disagreement about the accusative of "al-haqq" in "wal-haqqa aqulu", and the details of this were discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Fatiha.

The clause "la-amla'anna jahannam minka" etc. explains the clause "fa-al-haqq", and it is emphasized by the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and the nun of emphasis.

The fronting of the object in "wal-haqqa aqulu" serves exclusivity, i.e., "and I say nothing but the truth."

The "min" in His saying ﴿minka wa-mimman tabi'aka﴾ is explicative (bayaniyya), the one that enters upon a specifier (tamyiz); the specifier is in the accusative by implying its meaning. It also enters upon the specifier of "kam" as in ﴿How many generations have We destroyed before them?﴾ [Sad: 3]. Here it is an explanation of the undefined quantity implied by "la-amla'anna", so it is clarified by the words ﴿minka wa-mimman tabi'aka﴾.

Since the nature of what follows the explicative "min" is to be indefinite, it is necessary to consider the second-person pronoun (kaf al-khitab) as having the sense of a generic noun, i.e., "of your kind, the devils", since Iblis's own person would not fill Hell; and since it is conjoined with ﴿and those among them who follow you﴾, i.e., those among the children of Adam whom you misled who follow you, it is not permissible that anyone other than these two groups of devils and jinn should fail to fill Hell.

"Ajma'in" is an emphasis for the pronoun in "minka" and for "man" in "wa-mimman tabi'aka".

Know that the narration of this exchange between the speech of God and that of Satan is a narration of what passed through Satan's mind, the perceptions arising and generated in the depths of his soul, and of what passed in God's will, the effects consequent upon their causes, from Satan's thoughts; for the world in which these causes and their effects occur is a world of reality in which only truth prevails, and there is no room in it for the promotion of equivocation or trickery. For this reason, the thoughts of Satan mentioned in it are not considered audacity against God's majesty, nor is God's requital of Satan considered a condescension by God to converse with a servant who is hateful to Him.

We have mentioned in the commentary on Surat al-Hijr what the statements exchanged between Satan and God, and the statements which God cast upon him, indicate.

﴿Say: "I do not ask you any wage for it, and I am not one of those who pretend."﴾ ﴿It is only a reminder to all the worlds.﴾ ﴿And you will surely come to know its news after a time.﴾ When God commanded His Messenger to convey the admonitions and lessons contained in this surah, He commanded him, at its end, to strike their ears with this statement, which serves as a recapitulation (*fadhlakah*) of the surah, closing it and recording against them that he brought them nothing but what benefits them, and that he does not seek any reward for it. That is, had he asked them for a wage, their accusation that he was a liar, made for the sake of his own benefit, would have been plausible. But since that is absent, the suspicion of his lying must also be absent, because the restraint of reason keeps its possessor from lying without some benefit he hopes to gain for himself.

The meaning is the general negation of his asking them for a wage from the day he was sent until the revelation of this verse. This is an inductive argument (*qiyas istiqra'*), since if they surveyed the Messenger's ﷺ conduct in the past, they would find that his not asking for a wage is a general matter, established by complete induction drawn from all the individual polytheists in all their dealings with him. It is therefore something widely known among them. This refutes their saying "a liar" (*kadhdhab*), reported of them at the beginning of the surah, and establishes the proof of the truth of his message, as will come.

The pronoun in *'alayhi* ("for it") refers to the Qur'an, which is understood from the context, since the surah begins with His saying "by the Qur'an, full of reminder" (38:1). This is a case of returning the end to the beginning (*radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr*).

The conjunction of ﴿and I am not one of those who pretend﴾ indicates the negation of all pretence (*takalluf*) from the Prophet ﷺ.

*Takalluf* means undertaking hardship (*kulfah*), which is that which is difficult for a person to do or to bind himself to, because it burdens him or is hard on him. The pattern *tafa''ul* indicates the effort to deal with what is not easy. Thus the one who pretends (*mutakallif*) is the one who seeks what is not his, or claims to know what he does not know.

So the meaning here is: I am not one who falsely claims prophethood without being revealed to. This is a rebuttal of their saying "a liar," and in this respect it serves as a conclusion to his saying ﴿I do not ask you any wage for it﴾, because one who pretends to something seeks from his pretence some benefit. The meaning is: I am not among those who claim what is not theirs. From this comes the hadith of al-Daraqutni from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The Messenger of God went out on some of his journeys and passed by a man sitting by his *miqra* (a water basin), so 'Umar said, 'O owner of the *miqra*, did the beasts of prey drink from your basin last night?' The Prophet ﷺ said to him, 'O owner of the *miqra*, do not inform him, this is *mutakallif*; for them is what they carry in their bellies, and for us is what remains, a drink and a purifier.'" And in the two *Sahihs* (al-Bukhari and Muslim) it is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "O people, whoever knows some knowledge should speak of it, and whoever does not know should say, 'God knows best,' for God said to His Messenger: ﴿Say: I do not ask you any wage for it, and I am not one of those who pretend.﴾"

From His saying ﴿and I am not one of those who pretend﴾ it is understood that what he brought of the religion involves no pretence, that is, no hardship in its obligations, and this is the meaning of the leniency (*samahah*) of Islam. This is an inference (*istirwah*) based on the principle that it is among God's wisdom to create a harmony between the nature of the Messenger ﷺ and the spirit of his law, so that his devotion to implementing his law is wholehearted, since that is more effective in removing hardship from him in carrying out what he was commanded.

The construction *ma ana min al-mutakallifin* ("I am not one of the pretenders") is stronger in negating pretence than saying *ma ana bi-mutakallif* ("I am not a pretender"), as was explained previously in the commentary on His saying ﴿He said: I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant﴾ (2:67) in Surat al-Baqarah.

The sentence ﴿It is only a reminder to all the worlds﴾ is a *badal al-ishtimal* (inclusive apposition) of the sentence ﴿and I am not one of those who pretend﴾, in the sense that the negation of one thing implies the affirmation of its opposite. Since by His saying ﴿I am not one of those who pretend﴾ he negated that he fabricated the Qur'an against God, it follows that the Qur'an is a reminder to people, which God reminded them by, that is, it is not myths or nonsense. You may also make it a *tadhyil* (concluding remark), since there is no conflict between the two here. This report about the Qur'an's standing with the whole community of the call, and not only with the polytheists who were the subject of the dispute, is because once it was established that the Prophet ﷺ

**Page 310**

does not seek a reward from his opponents, and it was established thereby that he does not invent what has not been revealed to him, the discourse moved on to establishing that the Qur'an is a reminder to people in general. This therefore includes the polytheists of Makkah and others among mankind. It is as if it were said: God will do without you and will bring other peoples, as He said: ﴿If you disbelieve, then God is independent of you﴾ (39:7).

The generality of *al-'alamin* ("the worlds") gives the sentence the sense of a concluding remark for the two sentences before it.

The restriction (*qasr*) contained in the sentence ﴿It is only a reminder to all the worlds﴾ is a *qasr qalb idafi* (restriction by reversal of a specific opposing claim): that is, it is a reminder, not myths, nor magic, nor poetry, nor anything else, in refutation of the polytheists who labelled the Qur'an with what is not its true attributes.

Its basis is that the word *al-ghuraf* occurs in it, in this form and not *al-ghurufat*, in His saying: ﴿For them are chambers above chambers﴾ (39:20).

It is wholly Makkan according to the majority. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that His saying ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of God's mercy﴾ (39:53), through the three verses, was revealed in Madinah. It has also been said that up to seven verses were revealed in Madinah, concerning the story of Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah. Its chain is weak, and the story bears the marks of fabricated tales.

It is also reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that those verses were revealed in Madinah concerning Hisham ibn al-'As ibn Wa'il, when he delayed his migration to Madinah after he had prepared for it. In another report, it is said that with him was 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, and that they had agreed to migrate to Madinah, but they were tempted and were tempted.

The more correct view is that it was revealed concerning the polytheists, as will come when its verses are explained. The claim that it is Madinan arose only because of the weak stories narrated about it.

It has also been said that His saying ﴿O My servants who believe, fear your Lord﴾ (39:10), up to the end of the verse, was also revealed in Madinah.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that His saying ﴿God has revealed the best discourse, a Book resembling itself in its parts﴾ (39:23), up to the end of the verse, was revealed in Madinah.

**Page 312**

Thus the verses in which there is disagreement number nine.

The more probable view is that all of it is Makkan, and that whatever seems to have been revealed concerning particular stories, if its chains are sound, then it was cited in those stories, and it was confused by some narrators as being the occasion of revelation.

It will come when explaining His saying ﴿And God's earth is spacious﴾ (39:10) that it was revealed shortly before the emigration of the believers to Abyssinia, that is, in the fifth year before the Hijrah.

It is the fifty-ninth surah in order of revelation according to the preferred view, revealed after Surat Saba' and before Surat Ghafir.

Its verses are counted by the people of Madinah, the Makkans, and the Basrans as seventy-two; by the people of Syria as seventy-three; and by the people of Kufa as seventy-five.

* * *

**Its aims:** This surah opens with what serves as an introduction to its main theme, namely glorifying the Qur'an's status, a glorification repeated in six places within this surah, because the Qur'an comprises its aims.

Its aims are many, revolving around establishing God's sole divinity and refuting association with Him.

Refuting the excuses of the polytheists for their association and their falsehoods.

Negating one kind of association, which is their claim that God has a son.

Arguing for God's unity in divinity by evidence of His sole creation of the upper and lower worlds, and of His governance of their order and what they contain, something the polytheists do not deny He alone does.

The wondrous creation in the stages of the formation of man and animal.

Arguing against them with evidence from their own conduct, namely their resorting to God when harm befalls them.

Calling to reflection upon what is delivered to them of the Qur'an, which is the best of speech.

Warning them about their ingratitude for the blessing.

Contrasting their state with the state of the sincere believers devoted to God.

That the religion of monotheism is what the messengers brought before.

Warning against the polytheists suffering what befell the earlier nations who associated partners with God.

Informing the polytheists that they and their associates are of no account with God and His Messenger ﷺ; God is independent of their worship, and His Messenger does not fear them or their idols, because God has sufficed him against them all.

Affirming the resurrection and recompense, so that every soul may be repaid for what it earned.

Illustrating the resurrection by the revival of the earth after its death, and presenting to them the parable of sleep and waking after it, and that it is the Day of Distinction between the believers and the polytheists.

Illustrating the states of the believers and the polytheists in the two lives, the life of this world and the life to come.

Calling the polytheists to desist from transgressing against themselves, and calling the believers to steadfastness in piety and to leaving the abode of disbelief. It concludes with a description of the state of the Day of Reckoning.

Interwoven through all of this are threats and promises, parables, intimidation and encouragement, admonition, and an allusion in His saying ﴿Say: Are those who know equal with those who do not know?﴾ (39:9), up to the end of the verse, that the lot of the believers is that they are people of knowledge, and that the polytheists are people of ignorance. This is a glorification of the elevated status of knowledge and a censure of ignorance.
